script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to reflect together on one question: what is service? The Lord Jesus said: “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28) Brothers and sisters, service is not only about what we do; it is even more about whom we do it for, and why we do it. Today we’ll look at it from three angles: the essence of service, the heart of service, and the scope of service.

Please be still for three seconds and answer in your heart: when you hear the word “service”, what is the first picture that comes to mind? Leading worship? Playing the piano? Wiping chairs, washing cups? Having a post, having a role? All of these are service. But if service is only these things, the scope is too narrow, the bar is too high, and the motives easily get mixed. A sister prepared the fellowship meals in the church kitchen for twenty years, yet when she stood up front she said, “I don’t serve.” Brothers and sisters, the problem is not that we aren’t diligent enough; the problem is that our definition of service is far too small.

Let’s look at the background. In Matthew 20, the Lord foretells for the third time that he is going up to Jerusalem to be crucified. But straight after that, the mother of the sons of Zebedee comes asking for two seats, and the other ten disciples are indignant. The Lord is speaking about laying down his life; the disciples are squabbling over seats. So the Lord says a short phrase: “It shall not be so.” He says: “Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26) The road of the kingdom of heaven is not climbing up but going down.

First, the essence of service is living out the life of Jesus. The original word for “serve” pictures the one who waits at table. The original word for “ransom” is the price paid to buy back a slave. His life was service; his living was giving himself away. He broke bread for the five thousand, he washed the disciples’ feet, and in the end he gave us his very life. So service is not a job; service is the overflow of a life. You can take leave from a job; you can’t take leave from a life.

The Bible says: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach,” (Mark 3:14) Brothers and sisters, look at the order: being with him first, being sent after. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years, and its conclusion is this: what determines a lifetime’s happiness is not wealth, not fame, but the quality of relationships. If that is true between people, how much more between us and God. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Life is the root, relationships are the trunk, ministry is the fruit.

Second, the heart of service is doing it for the Lord, not for ourselves. The Lord took a little child in his arms and said: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name, receives me.” (Mark 9:37) In those days a small child had the lowest standing of anyone. Yet the Lord said that to receive him is to receive me. Brothers and sisters, the key is not the size of the task, but whether it is done in the Lord’s name. Even for a cup of cold water, the Lord says, that person will in no way lose his reward.

The Lord also said: “Because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40) The Lord, it turns out, hides himself in the least of people. Psychology speaks of the “overjustification effect”: children who loved drawing, once they drew for a certificate, stopped drawing afterwards. When the motive changes, joy leaves. That is why 321 says: for Jesus, for others, not for yourself. This is the selfless life.

Third, the scope of service is the whole of life. Paul says: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31) Even eating and drinking count! In the Old Testament, “to work” and “to serve” come from the same root. At home, loving your family is service; at work, honesty and integrity are service; at school, studying hard is service. Whatever is done in the Lord’s name, for the good of others and for the glory of God, is service.

Before his ascension the Lord said: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8) True service is not just action; it is life touching life. In a forest, the great trees pass nutrients to the little ones through underground mycorrhizal networks. The church is the same. With selflessness, the Holy Spirit fills us; filled with the Spirit, life touches life. This is the road to revival.

Brothers and sisters, there are three practices today. First, do everything for the Lord: before each task, be still for three seconds and say, “Lord, this one I do for you.” Second, start with small things: a word of care, a helping hand, a smile — don’t wait for the big opportunity. Third, practise selflessness: this week, do one act of service that nobody knows about. Many people grow weary in serving because they are serving by themselves and serving for themselves. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and there is joy; rely on the brain and ourselves, and there is weariness.

Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we began with: what is service? Service is not how much you do, but whom you do it for. When you live for the Lord, everything you do becomes service. When you live out Christ, your life is full of influence. So today, hand the throne back to the Lord, open up the scope of your service, and give all the glory to him. Your kitchen, your desk, your sickbed — all of them are altars.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I declare: my life is lived to serve you. I no longer live for myself; I will live for you and for others. Whatever I do, I will do it in your name. Help me to live a selfless life, and let my whole life become service that glorifies you. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you. Brothers and sisters, take these new eyes with you and go and live today.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion we are going to reflect together on a subject that is utterly familiar and yet one of the easiest to misunderstand: what is service? Our theme text is a sentence the Lord Jesus spoke himself: “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28) Brothers and sisters, remember today’s one line: service is not only about what we do; it is even more about whom we do it for, and why. Today we’ll look at it from three angles: the essence of service, the heart of service, and the scope of service.

First, please be still for three seconds and answer one question in your heart: when you hear the word “service”, what is the first picture that comes to mind? Some picture leading worship, playing the piano or preaching; some picture wiping down chairs and washing cups; some think of driving people to and fro, welcoming, keeping the accounts, running the AV desk; and some think of “having a post, having a role”. Brothers and sisters, all of these are service, of course. But Jesus’ definition of service goes far beyond these.

If service is only these things, we run into three traps. First, the scope is too narrow. There are one hundred and sixty-eight hours in a week, and serving at church may take up only three to five of them — what about the rest of life? Our faith is cut in two. Second, the bar is too high. Older people say, “I can’t sing”; new believers say, “I don’t know the Bible well yet.” Third, the motives get too mixed. What was once done for the Lord comes to be done for applause; the work still gets done, but inside, everything has already dried up. I know a sister who prepared the fellowship meals in the church kitchen for twenty years, yet when she stood up to give her testimony she said, “I just wash vegetables in the kitchen — I don’t serve.” Brothers and sisters, the problem is not that we aren’t diligent enough; the problem is that our definition of service is far too small.

Let’s look at the background first. Matthew’s Gospel is generally held to have been written by the apostle Matthew, for believers from a Jewish background. By chapter 20 the Lord has already foretold for the third time that he is going up to Jerusalem to be crucified and will be raised on the third day. But what happens next is heartbreaking to read: the mother of the sons of Zebedee comes up to ask for the seats on his left and right for her two sons, and when the other ten disciples hear it, they are indignant. The Lord is speaking about laying down his life; the disciples are squabbling over seats. So the Lord says a short phrase: “It shall not be so.” He says: “Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26) Brothers and sisters, the road of the kingdom of heaven is not climbing up but going down.

The first angle: the essence of service is living out the life of Jesus. “Serve” in the original is the Greek diakoneō, whose most basic picture is the one who waits at table — bringing the dishes, pouring the water, bending down. “Ransom” in the original is lytron, the price paid to buy back a slave. When the Lord said these words, he wasn’t teaching a principle; he was describing his own life. He broke bread for the five thousand, he touched the leper, he waited by the well for a Samaritan woman. Brothers and sisters, his life was service; his living was giving himself away.

Paul distilled that whole life into one passage: “But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7). “Emptied himself” in the original means “to pour oneself out”. The Lord did not set aside his divinity; he set aside the glory, the rights and the honour that were his due. 321 puts it well: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness and living it out. So service is not a job, but the overflow of a life. A job can be outsourced; you can take leave from it or resign from it; a life cannot. An apple tree doesn’t have to strive to carry out a fruit-bearing ministry; it only has to be an apple tree, and in season it bears apples.

Now look at a vitally important verse: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach,” (Mark 3:14) Brothers and sisters, notice the order: being with him comes first, being sent comes after. Sadly, we often reverse it. When we recruit helpers we ask first whether you can do it, whether you have time, but we rarely ask first: have you met with the Lord this morning? The result is that the ministry grows bigger and bigger while life grows thinner and thinner. Martha was busy with much serving and troubled in heart; Mary sat at the Lord’s feet listening to his word. The Lord said: “But one thing is needed” (Luke 10:42). The Lord was not dismissing serving; he was dismissing serving that had lost its order.

This is the 321 Insight: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Life is the root, relationships are the trunk, ministry is the fruit. Only when the roots go deep does the fruit come in abundance. The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938 and has followed the same group of people for more than eighty years. Its director, Robert Waldinger, sums it up: what determines whether a person is happy and healthy in later life is not wealth, nor fame, but the quality of their relationships. If that is true between people, how much more between us and God. So 321 says: people matter more than tasks; first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

The second angle: the heart of service is doing it for the Lord, not for ourselves. In Mark 9 the disciples are once again arguing on the road about who is the greatest. The Lord sits down, calls the twelve, then takes a little child, takes him in his arms and says: “Whoever receives one such little child in my name, receives me.” (Mark 9:37) In the first century a small child had no standing, no productive value and no voice. Yet it was just such a child that the Lord took in his arms. The original word for “receive” carries the warmth of inviting someone into your home and setting food before them. And the centre of gravity of the whole saying is those three words — “in my name”.

The Lord also said: “Because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40) This is the parable of the final judgement. The reason for the Lord’s commendation isn’t “You built such a large church”, but “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was sick, and you looked after me.” The Lord, it turns out, hides himself in the least of people. That elderly brother in the hospital bed, that child in the corner whom nobody notices — what you do to them, you do to the Lord. So service is not only the pulpit; service is daily living. Service is not a time slot; service is a way of seeing.

So why does “whom we do it for” matter so much? In 1973 Lepper, Greene and Nisbett of Stanford took a group of children who already loved drawing, and one group was told, “When you finish, you’ll get a certificate.” Two weeks later, the children who had drawn for the certificate spent noticeably less time drawing of their own accord — the “overjustification effect”. Deci and Ryan’s Self-Determination Theory also points out that once the motive shifts from within to without, inner motivation is eroded. Isn’t that the story of so many who serve? Paul says: “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).

This is what 321 calls selflessness: for Jesus, for others, not for yourself. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. When the disciples argued over who was greatest, ten were indignant with two and two were on guard against ten — and both sides lost. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Paul’s testimony is the most beautiful: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Everyone we are connected with is our “2”; as we live out the “0” before them, the Holy Spirit bears his fruit in all nine of its expressions. This is the 920 practice.

The third angle: the scope of service is the whole of life. Paul says: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31) Brothers and sisters, look how wide that circle is — even eating and drinking count! In 1 Corinthians Paul is dealing with the dispute over food sacrificed to idols, and the standard he finally gives is not a rule but a direction: do all to the glory of God. The same task can be done for ourselves or for God; the difference lies not in the task itself but in whom it faces.

Hebrew gives us the same light. In the Old Testament, “to work” and “to serve” come from the same root. Genesis says: “Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.” (Genesis 2:15) The word “cultivate” here is the same word as “serve” when Moses said to Pharaoh, “that they may serve me”. In God’s original intention, tilling the ground and worship were never two separate things. So: at home, loving your family is service; at work, honesty and integrity are service; at school, studying hard is service. A saying commonly attributed to Mother Teresa goes: not all of us can do great things, but we can do small things with great love.

Before his ascension the Lord said: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8) Brothers and sisters, the Lord didn’t say, “You must go and try hard”; he said, “You will receive power.” Bearing witness isn’t reciting a prepared script; it is saying with your whole life: the One I have met is real. The map the Lord gives is a set of concentric circles: starting from Jerusalem and moving outwards ring by ring — from the individual, to the family, to the church, to the world.

So 321 says: with selflessness, the Holy Spirit fills us; filled with the Spirit, life touches life. This is the road to revival. Why is selflessness the key? Because if a vessel is full of self, there is no room for anything else. The forest ecologist Suzanne Simard showed in the journal Nature in 1997 that the trees of a forest are linked to one another through underground mycorrhizal networks, and that great trees can pass nutrients to little saplings. The church is the same. This is the 235 relationship: become a “2” with a selfless person, build the “3” of spiritual parents and children, and grow into the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Next come three practices. First, practise doing everything for the Lord. Every day, before you do anything, ask yourself: whom am I doing this for? Then be still for three seconds and say, “Lord, this one I do for you.” Second, practise serving, starting with small things. Don’t wait for the big opportunity; start with a word of care, a helping hand, a smile. The Lord said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). Research published in Science in 2008 by Dunn, Aknin and Norton found that people who spent money on others were happier. The outward direction of giving brings joy in itself.

Third, practise a selfless life of service. Keep examining yourself: am I doing this for myself or for the Lord? Am I trying to perform, or seeking to glorify God? This week, deliberately do one act of service that nobody knows about. When no one praises you, if you feel disappointed inside, that is the place where “self” is still alive. Brothers and sisters, many people grow weary after serving for a long time, not because there is too much to do, but because they are serving by themselves and serving for themselves. Maslach divided burnout into three dimensions: emotional exhaustion, cold detachment from people, and a diminished sense of accomplishment. But the Lord’s invitation still stands: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:30)

Let’s set today’s message back within the framework of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. Change has an order: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This morning’s devotion is the first step — a change of mindset. From man’s perspective to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal. The focus is Jesus — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we began with: what is service? Service is not how much you do, but whom you do it for. When you live for the Lord, everything you do becomes service. So today I want to issue three calls. First, hand the throne back to the Lord. Second, open up the scope — your kitchen, your desk, your sickbed are all altars: “present your bodies a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). Third, give the glory to him. It is commonly said that in 1732, when young men of the Moravian Brethren set out as missionaries, they cried out: may the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of his suffering.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I declare: my life is lived to serve you. I no longer live for myself; I will live for you and for others. Whatever I do, I will do it in your name. Forgive our comparing, our competing and our weariness in service. Renew our mindset, so that we first are with you, and then are sent by you. Fill us with the Holy Spirit, make us faithful in the smallest things and joyful in places no one sees. Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and give you peace.

sections.heading: Introduction: A Sigh from the Depths of the Heart
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me start by describing a scene that is very common in churches.

There was a sister who had served in her church for twelve years. She had led children’s Sunday school, she had been in charge of welcoming, and later she took on pastoral care in her small group. Every week she was always the first to arrive and the last to leave. One day after the meeting had ended, she sat in the empty sanctuary and said to her pastor, “Pastor, it isn’t that I don’t love the Lord. I’m just… so tired.”

She paused, and the tears began to fall. Then she said, “I often feel as if everything gets pushed onto me. When people have a need, I go and do it; when the church has a gap, I go and fill it. But somewhere along the way, I lost track of what I’m even doing.”

Brothers and sisters, have you ever heard a sigh like that? Or has a sigh like that ever risen from the depths of your own heart?

If so, please don’t blame yourself, and don’t assume it means you aren’t spiritual. That kind of weariness is actually pointing to something very important — our mindset about service needs to be renewed by God.

Many of us began serving for two reasons.

The first reason: other people have needs. Someone is ill, someone is weak, someone has fallen; I see it, so I go and help.

The second reason: the church has needs. Sunday school is short of teachers, the worship team is short of members, the fellowship meal is short of helpers; the pastor makes an appeal from the platform, my heart softens, and up goes my hand.

Neither of these reasons is bad; you could even say they are good. God often calls us through other people’s needs. But brothers and sisters, please hear this clearly: if the drive behind our service stops “only” at the needs outside us, then sooner or later that drive will run out.

Why? Because the needs out there are endless, and our strength is limited. You fill this gap, and a hole opens over there; you help one person up, turn round, and three more have fallen. If it is “need” that drives us, we will be crushed by need. In the end, service becomes a burden, the burden becomes complaint, complaint becomes withdrawal, withdrawal becomes hurt, and hurt leads people to leave.

This cycle repeats itself over and over in churches. Not because those people don’t love the Lord, but because the drive did not come from within.

Today God wants to show us a crucial truth, one that will turn our mindset about service completely upside down.

The first statement: service is not only about other people’s needs.

The second statement: service is a need of our own life.

Please meditate on those two statements once more. Do other people need my service? Yes. But at a deeper level — do I need to serve? I need it very much.

It’s like exercise. When you go to the gym and lift weights, do the weight plates need you? No, they don’t. It is you who need to lift them. As you lift, you sweat, you ache, you gasp for breath — but a few months later, what has changed is not the dumbbell. It is your muscles, your heart and lungs, your whole physique.

Service is the same. When we go out to serve someone, the person most deeply changed is often not them, but ourselves.

That is why the vision of Kingdom 321 says: the fivefold change begins with mindset — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This morning we ask God first to change our mindset about service. For once the mindset changes, our service will move from “reluctance” to “joy”, from “just getting by” to “delight”, from “being drained” to “being built up”.

Brothers and sisters, may God speak to us this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Sent from Prison
sections.html:
Our theme text today comes from Ephesians 2:10. To truly understand this verse, we first need to get to know the letter it belongs to.

First, who was the author?

The author of Ephesians is the apostle Paul. The letter opens with these words: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus:” (Ephesians 1:1)

Second, when was it written, and in what circumstances?

When Paul wrote this letter, he was in prison. He says so himself: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,” (Ephesians 4:1) It is generally held that this was during Paul’s first house arrest in Rome, around AD 60–62. Philippians, Colossians and Philemon come from the same period, and together they are called the “Prison Epistles”.

Notice the contrast: a man with chains on his wrists, his movements restricted, wrote the loftiest, broadest and most glorious teaching on the church in the whole Bible. Paul couldn’t go out to serve, so he served with his pen; he couldn’t go and stand before people, so he knelt before God and prayed for them. That in itself is a fine sermon — the heart of service lies not in how big a stage our circumstances give us, but in whether we have within us a heart that lives for the Lord.

Third, to whom was it written?

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, a thriving harbour and a great commercial city. It was home to the temple of Artemis, famous throughout the ancient world and counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Acts records that Paul lived in Ephesus for about three years (Acts 20:31), and also tells how Demetrius the silversmith, because Paul’s preaching had hurt the trade in idols, stirred up a great riot throughout the city (Acts 19:23–41).

In other words, the believers in Ephesus had been rescued out of a system that worshipped idols, money, lust and power. They had once lived in a city that asked only, “What can I get?” Paul wants to tell them: you have not only been saved “out of” something; you have been saved “into” something — into God’s eternal plan.

Fourth, the context.

Ephesians 2:10 is not an isolated verse. It is a summit, with nine whole verses of build-up before it.

Paul begins with our original condition: “You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins,” (Ephesians 2:1) “Dead” means utterly powerless. The dead cannot save themselves, the dead cannot do good, the dead cannot even stretch out a hand to cry for help.

Then Paul speaks of what God has done: “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved.” (Ephesians 2:4–5)

Next Paul nails down the foundation of salvation: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9)

See it clearly: salvation is absolutely not by works, not by service, not by merit. Anyone who tries to earn salvation through service has turned the gospel upside down.

Then Paul writes verse 10: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.”

In the Greek, the second word of this verse is the connective γάρ (“for”), which carries the thought straight on: “For we are…” Paul’s meaning is this: precisely because salvation is entirely grace, our good works and our service are not in any way meant to earn something; they are the fruit that grace inevitably bears.

Brothers and sisters, fix this order firmly in your mind:

We are not “saved because we serve”; we “serve because we are saved”.

The first order is religion; only the second is the gospel.

And today’s lesson takes us a step further: this “serving because we are saved” is not a burden God lays on us; it is a need God has placed within us.

Key Point 1: Service Is the Purpose of Our Salvation

sections.heading: 1. We Are God’s “Masterpiece”
sections.html:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10)

This verse is only a few words long, yet it makes clear the place of a Christian’s whole life. Let’s go through it phrase by phrase.

“For we are his workmanship.” The word “workmanship” in Greek is ποίημα (poiēma). It appears only twice in the New Testament; the other occurrence is Romans 1:20, where it refers to the things God has made. The word does not mean “an odd item”; it means “a work” — a finished piece the craftsman has made with his own hands and takes delight in. The English word “poem” comes from it.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? In God’s eyes you are not a part on an assembly line; you are a poem he has written in his own hand.

“Created in Christ Jesus.” “Created” in Greek is κτίζω (ktizō), a word the Septuagint and the New Testament use specifically for God’s work of creation. By using this word, Paul is saying that when a person is born again and saved, it carries the same weight as a fresh act of creation. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

“For good works.” The “for” here introduces a purpose clause. God re-created us with a purpose. And what is the purpose? “Good works.” And these “good works” are not worldly moral charity, but “which God prepared”.

“Which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” “Prepared before” in Greek is προετοιμάζω (proetoimazō); the prefix προ means “beforehand”. It means that God had already arranged these good works in advance, before we were even born.

Brothers and sisters, think how wonderful this is.

God has not only prepared salvation for us to receive; God has also prepared work for us to complete.

sections.heading: 2. Your Life Is a Picture God Sketched Long Ago
sections.html:
Before a painter lifts the brush, the composition is already in his mind. He knows a tree goes here, and a shaft of light must be left there. We see one brushstroke of paint after another; he sees the finished painting as a whole.

So it is with God and our lives.

“Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.” (Psalm 139:16)

So, before you were even born, God had already prepared:

which good works you would do;

which people you would influence;

and what kind of testimony you would live out.

All of this is contained in the one word “service”.

Brothers and sisters, this is why we say — service is the purpose of our salvation.

We are not saved merely so that we can go to heaven one day. If God only wanted us in heaven, he could have taken us home the moment we made our decision for Christ. Why leave us for decades in a world so full of tears?

He leaves us here because he still has work for us to do. He leaves us here because there are people who will come to know Jesus only through you.

We are saved to live out God’s will. And God’s will, worked out concretely on earth, is service.

sections.heading: 3. The Parable of the Talents: What the Non-Serving Lose
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable. A master about to travel to another country entrusted his property to his servants, each according to his ability: to one five thousand, to one two thousand, to one a thousand. The ones who received five thousand and two thousand went and traded and doubled what they had been given. When the master returned he commended them: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.” (Matthew 25:21)

But the one who received a thousand buried the money in the ground. His reason even sounded devout: he said he was afraid; he said his master was a hard man. Yet the master answered, “You wicked and slothful servant…” (Matthew 25:26), and finally said:

“Throw out the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” (Matthew 25:30)

Brothers and sisters, notice: that servant didn’t steal the money, didn’t squander it, didn’t do anything wicked. What was his sin? His sin was — doing nothing at all.

This parable reminds us of two things.

First, not serving is not just a loss to ourselves. What is lost is the people who could have been blessed through you.

Second, not serving means losing the meaning of life. The master calls him an “unprofitable servant”. “Unprofitable” in Greek is ἀχρεῖος (achreios), meaning “useless, of no use”. A life that doesn’t serve is a life left in a corner, never put to use.

A fine violin locked away for ever in its case — is it still a fine violin? In terms of its materials, yes; but in terms of its purpose, it has lost what it means to be a violin.

sections.heading: 4. The Deep Human Longing for “Meaning”
sections.html:
On this point, psychology bears witness alongside Scripture.

The Jewish psychiatrist Viktor Frankl (1905–1997) was imprisoned in the Nazi concentration camps. In Man’s Search for Meaning, published in 1946, he observed that in extreme suffering, what best sustained a person’s will to live was not physical strength, nor luck, but a “sense of meaning” — a task still unfinished, someone still waiting for them. From this Frankl developed “logotherapy”, which holds that humanity’s most fundamental drive is the search for meaning in life.

Martin Seligman, the founder of positive psychology, served as president of the American Psychological Association (APA) in 1998. In Flourish, published in 2011, he set out five elements of well-being, known as PERMA. The M stands for Meaning, which he defined as “belonging to and serving something bigger than the self”.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Even psychology has reached this conclusion: unless a person serves something greater than themselves, they cannot find meaning.

And more than sixteen hundred years ago, the Church Father Augustine (354–430), at the very start of Book One of his Confessions, wrote the prayer that has echoed down the ages: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

Frankl tells us that people need meaning; Seligman tells us that meaning comes from serving something greater than ourselves; Augustine tells us who that “something greater” is — God himself.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight
sections.html:
The vision of Kingdom 321 gives us two statements here:

We were created for God.

We were saved to serve.

When a person does not live a life of service, their life slowly collapses inwards. Their attention shifts from “Whom can I give to?” to “Who can give to me?”; from “Whom did I serve today?” to “Did anyone notice me today?” That is how being self-centred begins. And once life is centred on the self, it loses its direction and loses its worth.

321 says: the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This first key point is meant precisely to change our mindset — service is not an “add-on” to my life; service is my life’s “factory setting”.

Do you remember the Three Foundations? Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When we accept that service is the purpose of our salvation, we are letting the Bible be our standard rather than letting our own feelings be the standard. Feelings say, “I don’t feel like serving today,” but the Bible says, “For we are his workmanship… for good works.”

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please take this to heart: my being alive is no accident; my salvation is not the finishing line. Before I was born, God had already prepared a path of service for me.

Key Point 2: Service Is the Way We Train to Reign with the Lord

sections.heading: 1. Two Completely Opposite Value Systems
sections.html:
“Whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Mark 10:43)

In what setting were these words spoken? We have to look at the context.

James and John, the two sons of Zebedee, came to Jesus and said, “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand, and one at your left hand, in your glory.” (Mark 10:37) When the other ten disciples heard it, they were indignant with them. So Jesus called the disciples together and said:

“You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever of you wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all.” (Mark 10:42–44)

Brothers and sisters, two completely opposite systems are set out here.

In the world’s system, the great are the ones who are served; the high are the ones who hold power. One person stands at the tip of the pyramid, and everyone beneath lives for him.

In God’s kingdom, the great are the ones who serve others; the high are the humble. The pyramid is turned upside down, and the One at the top holds everyone else up.

“Servant” in Greek is διάκονος (diakonos), originally “the one who carries dishes to the table at a meal”, later the title for a “deacon” in the church. “Bondservant” in Greek is δοῦλος (doulos), a heavier word still — a “slave”, someone with no sovereignty of their own.

The Lord Jesus doesn’t say, “You must not seek to be great.” He says, “You must be great in a completely different way.” God’s kingdom doesn’t forbid us to aspire upwards; it simply turns the ladder round a hundred and eighty degrees — in God’s kingdom, the way down is the way up.

sections.heading: 2. Jesus Himself Is That Role Model
sections.html:
“But I am among you as one who serves.” (Luke 22:27)

The setting of these words is even more astonishing. This is the Last Supper; the Lord Jesus is about to be betrayed and crucified. And on that very night, Scripture records: “A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest.” (Luke 22:24)

Brothers and sisters, can you imagine it? The Lord is preparing to go to the cross, and the disciples are arguing about whose seat is the grandest.

The Lord doesn’t lose his temper. He says, “For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves.” (Luke 22:27)

On the same night, John’s Gospel records that eternal picture: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.” (John 13:3–5)

Pay special attention to the word “knowing”. He knew that the Father had given all things into his hands — and then he went and washed feet.

In other words, he didn’t wash feet out of a sense of inferiority; it was because he had absolute authority and absolute security that he could stoop down and wash feet.

The less sure people are of their identity, the more they need others to serve them to prove their worth; the more secure people are in their identity, the more freely they can serve others.

He had all authority, yet he chose to become a servant. That turns our values completely upside down.

The Reformer Martin Luther (1483–1546), in his 1520 The Freedom of a Christian, summed up the Christian life in two seemingly contradictory sentences: “A Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none. A Christian is a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.”

Because we are perfectly free in Christ, we can gladly become the servant of all. That is the logic of the gospel.

sections.heading: 3. Serve First, Then Reign
sections.html:
“That you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” (Luke 22:30)

Notice the verse just before it: “I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me,” (Luke 22:29)

Having rebuked the disciples for arguing over who was greatest, the Lord then turns round and promises that they will sit on thrones. This is no contradiction; it reveals a profound spiritual law:

Serve first, and then you can reign.

Be humble first, and then you can receive glory.

Paul says too, “If we endure, we will also reign with him.” (2 Timothy 2:12) And Revelation says of God’s people that he “made us kings and priests to our God, and we will reign on the earth.” (Revelation 5:10)

Brothers and sisters, what does this mean? It means that every little act of service we do today is not wasted.

That stack of dishes you wash in the kitchen today is preparing your future crown.

That tear you shed today for a struggling brother is preparing your future place.

That row of chairs you set out today in a corner where no one saw — God saw it all.

Service is really God preparing our future:

preparing our life — a character that has not been shaped through service cannot bear the weight of glory;

preparing our identity — only those who start as servants can one day reign without becoming tyrants;

preparing our place in the kingdom — the one who is faithful in small things, the Lord will set over many things.

sections.heading: 4. The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
sections.html:
Israel has two seas, and both are fed by the same river, the Jordan.

The Sea of Galilee, in the north, has both an inflow and an outflow. The Jordan flows in from the north and flows out again to the south. So it teems with fish, its shores are shaded with green trees, and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place in that region.

The Dead Sea, in the south, only takes in and never gives out. Once the Jordan flows in, it never flows out again; the water can only evaporate. Day after day, year after year, the salt grows ever more concentrated. The salinity of the Dead Sea is about 34 per cent, close to ten times that of ordinary seawater, so fish cannot live there and water plants cannot grow — which is why it’s called the “Dead Sea”.

Brothers and sisters, the same source of water — so why is one teeming with life and the other lifeless?

The difference comes down to a single word: outflow.

A life that only receives and never gives — grace flows in but never flows out — in time grows “salty”, “bitter” and “hard”. A life with both inflow and outflow, through which grace flows on, becomes a Galilee full of fish and trees.

Service is that outlet. God doesn’t lack our service; it is our lives that lack that outlet.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight
sections.html:
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

The 321 vision says it very clearly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

When James and John asked for the seats on the right and the left, that was “leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights”; when the Lord Jesus wrapped a towel around himself and washed feet, that was “laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position”.

321 also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Look at the ten disciples: the moment they heard James and John asking for seats, they were indignant — that is pride provoking pride. But as soon as the Lord washed their feet, the atmosphere that night grew quiet — that is humility drawing out humility.

What are the Two Core Values? Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, when we practise serving here on earth today, we are practising “letting Jesus be King”; when we learn today not to grab the credit, we are practising “letting Jesus receive all the glory”. Only people like this will one day reign with the Lord. For someone who is willing today to let Jesus be King will, when one day seated on a throne, still take off their crown and lay it before the Lamb.

Key Point 3: Without Service, We Easily Slip into the Self-Centred Life

sections.heading: 1. The Son of Man Came to Serve
sections.html:
“For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45)

Many commentators call this verse the key verse of Mark’s Gospel. The whole of Mark is an unfolding of this one sentence.

“Serve” in Greek is διακονέω (diakoneō), from the same root as “servant” above. “Ransom” in Greek is λύτρον (lutron); in the society of the day, it was the money paid to buy a slave’s freedom. By using this word, the Lord Jesus is saying that his service was no mere show, no simple carrying of plates; his service went all the way — all the way to the cross, all the way to laying down his life.

Brothers and sisters, notice the structure of the verse: “not to be served, but to serve.”

There are two roads, and only these two. Every human life is walking either the road of “being served” or the road of “serving others”; there is no middle ground.

sections.heading: 2. Where Do Those Who Won’t Serve End Up?
sections.html:
If someone is unwilling to serve, they won’t stay where they are; they will naturally slide onto the other road.

They will want to be served. When the meeting ends, they’ll be watching to see whether anyone comes over to care for them.

They will want to be affirmed. When they’ve done a little something, they’ll mind whether anyone says “thank you”.

They will want to be exalted. When they see someone else on the platform, they feel a twinge of envy; when they see someone else praised, their heart goes cold.

Brothers and sisters, this is what 321 calls the self-centred life.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. In the Garden of Eden, Satan said to the woman, “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) At the heart of those words is “self” — I want to be my own god; I want to sit in the seat at the centre.

The self-centred life does not always show itself as wickedness; far more often it shows itself as touchiness, comparison, feeling hard done by, withdrawal. The more self-centred a person is, the more easily they are hurt; the more easily they are hurt, the more they wrap themselves up; and the more they wrap themselves up, the bigger that “self” becomes.

Paul tells of the opposite road: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

sections.heading: 3. Service Is God’s Training Ground for Us
sections.html:
Service is precisely the training ground God gives us for dealing with “self”. Through service, God trains us in three things.

First, training in denying of self. The Lord says, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24) Denying of self is not an abstract idea; it is concrete. It is when you meant to rest but went visiting instead; when you meant to speak but kept quiet and heard the other person out; when you should have been praised but passed the credit on to someone else.

Second, training in humility. “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” (Philippians 2:5–7) “Emptied himself” — that is selflessness. Nothing exposes the pride in us like service — when the person I serve doesn’t appreciate it, when I’ve done a great deal and nobody mentions it, what I am really like inside comes to the surface.

Third, training in loving people. Love is not an emotion; love is a verb. We often say, “I don’t have enough love, so I can’t serve,” but in fact the order is often the reverse: it is because we serve that love grows. Pray for someone for a month, and you will begin to love them.

When a person keeps on serving:

the self is dealt with, because service will always bring you up against people and situations you would rather avoid;

life is renewed, because every denying of self is a small resurrection;

love is enlarged, because your world no longer contains only you.

sections.heading: 4. Supporting Evidence from Science and Psychology
sections.html:
Even science has seen this.

Stephanie L. Brown of the University of Michigan and her colleagues published a study in the journal Psychological Science in 2003. They followed four hundred and twenty-three older married couples for five years and found that, after controlling for health, finances and other variables, those who regularly “gave” practical help to others had a significantly lower risk of death than those who did not, while “receiving” help from others did not bring the same benefit. The title of the study was blunt: providing support may be more beneficial than receiving it.

Then there is the Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in human history; its current director is Robert Waldinger. Spanning more than eighty years, its core conclusion is this: what keeps people healthy and happy throughout their lives is not wealth, nor fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this echoes the order of 321 exactly: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Let’s take another picture from the body. Your heart beats about a hundred thousand times a day, pumping blood to your whole body without a moment’s rest. How much of that blood does the heart keep for itself? It keeps only a tiny portion to supply itself and sends all the rest out. A heart that only wanted to hold on to blood wouldn’t be called healthy; that’s called heart failure.

Everywhere in the bodies God has made, the same thing is being said: to live is to let things flow.

sections.heading: 5. There Can Be No Revival Without Service
sections.html:
That is why we say: for there to be revival, there must be service.

Because life is shaped in service.

Because in service, life touches life.

321’s “920 practice” becomes very practical here. Everyone we are connected with is our “2”; as we practise living out the selfless (0) life towards them, the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit will grow.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that not one of these nine graces can be produced in isolation? Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; gentleness needs someone to be gentle towards. When God places people beside you, he is placing the soil for your fruit tree beneath your feet.

Without service, there is no one to grow towards; with no one to grow towards, no fruit can grow; and with no fruit, life stays exactly where it is.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s bring today’s message together with the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. He had all authority, yet he wrapped a towel around his waist and washed the disciples’ feet. The highest standard of service is not a method; it is a person — it is Jesus.

The Bible is my standard. Whether or not I serve is not decided by feelings or by mood but by God’s word. And God’s word says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.” (Ephesians 2:10)

The Holy Spirit is my guide. The thing to avoid above all in service is “making our own plans and then asking God to bless them”. The right order is to ask the Holy Spirit first: Lord, whom do you want me to serve today?

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King. The essence of service is giving up the throne. On my schedule, who is King? Over my wallet, who is King? Over my emotions, who is King?

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The greatest temptation in service is quietly keeping a little of the glory for ourselves. When we learn to pass every word of praise straight on as an offering to him, our service becomes worship.

Establish God’s system. We are not doing scattered good deeds; we are building. A family, a small group, a church, a workplace — each can become a brick in God’s system.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Today’s lesson begins precisely with the first link: exchanging the mindset that “service is other people’s need” for the mindset that “service is my life’s need”. Once the mindset changes, life changes; once life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; and once relationships change, ministry flows out naturally.

Brothers and sisters, remember that the order cannot be reversed. Many people are worn out because they skipped over life and relationships and charged straight into ministry. Ministry built on life is living water; ministry built on the flesh will sooner or later run dry.

Four Shifts of Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective — not asking, “Is this person worth my serving?” but asking, “How does God see this person?”

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective — not asking, “Will this produce results people can see?” but asking, “Will this last in heaven?”

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective — the bowls washed today will get dirty again, the chairs set out today will be stacked away, but the heart offered to the Lord lasts for ever.

From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective — the world says “climb up”, God says “go down”; the world says “get more”, God says “give more”.

The 235 Relationships

Service is not a solo battle. 321’s “235 relationships” tell us: become a “2” with a selfless person — that is a spiritual companion; build a “3” — that is spiritual parents and spiritual children; and then become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

For that sister who had served for twelve years and was worn out, the problem was often not that she did too much, but that she had always been doing it alone. God never meant for us to carry a church on our own. The Lord Jesus himself chose twelve disciples, and sent out seventy two by two (Luke 10:1).

Brothers and sisters, find your “2” today. When someone walks with you, service is no longer a heavy burden.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will take these three practices deeper by placing them within 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Treat Service as “the Purpose of Life”

Every morning remind yourself of two sentences: today I am not living for myself; I am living for God and for others.

In every setting, ask one question: whom can I serve today?

At home, whom can I serve? At work, whom can I serve? At church, whom can I serve? Online, whom can I serve?

Let service be the direction of your daily living, not an item in your diary.

Going deeper with the eight stages:

Information — first memorise Ephesians 2:10 and let the truth enter your mind.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to bring this verse down from your head into your heart, so that you truly see: I am God’s masterpiece; my whole life was prepared by God long ago.

Conviction — make a decision: from today, I will no longer ask, “Shall I serve today?” I will only ask, “Whom shall I serve today?”

Implementation — do one thing today, even if it’s just sending a message to greet someone.

Evaluation — in the evening spend three minutes looking back: whom did I serve today? What was my motive?

Correction — if you find your motive was to be seen, confess it to the Lord at once and ask him to cleanse you.

Repetition — forty days in a row without a break. A change of mindset takes time; it doesn’t come from one moment of being moved.

Multiplication — teach this practice to someone else, and take them along with you as you do it.

Practice 2: Learn Humility through Service

When you serve, don’t seek to be seen, don’t seek to be praised.

Instead, learn three things: serve in secret, serve gladly and willingly, serve without counting the cost.

The Lord Jesus says, “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your merciful deeds may be in secret, then your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.” (Matthew 6:3–4)

Peter also urges the elders: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly;” (1 Peter 5:2)

Let service become a way of dealing with pride.

Going deeper with the eight stages:

Information — read Matthew 6:1–4 and see clearly the Lord’s warning against “doing it to be seen”.

Revelation — ask the Lord to shine his light: the last time I was upset, was it because my service went unnoticed?

Conviction — admit that pride is the deepest problem in my life, and that humility is the only way out.

Implementation — this week, do one act of service that nobody at all knows about.

Evaluation — when it’s done, is your heart at peace, or a little disappointed? Disappointment is the proof that “self” is still there.

Correction — turn that disappointment into a matter for prayer, and ask the Lord to take back the throne.

Repetition — do at least one unseen act of service every month.

Multiplication — when you see others serving quietly, go and thank them and pray for them, and pass on this unseen faithfulness.

Practice 3: Serve Faithfully in Small Things

Don’t wait for a big platform; start from the smallest places.

Help one person. Care for one person. Bless one person.

What God values is not size but faithfulness.

The Lord Jesus says, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10)

And the prophet says, “Who despises the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10)

Before David became king, he was a boy keeping sheep in the wilderness (1 Samuel 16:11); before Moses led the Israelites, he spent forty years tending sheep in the wilderness of Midian. God’s training ground has always been in the “small”.

And the Lord himself put it most movingly: “Because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)

Brothers and sisters, that cup of water you hand out — the Lord has taken it into his own hands.

Going deeper with the eight stages:

Information — list three people in your circle who have had a need recently.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to point out the one “the Lord wants you to go to first”.

Conviction — believe that small things are not small in God’s eyes.

Implementation — this week, do one specific small thing for that person.

Evaluation — write it down: what did I do? How did they respond? What changed in my heart?

Correction — if you did it and saw no result, don’t give up; adjust your approach and try again.

Repetition — turn this small thing into a long-term habit.

Multiplication — invite a brother or sister to become your “2”, to remind each other and go and do it together.

An Important Reminder: Why Serving Wears Us Out

Brothers and sisters, if you find serving exhausting, please don’t immediately blame yourself. First be still and ask three questions.

Am I doing it “for people”? If I’m doing it for people, the moment they don’t appreciate it, I collapse.

Am I doing it “for the task”? If I’m doing it for the task, the moment things don’t go smoothly, I collapse.

Am I doing it “for myself”? If I’m doing it for myself, the moment someone else is praised, I collapse.

True service comes down to three phrases:

Do it for the Lord. “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)

Do it by the Lord. “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Work together with the Lord. We are not working for God in his place; we are working together with God. The heavy burden is on him, not on us.

321 has a saying that puts it superbly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and there is joy; rely on the brain and ourselves, and there is exhaustion.

Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad at heart; rely on the brain and you’ll be weighed down with worry.

For “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

The Lord also says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

Brothers and sisters, the Lord’s yoke is a “yoke for two”. When you feel the whole weight pressing on your shoulders, it may well be that you have asked the Lord to step out from the other side of the yoke and are pulling it all by yourself.

A Declaration of Faith

Let us declare together:

Lord Jesus, I declare: service is not a burden; it is my calling.

I was saved to serve you and to live out your life.

I will learn humility through service, and practise denying of self through service.

Lead me, so that my whole life is lived in service, preparing myself to reign with you one day.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, this morning we have seen three things together.

First, service is the purpose of our salvation. We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.

Second, service is the way we train to reign with the Lord. Serve first, then reign; be humble first, then receive glory.

Third, without service, we easily slip into the self-centred life. Service is the training ground God gives us for dealing with the old self and living out Christ.

So let’s say the lesson’s final sentence once more:

We serve not because others need you, but because — you need to serve.

Because service lets you live out your true self — the self created in the image of God and re-created in Christ.

Because service brings you into God’s plan — the plan prepared before you were born.

Because service prepares you for eternal glory — the crown that one day will be taken off and laid before the throne of the Lamb.

When you understand this, you will move from “serving because you have to” into “serving with joy”.

This is the life of an overcomer.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord is asking us a question: are you willing?

He isn’t asking whether you have the gifts; he isn’t asking whether you have the time; he isn’t asking whether you’re qualified. He asks only one thing: are you willing?

If you are, then say to the Lord in your heart, “I am willing.”

Then walk out of this morning devotion and go and find that one person. It needn’t be anything big — handing someone a cup of water is enough; you needn’t wait for a platform — one phone call is enough.

Let Jesus reign as King in your service.

Let Jesus receive all the glory through your service.

“Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.” (1 Corinthians 15:58)

Learn humility through service

prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you, for our salvation is entirely by grace, through faith; it is not of ourselves, and not of works. Plant this gratitude deep in our hearts first of all.

Lord, renew our mindset about service. We confess that at times we serve for people, for the task, for ourselves — and so we grow weary, resentful and ready to give up. Today, turn our service from “other people’s need” into “our life’s need”.

Lord, deal with the “self” within us. The heart that wants to be served, the heart that wants to be affirmed, the heart that wants to be exalted — deal with them by the cross. Make us like you: though you had all authority, you gladly wrapped a towel around your waist and stooped to wash feet.
Lord, give us eyes that see people, a heart willing to give, and hands ready to do small things. Make us faithful in small things, glad and willing in secret, and never losing our joy in hard labour.
Help us to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Let us share the yoke with you every day and find rest in you.
Lead us to live our whole lives in service; prepare our life, our identity and our place in the kingdom, that one day we may reign together with you.
Reign as King in our service, and receive all the glory through our service.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Ephesians 2:10: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” Looking back over your experience since you came to faith, which “good work” do you think God prepared for you before you were born — one that others could not easily do in your place? Are you walking that path now?

Mark 10:45: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” Please share honestly: the last time you felt weary or hard done by in your service, were you doing it “for people”, “for the task” or “for yourself”? If you changed that to “doing it for the Lord, by the Lord, and together with the Lord”, how would you adjust? Please pray for one another.

blog.title: Worn Out by Serving?

blocks.x: Subtitle: perhaps you’ve been asking the wrong question
A sigh in an empty sanctuary

A sister had served in her church for twelve years. She had led Sunday school, been in charge of welcoming and taken on pastoral care; every week she was always the first to arrive and the last to leave.
One day after the meeting had ended, she sat in the empty sanctuary and said, her eyes red: “It isn’t that I don’t love the Lord. I’m just… so tired.”

Have you ever heard a sigh like that? If so, please don’t rush to blame yourself for not being spiritual. That weariness is actually pointing to something: our mindset about service needs to be renewed.
Most of us began serving for two reasons — other people have needs, and the church has needs.

Neither of these reasons is bad. But if the drive stops only at the needs outside us, sooner or later it will run out. Because the needs out there are endless, and our strength is limited. You fill this gap, and a hole opens over there. And so service becomes a burden, the burden becomes complaint, and complaint becomes withdrawal.
In fact, you are the one who needs to serve
The Bible gives us a perspective that turns this upside down:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10)

The word “workmanship” in Greek is ποίημα, meaning a work, a masterpiece; the English word “poem” comes from it. In God’s eyes you are not a part on an assembly line; you are a poem he has written in his own hand.

And the original word for “prepared” carries the sense of “beforehand” — before you were even born, God had already prepared the good works you would do, the people you would influence and the testimony you would live out. So we are not saved merely to go to heaven; he leaves you here because there are people who will come to know Jesus only through you.

Picture the dumbbells at the gym. Do the weight plates need you? No. It is you who need to lift them. A few months later, what has changed is not the dumbbell, but your muscles and your heart and lungs.
Service is the same. The person most deeply changed is often not the one being served, but ourselves.
The difference between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea
Israel has two seas, and both are fed by the same river, the Jordan.

The Sea of Galilee has both an inflow and an outflow, so it teems with fish and its shores are shaded with green trees. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out; its salt grows ever more concentrated, to a salinity of about 34 per cent, close to ten times that of ordinary seawater, so no fish can live there.
The same source of water; the difference comes down to a single word: outflow.
The Lord Jesus said: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45)

There are two roads, and only these two. If someone doesn’t serve, they won’t stay where they are; they will slowly drift towards “wanting to be served, wanting to be affirmed, wanting to be exalted” — which is exactly what the old, self-centred life looks like.
Service is the training ground God gives us for dealing with ourselves: training in denying of self, training in humility, training in loving people.

Psychology has seen the same thing. Stephanie L. Brown of the University of Michigan and her colleagues published a study in Psychological Science in 2003 that followed four hundred and twenty-three older married couples for five years and found that those who regularly gave practical help to others had a significantly lower risk of death.
From serving because we must to serving with joy
If you find serving exhausting, first be still and ask three questions: Am I doing it for people? Am I doing it for the task? Am I doing it for myself?

If I’m doing it for people, the moment they don’t appreciate it, I collapse; if I’m doing it for the task, the moment things don’t go smoothly, I collapse; if I’m doing it for myself, the moment someone else is praised, I collapse.
True service comes down to three phrases: do it for the Lord, do it by the Lord, work together with the Lord.
Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and there is joy; rely on the brain and ourselves, and there is exhaustion.
So start today, in the smallest places. You needn’t wait for a big platform: help one person, care for one person, bless one person. What God values is not size but faithfulness.
Because we serve not because others need you, but because — you need to serve.
Service lets you live out your true self, brings you into God’s plan and prepares you for eternal glory. This is the life of an overcomer.
A question for reflection
If, from today, you no longer asked “Shall I serve today?” but only “Whom can I serve today?”, how would your day be different?

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning.
Today we are looking together at a question: whose need is service? Service — whose need is it, really?
Our theme verse is Ephesians 2:10: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.”
This lesson wants to tell us one thing: service is not others’ need, but the need of our own life.

There was a sister who had served in her church for twelve years. One day after the meeting had ended, she sat in the empty sanctuary and said, “Pastor, it isn’t that I don’t love the Lord. I’m just… so tired.”
Brothers and sisters, have you ever heard a sigh like that?
Many of us began serving for two reasons: other people have needs, and the church has needs.
Neither of these reasons is bad. But if the drive stops only at what is outside us, sooner or later that strength will run out.
Because the needs out there are endless, and our strength is limited.
It’s like the dumbbells at the gym. Do the weight plates need you? No. It is you who need to lift them.
Service is the same. The person most deeply changed is often not them, but ourselves.
Let’s look at the background first.
The author of Ephesians is Paul. When he wrote this letter, he was in prison. He says: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you.” (Ephesians 4:1) That was around AD 60–62.
Brothers and sisters, a man with chains on his wrists wrote the most glorious teaching on the church. Since he couldn’t go out, he served with his pen.
Notice what comes just before: “For by grace you have been saved through faith… not of works, that no one would boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9)
Salvation is absolutely not something we earn by serving.
So the order is this: we are not saved because we serve; we serve because we are saved.
The first key point: service is the purpose of our salvation.
“For we are his workmanship.” The word “workmanship” in Greek is ποίημα, meaning a work, a masterpiece. The English word “poem” comes from it.
Brothers and sisters, in God’s eyes you are not a part on an assembly line; you are a poem he has written in his own hand.

“Which God prepared before that we would walk in them.” The prefix of “prepared before” means “beforehand”. Before you were even born, God had already prepared the good works you would do, the people you would influence and the testimony you would live out.
So we are not saved merely to go to heaven. He leaves you here because there are people who will come to know Jesus only through you.

The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable. A master entrusted money to his servants: the ones who received five thousand and two thousand went and traded; but the one who received a thousand buried the money in the ground.
The master said: “Throw out the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness.” (Matthew 25:30)
Brothers and sisters, that servant didn’t steal, didn’t squander, didn’t do anything wicked. His sin was doing nothing at all.
So not serving is not just a loss; not serving means losing the meaning of life.
A fine violin locked away for ever in its case — is it still really a violin?
The second key point: service is the way we train to reign with the Lord.
“Whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Mark 10:43)
When were these words spoken? When James and John asked to sit at the Lord’s right and left.
Brothers and sisters, two opposite systems are set out here. The world: the great are served, the high hold power. God’s kingdom: the great serve others, the high are humble.
God doesn’t forbid us to aspire upwards; he simply turns the ladder round a hundred and eighty degrees. In God’s kingdom, the way down is the way up.
“I am among you as one who serves.” (Luke 22:27)
Brothers and sisters, this was said at the Last Supper. The Lord was about to go to the cross, and the disciples were arguing about who was the greatest.
That night the Lord, “knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands”, wrapped a towel around his waist and washed the disciples’ feet. (John 13:3–5)
He didn’t wash feet out of a sense of inferiority; it was because he had absolute security that he could stoop down.
Then the Lord said: “You will sit on thrones.” (Luke 22:30)
This is a spiritual law: serve first, and then you can reign; be humble first, and then you can receive glory.
That stack of dishes you wash today is preparing your crown.
The third key point: without service, we easily slip into the self-centred life.
“For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve.” (Mark 10:45)
Brothers and sisters, there are two roads, and only these two. If someone doesn’t serve, they will want to be served, want to be affirmed, want to be exalted.
This is what 321 calls the self-centred life, the root of humanity’s fall.
But Paul says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)
Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into fullness and living it out.
Service is precisely the training ground God gives us: training in denying of self, training in humility, training in loving people.

Israel has two seas, both fed by the Jordan. The Sea of Galilee has both an inflow and an outflow, and it teems with fish; the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out, with a salinity of about 34 per cent, close to ten times that of seawater, so there is no life in it.
The difference comes down to one word: outflow. God doesn’t lack our service; it is our lives that lack that outlet.
So we say: for there to be revival, there must be service. Because in service, life touches life.
This is 321’s 920 practice — everyone I relate to is my “2”; live out selflessness, and the ninefold fruit of the Spirit will grow.
We have three practices.
First, treat service as the purpose of life. Every day ask one question: whom can I serve today?
Second, learn humility through service. Serve in secret, gladly and willingly, without counting the cost.
Third, be faithful in small things. Don’t wait for a big platform. Help one person, care for one person, bless one person.
The Lord said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” (Luke 16:10)
Take these deeper with the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.
Brothers and sisters, if you find serving exhausting, first ask three questions.

Am I doing it for people? The moment they don’t appreciate it, I collapse. Am I doing it for the task? The moment things don’t go smoothly, I collapse. Am I doing it for myself? The moment someone else is praised, I collapse.
True service is this: do it for the Lord, do it by the Lord, work together with the Lord.
Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and there is joy; rely on the brain and ourselves, and there is exhaustion.
So the conclusion says: we serve not because others need you, but because you need to serve.
Service lets you live out your true self, brings you into God’s plan and prepares you for eternal glory.
This is the life of an overcomer.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, thank you that our salvation is entirely by grace.
Renew our mindset about service; turn it from “other people’s need” into “our life’s need”.
Deal with the self within us, and make us like you — gladly wrapping a towel around our waist and stooping to wash feet.
Help us to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; to live our whole lives in service, and one day to reign together with you.
Reign as King in our service, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
