script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today is Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 159, and our title is “Service Is My Own Need”.

In the last lesson we came to understand one thing: serving is actually our own need. Today we’re going to take three steps further in: serving brings growth in our lives; serving is the way to invest in eternity; serving makes us useful people.
Brothers and sisters, serving is not only giving; serving is a tremendous blessing and opportunity that God gives us.
Let me first take you on a trip to Israel.

There’s a river called the Jordan, running from north to south. It first flows into the Sea of Galilee and flows out again; finally it empties into the Dead Sea, and from there it never flows out again.

The Sea of Galilee has water coming in and going out; its water is living, fishing boats come and go, and fish gather in shoals. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out; its salinity is above about 33 per cent, nearly ten times that of seawater, and not a single fish can survive in it.
The same river water — so where is the difference? Not in how much each receives, but in whether it is willing to give out.
Brothers and sisters, ask yourself: is my life more like the Sea of Galilee, or more like the Dead Sea?
Our theme verse says, “While we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

Paul wrote these words. While he was being misunderstood, he was pouring out his life for the church day after day. The word “look at” in the original means to fix your gaze, like an archer keeping his eye locked on the target.

On the other side, in Mark 10, there is a rich young man. Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him: go, sell whatever you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. But he went away sorrowful.
One gave himself away; the other couldn’t. Brothers and sisters, this morning we stand between these two pictures.
The first key point: serving is the path to growth in life.
The principle of life comes down to a few simple words: what comes in must go out.
Breathing is breathing in and then breathing out. The body takes food in and then eliminates. Life is receiving and then giving out.
An adult breathes about twenty thousand times a day, and the heart beats about a hundred thousand times. They can keep going because they keep on giving out.
The law God wrote into the natural world he has also written into your spiritual life and mine.
Only hearing the word and never doing it, our spiritual life stagnates. James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)
Only receiving and never sharing, our spiritual life grows weak. Brothers and sisters, collecting is not absorbing, and absorbing is not growing.
The Lord Jesus said that from within whoever believes in him will flow rivers of living water. Notice: it says “flow”, not “store up”.

Paul said, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35) A five-year study published by the University of Michigan in 2003 also found that people who regularly help others have a markedly lower risk of dying.
A 321 insight: life grows by giving out; selflessness is shaped in serving.
When you begin to serve, you’ll discover that you become more loving, more patient, more like Jesus.
The second key point: serving is the way to invest in eternity.
The Lord Jesus said to the rich young man, “You will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Mark 10:21)
The Lord reminds us: everything on earth is temporary; the values of heaven are eternal.
In the Sermon on the Mount the Lord said earthly treasure has three enemies: moth, rust and thieves. Brothers and sisters, there is not one thing in this world that you can keep for ever.
The Lord also said: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The reverse is true as well — look at your diary, and you’ll know where your heart is.
So what can be stored up in heaven?
Not how much you own, but how much you give away.
The Lord said, “Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)
What is “it”? Giving people food, giving them drink, taking them in, visiting the sick. All of them small things.
So when you help someone, when you care for someone, when you give your time and your love, you are really investing in heaven.
A 321 insight: only what we give away is eternal; everything we hold on to will pass.
Every act of service is an eternal investment.
The third key point: serving makes us useful people.
The master said, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” (Matthew 25:21)
God gives each person different gifts: some five talents, some two, some one.
But brothers and sisters, the one who received five and the one who received two were given exactly the same praise. For the master was looking not at how much, but at faithfulness.
The point is not how much, but whether it is used. Used, it has value; unused, it becomes useless.
God’s principle is very clear: “For to everyone who has will be given.” (Matthew 25:29) The more you use, the more you have; unused, even what you have is lost.
Muscles are just like that. In the weightlessness of space, astronauts who don’t exercise lose muscle and bone mass quickly, so they must exercise about two hours every day.
Many people don’t serve because they feel they’re not good enough, don’t have enough, aren’t capable enough.

But back in 1977 the psychologist Bandura found that confidence comes mainly from the first-hand experience of getting something done. You don’t first have confidence and then do it; you do it, and then you have confidence.
Brothers and sisters, don’t wait until you’re better to serve; use it first, and then you’ll get better.
Let’s practise three things.
First, practise letting your life have both in and out. When you’ve heard a message, share it with someone in your own words.
Second, practise investing in eternity through serving. Ask every day: who can I give myself for today?
Third, practise using everything God has given you. A word, an act of care, a little time — all of them can be used by God.

The 321 eight stages of changing our mindset are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, start today with the stage of Implementation.
Let’s go back to that River Jordan.
The same water, flowing out, becomes living water; held back, it becomes dead water.
In serving, you will grow; in serving, you will store up eternity; in serving, you will be used by God.
Once you understand this, you will no longer ask, “Why should I serve?” You’ll begin to say, “Lord, give me more opportunities to serve!”
Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for letting me see that serving is a blessing and an opportunity you have given me.
Please turn the Dead Sea in me into a Sea of Galilee; open up the outlet of my life, so that your grace can flow out.
I am willing to serve with everything you have given me, investing it in eternity. I believe that when I am willing to use it, you will add to it.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you, and give you an opportunity to give out today.
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today is Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 159, and our title is “Service Is My Own Need”.

In the last lesson we came to understand that serving is actually our own need. Today we’re going three steps further — serving brings growth in our lives, serving is the way to invest in eternity, and serving makes us useful people.
Brothers and sisters, please first remember one sentence: serving is not only giving; serving is a tremendous blessing and opportunity that God gives us.
Let me first take you on a trip to Israel. There’s a river there called the Jordan; it rises from the snowmelt of Mount Hermon in the north and flows all the way south.

It first flows into the Sea of Galilee, and then flows out again. There the water is living, fishing boats come and go, and fish gather in shoals; it was there that the Lord Jesus called his disciples and fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish.

Then it carries on south and empties into the Dead Sea, and from there it never flows out again. Water that goes in can only evaporate; the salinity is above about 33 per cent, nearly ten times that of seawater. Not a single fish can survive in it, and not a blade of grass grows on its shores.
The same river water, the same sunshine, the same land. So where is the difference? Not in how much each receives, but in whether it is willing to give out.

Brothers and sisters, when we understand that “serving is our own need”, our lives turn from passive to active. We no longer serve only when there’s a need, no longer serve only when we’ve been rostered on; instead, whenever we see an opportunity we serve, and we make serving part of our lives.
Did you hear the difference? In the first two, serving is a task someone else gives me; in the last two, serving is my own life.
So please quietly ask yourself: right now, is my life more like the Sea of Galilee, or more like the Dead Sea?
Let’s first look at today’s theme verse.

“While we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

This letter was written by the apostle Paul, around AD 55–56, to the church in Corinth. At the time some were questioning him: he’s weak, he’s always being beaten and imprisoned — how could he possibly be an apostle?

Paul didn’t argue for any splendour of his own. He said, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) Clay vessels were the cheapest, most easily broken containers. I am a clay vessel, yet inside me there is a treasure.

The word “look at” in Greek is skopeō; it means to fix your gaze on, to make something your target, just as an archer keeps his eye locked on the bullseye. Brothers and sisters, Paul moved the sights of his life from what can be seen to what cannot be seen.
Now to the first key point: serving is the path to growth in life. The principle of life comes down to a few simple words — what comes in must go out.
Look at your breathing: you breathe in, and then you breathe out. An adult breathes about twenty thousand times a day. If you only breathed in and never out, you couldn’t last a minute.
Look at your heart: it beats about a hundred thousand times a day. The reason it can keep beating is that it keeps on giving out.
Brothers and sisters, the law God wrote into the natural world he has also written into your spiritual life and mine.
If there is only in and never out, life stagnates, and can even die. Spiritual life is the same.
Only hearing the word and never doing it, our spiritual life stagnates. James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

Notice those words: deluding your own selves. When someone hears a great deal of preaching but never puts it into practice, over time they think they’re very spiritual. In fact, only their knowledge has grown; their life hasn’t grown up.
Only receiving and never sharing, our spiritual life grows weak. One phone can hold hundreds of sermons, but brothers and sisters, collecting is not absorbing, and absorbing is not growing.
So where is the outlet? The outlet is serving.

The Lord Jesus said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.” (John 7:38) Notice, the Lord did not say a reservoir will be stored up inside you; he said rivers will flow out.

The Lord also said, “The water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.” (John 4:14) A pond waits for someone to pour water in; a spring wells up from below. Only someone who starts giving out discovers that there was a spring inside them all along.
At Miletus Paul said to the elders, “Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’” (Acts 20:35)

The University of Michigan psychologist Stephanie Brown and her colleagues published a study in 2003 that followed 423 older married couples for five years. They found that those who regularly helped others had a markedly lower risk of dying, while those who simply received help showed no such benefit.
Solomon had said it three thousand years earlier: “The liberal soul shall be made fat. He who waters shall be watered also himself.” (Proverbs 11:25)
Here is today’s first 321 insight: life grows by giving out; selflessness is shaped in serving.
The old self, the self-centred life, is always calculating “What do I get?”; the new self, living in selflessness, begins to ask “What can I give?”

Brothers and sisters, when you begin to serve, you’ll discover that you become more loving, more patient, more like Jesus. That isn’t something you squeeze out of yourself; it’s because the water has started to flow, and the spring wells up.
The second key point: serving is the way to invest in eternity.
Mark 10 records that as the Lord Jesus was on the road to Jerusalem, a young man ran up and knelt before him. He was young, he was rich, and he was devout and kept the commandments.

Scripture records a deeply moving sentence: “Jesus looking at him loved him.” The Lord was not trying to make things hard for him. It was because the Lord loved him that he said to him, “One thing you lack. Go, sell whatever you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Mark 10:21)

See the Lord’s logic: first give it away, and then you will have treasure in heaven. This is not a harsh command; it’s a piece of better investment advice. Sadly, the young man’s face fell, and he went away sorrowful. It wasn’t that he didn’t believe. It was that he couldn’t give it away.
Why couldn’t he give it away? Because he couldn’t see clearly the difference between two worlds.

The Lord said, “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal.” (Matthew 6:19) Moths eat clothing, rust corrodes metal, thieves steal money. In this world there is not one thing you can keep for ever.
The Lord went on, “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:21)
Brothers and sisters, the reverse is also true. Do you want to know where your heart is? Open your diary, look at your bank statements, and the answer is right there.
So what can be stored up in heaven? Not how much you own, but how much you give away.
The Lord Jesus said, “Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” (Matthew 25:40)

What is “it”? I was hungry and you gave me food, thirsty and you gave me drink, sick and you visited me — all the most ordinary little things. The Lord also said that whoever gives one of these little ones just a cup of cold water to drink will in no way lose his reward.
Do you remember that poor widow? She put in two small coins, and the Lord said she had given more than all the others. Earth counts how much you gave; heaven counts how much you kept back.
In 1949 a 22-year-old American wrote a sentence in his journal: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.”
His name was Jim Elliot. In 1956, he and four co-workers, seeking to bring the gospel to the Auca people of Ecuador, were speared to death on a river beach. He was 28 that year.

By earthly arithmetic it was a colossal loss. But that tribe later came to the Lord in large numbers, and their story has, for more than sixty years, inspired countless people to take up the path of mission.

This is the second 321 insight: only what we give away is eternal; everything we hold on to will pass. The 321 vision speaks of a shift in perspective: from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one.

In Revelation John heard a voice saying, “that they may rest from their labors; for their works follow with them.” (Revelation 14:13) Brothers and sisters, on the day we leave this world we can take nothing with us; only our works will go with us.
The third key point: serving makes us useful people.
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things.’” (Matthew 25:21)
This is the parable of the talents. The master gave to each according to his ability: one five talents, one two, one one.

That “one talent” — talanton in the original — was about six thousand denarii, and one denarius was a labourer’s wage for a day. Do the sums: the servant who “only got one” was holding nearly twenty years’ wages in his hand.
Brothers and sisters, God has never given anyone “just a little”. In God’s eyes, even the smallest entrustment is a fortune.
Notice how the parable ends. The one who received five gained five more; the one who received two gained two more. What the master said to them was word for word exactly the same.
The master was looking not at quantity, but at faithfulness.
“Faithful” in Greek is pistos, from the same root as “faith”. Paul says, “Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:2)
And the one who received one talent? He said, “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.” He didn’t gamble it, he didn’t spend it. He simply — didn’t use it.
And the master’s verdict on him was: you wicked and slothful servant. Brothers and sisters, in the ledger of the kingdom of heaven, “not using” is itself a debt left unpaid.
So God’s principle is very clear: “For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.” (Matthew 25:29)

Just look at your muscles and you’ll understand. In the weightlessness of space, unless astronauts deliberately exercise, they lose muscle and bone mass rapidly, which is why on the International Space Station they are required to exercise about two hours every day. Brothers and sisters, muscles aren’t ruined by use; muscles are ruined by sitting idle.

The brain is the same: circuits used often are strengthened, and connections left unused are pruned away. A language you’ve learned but never speak will be forgotten; a piece you can play but never practise will grow rusty. Spiritual gifts follow this same law — the more you use them, the more you have; unused, even what you have is lost.
Many people don’t serve because three sentences are running in their hearts: I’m not good enough, I don’t have enough, I’m not capable enough.
But God says: it isn’t about how much; it’s about whether you’re willing to use it.

In 1977 the psychologist Bandura put forward the theory of self-efficacy. He found that the main source of people’s confidence in their own abilities is the first-hand experience of success. In plain words: you don’t first have confidence and then do it; you do it, and then you have confidence.

Moses said he was slow of speech, Jeremiah said he was only a child, yet God still sent them. That boy had only five loaves and two fish, but he handed them over, the Lord broke them, and the crowd was fed.

This is the third 321 insight: unused becomes useless; used is enlarged. This is exactly the 920 practice — everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we live out the selfless “0”, and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Love needs someone to love; patience needs someone to be patient with. God has put people around you precisely so that you have somewhere to “use” it.
Let’s practise. First, practise letting your life have both in and out. Each day, don’t only receive; give out as well. When you’ve received a grace, become a blessing to someone else.

After this morning’s devotion, pick out the one sentence that touched you most, and pass it on to someone in your own words. Don’t forward the whole thing. Forwarding is just passing water through; saying it in your own words is digesting.
Second, practise investing in eternity through serving. Ask yourself every day: who can I give myself for today? How can I invest in heaven today?
Today, choose one person and do one small thing: a phone call, a prayer, some time spent together. It needn’t be big, but it must be real.
Third, practise using everything God has given you.
Don’t belittle yourself. A word, an act of care, a little time — all of them can be used by God.
Please list three things God has given you, and after each one write a name: who can I use this for?
One last gentle reminder. Many people think: I’ll serve once I’m better. But God’s principle is: use it first, and then you’ll get better.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll grow; rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll stagnate. Brothers and sisters, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Lord said, “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve.” (Mark 10:45) When the Lord of the universe himself bent down to serve, can we still stand on our own status?
The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system.

The order of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

There are eight stages in changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. What you heard today is information; ask the Holy Spirit to turn it into revelation for you. Once convinced, implement it; evaluate it tonight; correct it tomorrow; then repeat it; and finally bring someone to serve alongside you — that is multiplication.
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the River Jordan we visited this morning. The same water, flowing out, becomes living water; held back, it becomes dead water.
Serving is not merely giving; it is the beginning of growth, of investment and of worth.
In serving, you will grow; in serving, you will store up eternity; in serving, you will be used by God.
Once you understand this, you will no longer ask, “Why should I serve?” You’ll begin to say, “Lord, give me more opportunities to serve!”

That young man went away sorrowful, because he couldn’t bear to let go. Paul joyfully finished the whole race, because he had long since given himself away. This morning the Lord is looking at you too, and loving you, and saying to you: come, follow me.
Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let’s pray together.
Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for letting me see that serving is not an extra burden, but a blessing and an opportunity you have given me.
Lord, forgive me. So often I only want to receive and not give out; so often I say I’m not good enough, not capable enough — when really I can’t bear to let go, and I’m afraid.
Please turn the Dead Sea in me into a Sea of Galilee; open up the outlet of my life, so that your grace can flow out and become a blessing to others.

Please help me turn my time, money, energy and love into treasure in heaven. Teach me to use what I have first, and grow better by using it. However much you give me, I am willing to bring it out and use it.
Lord, be King in my life, and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Brothers and sisters, may the Lord bless you and keep you. May you have an opportunity to give out today.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Moment of Raising Your Hand
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we come together before God to listen quietly to a question that is very short, yet one that will follow us all our lives.

Let me first describe a scene that has played out in many churches. The Sunday service ends, and the pastor stands at the front and says, “Next month we’re starting a new area of service, and we need a few brothers and sisters. If you’re willing, please raise your hand.”

What happens next?

A silence. A very curious silence. Suddenly everyone’s eyes are very busy — some look down at the bulletin, some sort out their bags, some study their own shoes intently. It isn’t that they don’t love the Lord, nor that they’re unwilling; it’s that in those few short seconds, a voice is speaking in each person’s heart.

That voice says, “I’m not good enough yet.”

That voice says, “I don’t have the gift.”

That voice says, “I don’t have the time.”

Brothers and sisters, do these three sentences sound familiar? I believe there’s no one here to whom they are completely foreign. These three sentences are practically the common language of Christians the world over. They sound humble, honest, perfectly reasonable. Yet today we are going to see together that none of these three sentences is really “a statement of fact”; each is “a stronghold of mindset”.

In the last lesson we saw together that serving is our need. It isn’t that God needs us to serve, but that we need to serve; a life that doesn’t serve will dry up, become self-centred, and gradually lose the glory that God’s children ought to have. Once we understand that “serving is our need”, a very practical question follows —

Who can serve?

Who is qualified to stand in God’s work? Who is good enough to be used by God? Those who have studied theology? Those who speak well? Those with plenty of time? Those whose gifts are obvious, who shine the moment they step onto the platform?

Scripture’s answer is so simple it’s startling — and so simple there’s nowhere to hide from it —

The willing can all serve.

Notice that God has never asked, “Are you able?” What God asks is, “Are you willing?” The words Isaiah heard in the temple were not “Who is able to go for me?” but “Who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6:8). “Will go” — that is willingness. God’s call-up has never been a checklist of abilities, but an invitation to the heart.

Brothers and sisters, this is a turning point in our mindset. Most of the stagnation in our lives comes not from a lack of ability, but from a wrong mindset. The light of 321 says it clearly: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Today’s lesson is about removing four wrong mindsets from our hearts, one by one, and putting God’s perspective in their place.

Today we’ll look at four things: first, we don’t serve once we’re equipped; we are equipped in serving. Second, we don’t serve because we have the gift; we experience God’s provision in serving. Third, it isn’t that we have no time; it’s that we haven’t put God first. Fourth, serving is grace, not a burden.

Four key points, all pointing to the same conclusion: whether you are able to serve has never been the question; whether you are willing is the only question.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An “Unworthy” Man Writes “I Am What I Am”
sections.html:
Our theme verse today comes from 1 Corinthians 15:10. To really taste this verse, we need to know who wrote it and under what circumstances.

The author of 1 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It was written around AD 55, when he was in Ephesus during his third missionary journey (1 Corinthians 16:8 says, “But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost”). Its recipients were the church he himself had planted in Corinth.

What kind of place was Corinth? Corinth lay on the isthmus in southern Greece. It was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, and its two ports, east and west, made it one of the busiest commercial cities in the Mediterranean. The city was wealthy, mixed in population, confused in religion and corrupt in morals. A church in a city like that naturally had plenty of problems: factions and quarrels, sexual immorality, believers suing one another, disorder at the Lord’s Supper, and comparing and boasting over spiritual gifts. In 1 Corinthians 12 to 14, Paul spends three whole chapters on gifts — because that church’s greatest sickness was using gifts to rank one another.

Then Paul comes to chapter 15, on the resurrection. He first lists the witnesses of the resurrection: Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred brothers, James, all the apostles. Finally he says, “And last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also. For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.” (1 Corinthians 15:8–9)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to Paul’s self-assessment: the least, unworthy, one who had persecuted the church. Judged by qualifications, Paul was the least qualified of all to serve. With his own hands he had thrown believers into prison; when Stephen was stoned to death, he stood by, minding the clothes. If “serving” required an impressive CV, Paul would be the first one out.

Yet next he writes the most moving sentence in the whole letter: “But by the grace of God I am what I am.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

“But” — this word is the turning point of the gospel. Human qualifications end here; God’s grace begins here.

“The grace of God” — the word for grace here is the Greek charis, meaning a free, undeserved gift. Interestingly, the New Testament word for “gift” (charisma) comes straight from charis — a gift is grace made concrete. That is to say: whatever ability you have in your hands, you didn’t earn it; it is the fruit that grace has borne.

In the same verse Paul says three more things, and with them he lays out the whole logic of serving. First, “His grace which was given to me was not futile” — when grace comes, it must bear fruit. Second, “I worked more than all of them” — those who receive grace don’t lie back; they’re the ones most willing to work. Third, “Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” — when the work is done, the credit doesn’t go to ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, this one verse answers both extremes at once. To the one who says, “I’m not good enough”, Paul says: I wasn’t worthy either, but God’s grace has made me what I am today. To the one who says, “I’m very capable”, Paul says: Yet not I, but the grace of God. The first is lifted up, the second is brought down. This is how the gospel works: it lifts up the lowly and humbles the proud.

This is exactly what 321 says: the old self, the self-centred life, is always weighing whether it’s good enough, whether it’s better than others; the new self, living in selflessness, sees only grace and lets Jesus alone be King. Paul’s “not I, but the grace of God” is the finest declaration of selflessness there is.

Now, carrying this verse with us, let’s walk step by step into today’s four key points.

sections.heading: 1. We Don’t Serve Once We’re Equipped; We Are Equipped in Serving
sections.html:
That voice in our hearts: “I’m not ready yet”

Many people are afraid to serve, and their reasons sound entirely reasonable: “I’m not ready yet”, “I’m not mature enough yet”, “Once I’ve read the Bible for a few more years, heard a few more sermons, become a bit more stable, then I’ll come and serve.”

Brothers and sisters, I have to be very honest: this “waiting” often lasts ten years, twenty years, even a lifetime. Because “ready” never has a clear line. Today you finish reading one book of the Bible, and tomorrow you find there are sixty-five more; today you overcome one weakness, and tomorrow the light shows up another gap. If we wait until we’re perfect, we’ll never begin.

And there’s a deep myth hidden here: we think spiritual growth means “first you know how, then you do it”. The truth is just the opposite — the spiritual principle is “first you do it, then you know how”.

Not knowing first and then doing; doing first and then knowing.

God’s order: first he sends, then he equips

Let’s look at a few people in the Bible.

Moses. God called him from the flames at Horeb, and Moses’ first reaction was to make excuses: “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10) He was telling the truth — he really wasn’t a good speaker. But God didn’t first send him on a public-speaking course. God said, “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” (Exodus 4:12) Notice the order: first “go”, then the gift.

Even more interesting is the passage just before. God asked Moses, “What is that in your hand?” Moses said, “A rod.” (Exodus 4:2) It was nothing but a shepherd’s stick, the most ordinary thing of his forty years in the wilderness. Yet when Moses obediently threw it on the ground and picked it up again at God’s word, from then on Scripture calls that rod “God’s rod”. Brothers and sisters, God doesn’t first give you a new rod; God wants to use the one you already have in your hand.

Gideon. When the angel appeared to him, he was threshing wheat in the winepress, hiding from the Midianites. God said, “Go in this your might, and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Haven’t I sent you?” (Judges 6:14) Gideon immediately replied, “O Lord, how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.” (Judges 6:15) The poorest family, the least person — his self-assessment wasn’t wrong at all. But God’s answer was: “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.” (Judges 6:16)

Jeremiah. When God called him, he said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” (Jeremiah 1:6) God said, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for you must go to whomever I send you, and you must say whatever I command you.” (Jeremiah 1:7)

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed what they have in common? The first thing every one of those called said was, “I can’t.” And God’s answer was never “Yes, you can”, but “I will be with you.” God never denies our inadequacy; he simply adds himself to it.

Now look at how the Lord Jesus led his disciples. In Matthew 10, Jesus sent out the twelve disciples to preach, to heal and to cast out demons. Were the disciples mature at that point? Not in the least. Later they were still arguing over who was the greatest, still so frightened in the boat that they woke Jesus up, and Peter was still going to deny the Lord three times. Yet the Lord sent them anyway. The Lord didn’t wait until they were perfect before using them; he shaped them as he used them.

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” (James 1:17)

Brothers and sisters, notice “from above”. Since every good gift comes from above, “Am I enough?” isn’t the key; the key is “Will he give from above?” And God has already told us: in his giving there is no variation, no turning shadow — he won’t be willing to give to you today and change his mind tomorrow. You needn’t worry that the supply will run out.

Learning to ride a bicycle

My favourite picture for this is learning to ride a bicycle.

You could buy ten books and read the world’s most authoritative “Mechanics and Balance of the Bicycle”, memorising every formula for the gyroscopic effect, shifting your centre of gravity and the self-correcting front wheel. Then I ask you: can you ride now? No.

On the other hand, a six-year-old who understands none of the principles is lifted onto the bike by his dad, pushed a few metres, falls twice and skins his knee. Twenty minutes later he can ride. And he’ll never forget it as long as he lives.

Why? Because you don’t learn to ride a bicycle by “understanding”; you learn by “getting on”.

Brain science confirms this too. Skills like cycling, swimming and playing the piano belong to “procedural memory”, handled mainly by the cerebellum and the basal ganglia; this is a different memory system from the one we use to memorise facts, and it can only be built through actual, repeated practice. In other words, when God made us, he wrote “learning by doing” into our very bodies.

Serving is the same. A hundred classes on “How to Care for People” are worth less than actually going on one visit; ten books on prayer are worth less than actually kneeling down once to pray for someone.

In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward the theory of “self-efficacy”. He pointed out that the most powerful source of people’s confidence that “I can do this” is not other people’s encouragement, nor giving yourself a pep talk, but “mastery experience” — actually getting something done yourself. Brothers and sisters, this explains exactly why so many people become more afraid to serve the longer they don’t serve: they’ve never had a first time. Confidence isn’t something you wait for; confidence is something you get by doing.

Hudson Taylor, the founder of the China Inland Mission, is generally credited with saying, “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.” Notice the order of that sentence — first “done”, then “supply”.

A 321 insight: take the first step with your heart, and the Holy Spirit begins to work

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad.

Whose voice is “I’m not ready yet”? That is the voice of the “brain”. The brain calculates: Will I make a fool of myself? Am I qualified? What will people think of me? It calculates this way and that, and the conclusion is always “Wait a bit longer.”

Whose voice is “I’m willing”? That is the voice of the “heart”, the voice of the Holy Spirit’s prompting. The heart doesn’t calculate; the heart simply responds: Lord, here I am; send me.

And this “willingness” is exactly what 321 calls “selflessness”. The self-centred keep looking at themselves — my level, my face, my sense of security; the selfless look only at the Lord — you send, and I go. The old self is self-centred, so it is never enough; the new self is selfless, so it is ready to be used at any time.

So please remember these two sentences:

Take the first step with your heart, and the Holy Spirit begins to work.

When you’re willing to begin, you’ll fall, but you’ll learn; you’ll be imperfect, but you’ll grow. Serving itself is the best equipping there is.

sections.heading: 2. We Don’t Serve Because We Have the Gift; We Experience God’s Provision in Serving
sections.html:
Our God makes something from nothing and much from little

The second common reason is: “That isn’t my gift”, “I don’t have that gift; I can’t do it.”

To pull down this stronghold, we first need to know what kind of God we believe in.

“For he spoke, and it was done. He commanded, and it stood firm.” (Psalm 33:9)

Brothers and sisters, what a great verse this is. In Genesis 1, the earth was formless and empty, and darkness was on the surface of the deep. God didn’t first go and look for materials; God spoke just one sentence: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” (Genesis 1:3) Between nothing and something there was only a single word.

Our God is the God who creates. And what is creating? Creating is making something out of nothing, making much out of little.

So when you say, “I don’t have the gift”, you are really saying to a God who “spoke, and it was done”: this is something you can’t do.

Paul says, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God.” (2 Corinthians 3:5) Notice that Paul admits he is “not sufficient” — this isn’t low self-esteem; it’s a fact. But he doesn’t stop there; he goes on to say, “our sufficiency is from God”. Seeing clearly our own limits while looking up to God’s limitlessness — that is true humility.

Five loaves and two fish: hand them over, and it’s enough

The Lord Jesus gave us a picture we can never forget.

As evening fell, there were five thousand men out in the wilderness, besides women and children. The disciples said, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.” (Matthew 14:17)

Listen to that word “only”. “Only” is the word we use most. I only have a little time. I only have a little money. I only have a tiny gift. I only finished junior high. I can only cook. I can only drive. I can’t do anything — I can only pray.

John’s Gospel gives us more detail: these five loaves and two fish were a boy’s lunch, and they were barley loaves — barley was the food of the poor at the time (John 6:9). The disciples’ assessment was: “But what are these among so many?” By human reckoning, this was a sum that could only end in failure.

But Jesus said something very short: “Bring them here to me.” (Matthew 14:18)

And then? “He commanded the multitudes to sit down on the grass; and he took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven, he blessed, broke and gave the loaves to the disciples, and the disciples gave to the multitudes. They all ate, and were filled. They took up twelve baskets full of that which remained left over from the broken pieces.” (Matthew 14:19–20)

Not enough became more than enough; the limited became limitless. And there were still twelve baskets left over — twelve disciples, a basket each. God’s provision always has “some left over”.

Brothers and sisters, notice where the decisive action of the whole miracle lies. Not in the loaves, not in the fish, not in the disciples’ ability, but in “Bring them here to me” — in that act of handing over. Bread left in the boy’s hands is one meal; bread placed in Jesus’ hands is a banquet for five thousand.

We often get this wrong, thinking it has to become more before we hand it over. No. First we hand it over, and then it becomes more. The bread multiplied only after it was “broken”; if it had never been broken, it would have stayed five loaves for ever.

The picture of a single cell

God’s power to make much from little is actually written on our own bodies every day.

Every human life begins as a fertilised egg — a single cell almost invisible to the naked eye. And an adult body, according to an estimate published in 2013 in the Annals of Human Biology by Bianchi and colleagues at the University of Bologna in Italy, is made up of about 37 trillion cells. From one cell to 37 trillion.

Brothers and sisters, could the God who turned one cell into you not turn that little gift in your hands into a blessing?

A gift is not a qualification but an entrustment

We often have a misunderstanding about “gifts”: we think a gift is a certificate of qualification, and only with one can we step onto the field.

But Scripture says, “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” (1 Peter 4:10) The emphasis here is on “serving one another” and “good managers”. A manager is not the owner; a manager is the one entrusted. Gifts are not for proving who you are; they are for the benefit of others — “But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all.” (1 Corinthians 12:7)

What’s more, gifts are often discovered only in the “using”. Many brothers and sisters were first roped into leading a small group once, and only then discovered they had a shepherd’s heart; were first asked to drive an elderly member home once, and only then discovered the great joy they had in serving people. Gifts are like muscles: unused, they waste away; used, they grow.

God says, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) Notice — not in our strength, but in our weakness. You think weakness keeps you from serving; God says weakness is exactly where his power shows itself.

This doesn’t mean we should do everything or say yes to everything. We still need wisdom; we still need to discern before God. What we want to pull down here is that self-imposed limit, the sentence “I can’t do it, so God can’t either.” Don’t limit what God can do.

A 321 insight: placed in the Lord’s hands, the limited becomes limitless

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living out that fullness.

Five loaves in the boy’s hands were “something” — but a very small something. Once the five loaves were in Jesus’ hands, the boy had “nothing” — and yet that day five thousand people were fed because of him. This is selflessness: letting go of the small “something” in your hand and entering into God’s great limitlessness.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) No longer I — that is selflessness; but Christ lives in me — that is limitlessness.

So please remember:

Placed in the Lord’s hands, the limited becomes limitless.

You be willing first, and God will provide. When there is a need, God will give you strength, and God will enlarge your gifts.

sections.heading: 3. It Isn’t That We Have No Time; It’s That We Haven’t Put God First
sections.html:
The truth about “I don’t have time”

The third reason is the one used most often, and with the clearest conscience: “I’d really love to serve, but I genuinely don’t have the time.”

Brothers and sisters, I completely understand. Modern busyness is real busyness: work, overtime, ferrying children about, caring for elderly parents, the mortgage, health, relationships. None of these are excuses; they are real, heavy burdens.

But please allow us to face one thing honestly together.

Time is the fairest thing in the world. Rich or poor, high or low, everyone has twenty-four hours in a day and 168 hours in a week. The president and the cleaner, the billionaire and the student — exactly the same, not a minute’s difference.

So when we say, “I don’t have time”, strictly speaking, that isn’t accurate. The accurate version is: “This hasn’t yet made it to the front of my priorities.”

The time-management writer Laura Vanderkam has long studied people’s time logs, and she has said something that cuts to the quick: rather than saying “I don’t have time”, say honestly, “It’s not a priority.” She suggests we try replacing “I don’t have time to exercise” with “Exercise is not a priority”, and you’ll immediately hear the weight of that sentence.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t to condemn us, but to move our focus from “time” to “priority”. For we cannot add a single second to our time, but our priorities are something we can adjust today.

We always make time for what matters

Just think about it.

However busy someone is, if their child has a 40-degree fever, will they take time off work? Yes. However busy someone is, if their parent is in hospital for surgery, will they rush to the hospital? Yes. However busy someone is, if someone they love dearly asks to see them, will they squeeze out two hours? Without fail.

We never make time for things because we’re “free”; we make time for things because they’re “important”.

Even the busiest people make time for the people who matter.

So the question isn’t “Do I have time to serve God?” but “Is God the one who matters in my heart?”

The Lord Jesus said it directly: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) The word “first” is all about priority. The Lord didn’t say you needn’t look after your daily life; he said: put the order right, and he’ll take care of the rest.

Luke 10 records how Martha welcomed Jesus into her home, and “Martha was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). Notice that Martha wasn’t a bad person; she was the one who welcomed the Lord in — she was serving. But the Lord said to her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:41–42)

Brothers and sisters, Martha’s problem wasn’t doing too much; it was getting the order wrong. She did the work first and drew near to the Lord afterwards; Mary sat at the Lord’s feet first and then went to do the work. The same day, the same guest, the same kitchen — change the order, and life tastes completely different.

Moses prayed, “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” (Psalm 90:12) We count our days not to make ourselves anxious, but to gain a heart of wisdom, so that we spend our limited days on things that are eternal.

The Reformer Martin Luther is generally credited with saying, “I have so much to do today that I shall have to spend an extra hour in prayer.” By human reckoning that’s a waste; by God’s reckoning, it’s handing the whole day to the Lord who rules over time.

Serving isn’t adding one more thing; it’s doing everything with a different heart

At this point we need to pull down the biggest misunderstanding of all.

Many people think “serving” means “taking on one more role at church”, squeezing one more slot into a schedule that’s already full to bursting. If that were so, serving would of course become a burden — the last straw that breaks the camel’s back.

But the definition Scripture gives us is far broader:

“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Eating and drinking — the two most ordinary, least “spiritual” things in daily life. If even eating and drinking can be done to the glory of God, what can’t be?

Paul also says, “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)

Brothers and sisters, did you catch that? What makes something serving isn’t what the thing is, but who it’s done for. The same washing-up done for yourself is housework; done for the Lord, it’s worship. The same meeting held for sales targets is work; held for the glory of God, it’s ministry.

So:

Work can be serving. Family can be serving. Daily living can be serving.

Serving isn’t doing one more thing; it’s doing everything with God’s heart.

When you see it this way, you’ll suddenly realise: it isn’t that you have no time to serve; you can serve twenty-four hours a day.

A 321 insight: where your focus is, there your time will be

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Most of the weariness of our generation comes from having the order upside down: things first, then people, and last of all, barely squeezing out a little time for God. So the tasks multiply, the heart grows drier, and people grow ever more tired.

Put the order back the right way, and you’ll find you seem to have more time. Because when you align yourself with God first, you no longer need tasks to prove yourself; and when you don’t need to prove yourself, you don’t have to do so many things that never needed doing.

321’s 920 practice puts it very practically: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. Your spouse, your children, your parents, your colleagues, the person you meet every day — all of them are the “2” God has set before you. Live out a life of selflessness (0) towards them, and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, this is serving that needs no extra time set aside. You were going to eat with your family anyway, going to work with your colleagues anyway — just lay down the “self” and invite Jesus onto the throne, and all that time becomes time for serving.

So please remember:

Where your focus is, there your time will be.

Your diary is your heart’s confession.

sections.heading: 4. Serving Is Grace, Not a Burden
sections.html:
How Paul saw himself

The last key point is also the foundation of the whole lesson.

“But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Everything Paul achieved in his life — three missionary journeys, thirteen letters, countless churches — he summed up in one sentence: by the grace of God.

He also said to Timothy, “I thank him who enabled me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he counted me faithful, appointing me to service.” (1 Timothy 1:12) Notice the words “I thank him”. Paul doesn’t say, “Lord, look how much I’ve done for you”; he says, “Thank you for appointing me to serve.”

In Paul’s dictionary, serving was not something he gave to God; it was something God gave to him.

David was the same. When the Israelites gave willingly for the building of the temple, David prayed before God: “But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.” (1 Chronicles 29:14)

Brothers and sisters, what a way of seeing things. What we offer, what we lay down, what we serve with — it all came from God in the first place. We are simply giving God’s things back to God, and yet God still praises us and rewards us.

Even the ability to serve is God’s gift. So — there’s nothing to boast of, only thanks to give.

Understand that it’s grace, and three poisons lose their power

When we truly understand that serving is grace, three things are taken out of us.

First, we stop comparing. Comparison is the greatest killer of serving. That’s exactly what the Corinthian church was like: those who spoke in tongues looked down on those who didn’t; those who prophesied felt a cut above those who served at tables. Paul wanted them to know that the gifts are all worked by one and the same Spirit, and that no member of the body is superfluous. Since it is all grace, comparing is utterly meaningless — you wouldn’t take a present someone gave you, measure it against someone else’s, and then feel you were something special.

Second, we stop complaining. The root of complaining is “I’ve given so much — why does nobody notice?” The assumption behind that sentence is: serving is something I give out, so I ought to receive something back. But if serving is itself grace, an opportunity God has given me, then I’ve already received first — so what is there to complain about?

Third, we stop being lazy. In Matthew 25 the servant who received one talent said, “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.” (Matthew 25:25) And how did the master answer? “You wicked and slothful servant” (Matthew 25:26). Brothers and sisters, notice that his problem wasn’t small ability, but burying what God had entrusted to him. The root of laziness is often fear; and the root of that fear is seeing the Lord as a harsh master, not as a Father full of grace.

In their place come three beautiful things: gratitude, treasuring, and seizing the opportunity.

Because being able to serve is itself a blessing.

Those who serve are blessed first

This is not just a spiritual way of speaking; it is also an observable fact.

In a study published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough found that participants who kept a regular record of things they were grateful for did markedly better in well-being, optimism and physical comfort than control groups who recorded only their troubles or ordinary events. Gratitude isn’t self-consolation; gratitude really does change a person.

On the serving side, Rodlescia Sneed and Sheldon Cohen of Carnegie Mellon University in the United States reported, in a study published in 2013 in the journal Psychology and Aging, that adults over fifty who had volunteered at least two hundred hours in the past year had a significantly lower risk of later developing high blood pressure.

Brothers and sisters, this isn’t saying we serve for the sake of our health. It simply confirms once again what Scripture said long ago: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35) When God made us, he wrote “giving out brings greater joy” into our design.

Mother Teresa is generally credited with saying, “Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love.” This is exactly the attitude of grace — not because I am great, but because the Lord’s love is great.

A 321 insight: not that I can, but that the Lord can

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

“Not that I can, but that the Lord can” — these few words say everything about both core values.

“Not that I can” — this is letting Jesus be King. Only one can sit on the throne. When I say, “I can”, I climb onto a seat that doesn’t belong to me; that is exactly what 321 calls pride: leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. Humility, on the other hand, is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

“But that the Lord can” — this is letting Jesus receive all the glory. If our serving makes people see my competence, my eloquence, my sacrifice, then we’ve stolen the glory; if our serving makes people see the Lord’s grace, the Lord’s faithfulness, the Lord’s power, that is the very purpose of serving.

The secret of Paul’s whole life lies in that one sentence: “Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”

So please remember:

Not that I can, but that the Lord can.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From “I Can’t” to “I’m Willing”
sections.html:
Let’s put everything we’ve seen today back into the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45) The Lord is the ruler of the universe, yet he took a towel, wrapped it round his waist, crouched down and washed his disciples’ feet, and said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” (John 13:14) Who can serve? First look at the Lord who serves us.

The Bible is my standard. It isn’t my feelings that say whether I’m qualified, nor other people’s opinions that say whether I’m up to it, but what God’s word says. And God’s word says: the willing can all serve.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. We don’t grit our teeth in our own strength; we rely on the power of the Holy Spirit. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll have strength; rely on the brain and yourself, and all you’ll have left is anxiety.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King — King over my schedule, King over my sense of competence, King over my weakness.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when the serving is done, the applause goes to him; when it fails, we still trust him.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. One person’s serving is a point; a group serving together is a system. God has never set out to make a few stars; God is building his body.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

“I’m not good enough”, “I don’t have the gift”, “I don’t have the time” — brothers and sisters, all three sentences have the same subject: “I”.

The self-centred always have their eyes fixed on themselves: my level, my face, my schedule, my gains and losses. So the more they look, the less they dare to move.

The selfless have their eyes fixed on the Lord: the Lord sends, and I go; the Lord provides, and I have; the Lord values it, and I offer it.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Interestingly, “I’m not good enough” sounds very humble, but at its core it is still pride — because it is still calculating about the self, still insisting on being good enough before daring to step out. True humility isn’t thinking less of yourself; it’s not thinking about yourself. It isn’t feeling that you can’t; it’s knowing that the Lord can.

The Fivefold Change and the Shift in Perspective

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice that ministry comes last. So we don’t start by pushing people into serving roles; we first let the mindset change — when someone truly believes that “the willing can all serve”, their life begins to loosen, their daily living begins to adjust, their relationships begin to be filled with God’s love, and ministry naturally grows out of it.

The shift in perspective happens here too: from man’s perspective to God’s — man says, “I’m not worthy”; God says, “My grace is sufficient for you”; from earthly to heavenly — earth calculates gains and losses, heaven counts faithfulness; from temporary to eternal — a cup of cold water offered today will never lose its reward; from worldly to godly — the world looks at the size of the gift, God looks at whether the heart is willing.

920 and 235

The 920 practice: start with the one “2” beside you. You needn’t wait for the church to advertise a vacancy; your family, your colleagues, your neighbours are the ones you serve. Living a selfless life towards them and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — that is the most solid serving there is.

235 relationships: become a “2” with a brother or sister who is likewise selfless, supporting each other and starting out together; establish a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that the experienced lead those just starting out; and finally become a “5” — apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4:11) — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together.

Brothers and sisters, no one serves alone. If you’re afraid to take the first step, find a “2” and take it together.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them into practice one by one.

Practice 1: Practise taking the first step

Don’t wait until you’re ready to begin. Begin today: do one small act of service, help one person. Let action bring growth.

Information: first let the truth into your mind. Commit this sentence to memory — not knowing first and then doing; doing first and then knowing. God’s order is first sending, then equipping (Exodus 4:12).

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this sentence from your brain to your heart, so that you “see” it for yourself. You might pray like this: Lord, open my eyes, and let me see that you have never once despised my inadequacy; you are only waiting for my willingness.

Conviction: make a decision. Not “I’ll give it a try”, but “I believe God can use me right now.” Conviction is standing on God’s word before you’ve seen the outcome.

Implementation: this week, do one act of service so small it couldn’t be smaller. Pour a glass of water, wipe down a chair, send a message to say hello, pray for someone for five minutes, see an elderly member home. “Indeed, who despises the day of small things?” (Zechariah 4:10) The Lord says, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” (Luke 16:10)

Evaluation: when you’ve done it, be still for three minutes and ask yourself: What was I thinking about while I did it? Was I thinking about being seen, or about that person? Did I get upset because I didn’t do it well? Getting upset usually means I’m still looking at myself.

Correction: hand what you’ve discovered over to the Lord, adjust your motives, adjust your approach — but don’t give up. A child who falls off doesn’t stop learning to ride; he picks up the bike and rides again.

Repetition: don’t do it just once. Set a rhythm — at least one thing every week. Only repetition turns an “event” into “life”.

Multiplication: find a brother or sister who is just as afraid to step out, and invite them to do it with you. You’ll go from being someone who is equipped to someone who equips others. That is the “3” of 235.

Practice 2: Practise handing your limits to God

Place what you have — your time, your abilities, your resources — in God’s hands, and let God use it and enlarge it.

Information: God is the God who makes something from nothing and much from little (Psalm 33:9). Five loaves were handed over, and five thousand were fed (Matthew 14:19–21).

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you truly see what the “five loaves” in your own hands are. Don’t belittle them. A skill of yours, a free slot in your week, a car, a kitchen, a pair of ears willing to listen — they are all loaves.

Conviction: believe that “what is handed over doesn’t become less; it only becomes more.” This is the exact opposite of the world’s arithmetic, so it takes faith.

Implementation: this week, hand over one specific thing. It could be a fixed fifteen minutes each day to intercede for others; it could be a monthly offering; it could be opening up your skill for the church or your neighbours to use. As you hand it over, learn to say what the disciples said: Lord, take it — it’s yours.

Evaluation: check whether you’re handing it over with one hand and taking it back with the other. After handing it over, do you keep watching to see whether it’s being used properly?

Correction: if you find you’re still calculating gains and losses, come back to the cross and say to the Lord again: Yet not I, but your grace (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Repetition: keep on handing it over. Faith is like a muscle: hand it over once and it’s a moment of being moved; hand it over a hundred times and it’s life.

Multiplication: tell the story of your own “five loaves and two fish” — give your testimony. Your testimony will become someone else’s courage to step out.

Practice 3: Practise adjusting your priorities

Examine your life: is God in first place? Deliberately set aside time to draw near to God and to serve others. Let your life return to the right order.

Information: the Lord says, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) Get the order right, and God takes care of the rest.

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you see your real priorities. The method is very simple — lay out how you spent the past seven days. Where your time has gone, there your heart is.

Conviction: decide to believe that “giving my best time to God won’t cost me anything; I can only gain.”

Implementation: do two things this week. First, set a fixed time every day for morning devotion and prayer, write it in your diary, and treat it like an important meeting. Second, reserve a fixed slot in your diary for “serving others”. Whatever isn’t scheduled never happens.

Evaluation: at the weekend, look back and ask yourself: Where did I rank God this week? Is there something I keep saying matters, yet never seem to have time for?

Correction: don’t change too much at once. First protect the smallest, most sustainable unit — even if it’s just ten minutes a day. A small habit you can keep up beats a grand plan that collapses after three days.

Repetition: let it become the rhythm of your life, like eating and sleeping.

Multiplication: agree with a family member or your spiritual companion to remind each other and report back to each other. One person easily slackens; two people go a long way.

A Gentle Reminder: What is holding you back?

The lesson reminds us that what holds you back from serving is not ability, but three things: fear, limits and self-centredness.

Fear. Fear of not doing it well, fear of being judged, fear that once you commit you’ll never get out of it. Scripture says, “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.” (1 John 4:18) It isn’t that you stop being afraid first and then love; it’s that in love, fear is cast out.

Limits. These are the lines we draw for ourselves: “That isn’t my gift”, “Someone with my personality isn’t suited to it”, “I’m too old”, “I’m too young”. These lines weren’t drawn by God; we drew them. God says, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child.’” (Jeremiah 1:7)

Self-centredness. This is the deepest layer. At the core of fear is being afraid that “I” will lose face; at the core of limits is protecting “my” comfort. So 321 is right: the self-centred life is the root of every problem.

Rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll shrink back; rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll step out.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please hand these three things over to the Lord one by one, by name. Don’t just say vaguely, “Lord, please help me”; say specifically: Lord, this is what I’m afraid of; Lord, this is the line I’ve drawn for myself; Lord, this is the part of me I want to protect. What we name and hand over, God can take away from us, one thing at a time.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: The Willing
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we started with.

Who can serve?

Not the most capable. If it were, Moses would be out, because he was slow of speech and of a slow tongue.

Not those with the most time. If it were, Paul would be out, because he’d been in prison, was always on the road, and still had to make tents.

Not the most gifted. If it were, the boy who offered the five loaves would be out, because all he had was a lunch of barley bread.

Then who?

The willing.

“Your people offer themselves willingly in the day of your power, in holy array.” (Psalm 110:3) What God wants has always been a willing heart.

When you are willing, God goes to work. When you step out, God adds to you.

For “it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). Even that “willingness” is something God put in your heart first. So if this morning there’s even a little stirring in your heart, even a little desire — that isn’t just your emotions; that is God’s call.

“I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here I am. Send me!’” (Isaiah 6:8)

When Isaiah said this, he had only just seen that he was “a man of unclean lips”, and his mouth had only just been touched by a live coal from the altar. He didn’t go after becoming worthy; he went after being touched by grace.

Brothers and sisters, today, let Jesus reign as King in your life; today, pass the five loaves in your hands over to him; today, put him back in first place in your diary. And then you’ll see with your own eyes: not enough becomes more than enough, the limited becomes limitless, the ordinary becomes glorious.

This is — a life of serving in grace.

All glory to our Lord Jesus Christ.

blog.title: Who Can Serve? Not the Strongest, but the Willing

blocks.x: Morning Devotion 321, Lesson 160: “Who Can Serve?”

The Sunday service ends, and the pastor stands at the front and says, “Next month we’re starting a new area of service, and we need a few brothers and sisters. If you’re willing, please raise your hand.”
What follows is a very curious silence. Suddenly everyone’s eyes are very busy — some look down at the bulletin, some sort out their bags, some study their own shoes intently.
It isn’t that they don’t love the Lord. In those few short seconds, a voice is speaking in each person’s heart: I’m not good enough yet; I don’t have the gift; I don’t have the time.
These three sentences sound humble, honest, perfectly reasonable. Yet none of them is really a statement of fact; each is a stronghold of mindset.
God has never asked, “Are you able?”
The words Isaiah heard in the temple were not “Who is able to go for me?” but “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6:8)
“Will go” — that is willingness.
God’s call-up has never been a checklist of abilities, but an invitation to the heart. The question has never been “Are you able?” but “Are you willing?”

Look at the people God used. Moses said, “I am slow of speech”, yet God said, “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth” (Exodus 4:12) — notice the order: first go, then the gift. Gideon said he was the least in his father’s house; Jeremiah said he was only a child. The first thing every one of those called said was, “I can’t”; and God’s answer was never “Yes, you can”, but “I will be with you.”

The spiritual principle is the exact opposite of common sense: not knowing first and then doing, but doing first and then knowing. It’s like learning to ride a bicycle — you could memorise every formula of the mechanics and still not be able to ride; a six-year-old falls twice, and twenty minutes later he can ride, and never forgets it as long as he lives. The theory of self-efficacy put forward by the psychologist Albert Bandura in 1977 shows that the most powerful source of people’s confidence that “I can do this” is “mastery experience” — actually getting something done yourself.
Confidence isn’t something you wait for; confidence is something you get by doing.
The Key to the Five Loaves Is Not the Bread, but Handing It Over
The disciples said, “We only have here five loaves and two fish.” (Matthew 14:17)
Listen to that word “only”. I only have a little time. I only have a little ability. I can’t do anything — I can only pray.
Jesus said just one very short thing: “Bring them here to me.” In the end five thousand were fed, and there were still twelve baskets left over.

The decisive action of the whole miracle lies not in the loaves, not in the fish, not in the disciples’ ability, but in that act of handing over. We often think it has to become more before we hand it over; in fact, first we hand it over, and then it becomes more. The bread multiplied only after it was broken; if it had never been broken, it would have stayed five loaves for ever.

Our God is the God who “spoke, and it was done; commanded, and it stood firm” (Psalm 33:9). When you say, “I don’t have the gift”, you are really saying to a God who speaks things into being: this is something you can’t do.
It Isn’t That You Have No Time; You Haven’t Yet Put Him First

Time is the fairest thing there is: rich or poor, high or low, everyone has twenty-four hours in a day. So “I don’t have time”, put accurately, means: “This hasn’t yet made it to the front of my priorities.” If your child has a 40-degree fever, however busy you are, you’ll take time off. We never make time for things because we’re free; we make time for things because they’re important.
Even the busiest people make time for the people who matter.

What’s more, serving isn’t squeezing one more slot into an already full schedule. Scripture says, “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31) If even eating and drinking can glorify God, then work, family and daily living can all be serving. What makes something serving isn’t what the thing is, but who it’s done for.
Serving isn’t doing one more thing; it’s doing everything with God’s heart.

Last, and most important of all: serving is grace, not a burden. Paul says, “Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) Even the ability to serve is God’s gift, so there’s nothing to boast of, only thanks to give. When we understand this, we stop comparing, stop complaining and stop being lazy; instead we treasure it and seize the opportunity. Because being able to serve is itself a blessing.

The light of 321 says it clearly: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; not that I can, but that the Lord can. Rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll shrink back; rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll step out. Today, do one small act of service, and pass the five loaves in your hands over to him.
Who can serve? Not the most capable, not those with the most time, not the most gifted, but the willing.
When you are willing, God goes to work. When you step out, God adds to you. This is a life of serving in grace.
Reflection: “I’m not good enough, I don’t have the gift, I don’t have the time” — which of these comes up most often in your heart? This week, what is the small step you are willing to take?
