Understanding without Spirit becomes knowledge
Healthy service: the Spirit plus God’s word
Truth in one hand, power in the other
• Lesson point: Spirit without Understanding loses its foundation; Understanding without Spirit becomes mere knowledge.
• Warn of two distortions: stressing only experience drifts from the true way; stressing only doctrine is correct but cold.
• Truly healthy service: the power of the Holy Spirit plus the word of God.
• Picture: a sailing boat needs wind, and it needs a rudder.

brief21.title: Jesus Is the Best Example
notes: “He whom God has sent speaks the words of God”
“God gives the Spirit without measure”
(John 3:34)
Preaching the gospel and healing (Matthew 9:35)
• John 3:34 — “speaks the words of God” is truth; “the Spirit without measure” is power.
• In the Lord Jesus, truth and power are perfectly one.
• Matthew 9:35 — teaching and preaching are the word; healing every disease is power.
• Stress: truth in one hand, power in the other, both hands working together.

brief21.title: So It Was with the Apostles
notes: At Pentecost the Spirit came; Peter stood to preach
His whole sermon quoted the Old Testament
“Those who gladly received his word were baptized”
About three thousand added that day (Acts 2:41)
• Acts 2:14 — Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice.
• Peter’s sermon is almost entirely Old Testament quotation: Joel, Psalm 16, Psalm 110.
• Acts 2:41 — “those who gladly received his word were baptized”; about three thousand were added that day.
• Key: they weren’t baptised because they saw tongues of fire, but because they received his word.

brief21.title: The Spirit Is Electricity; the Bible Is Wiring
notes: Electricity without wiring: a flash and gone
Wiring without electricity: just copper
321 insight:
The Spirit lets us experience God; Understanding, know him
• Picture: electricity and wiring; electricity without wiring is a lightning strike, wiring without electricity is scrap copper.
• Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion: Scripture is like a pair of spectacles that brings God’s works into view.
• Scientific analogy: seeing needs light and focus; the Spirit is the light, the Bible the focus.
• 321 insight: the Spirit lets people experience God, Understanding lets people know God; neither can do without the other.
• Reminder: the Holy Spirit never leads anyone to go against Scripture.

brief21.title: 2. From the Letter to Revelation
notes: Many read the Bible and stop at the letter
Every word recognised, yet the heart untouched
“Man shall not live by bread alone,
but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth”
• Lesson point: many people read the Bible and stop at the letter.
• Describe stopping at the letter: every word recognised, reading plan ticked, yet not one sentence left in the heart.
• Matthew 4:4, “that proceeds out of God’s mouth”: the original rhema means a spoken word.
• God’s word is not a fossil lying on paper, but a living word carrying breath.

brief21.title: The Word of God Is Living
notes: “The word of God is living and active”
(Hebrews 4:12)
“Living”: in the original, simply alive
“Active”: in the original, at work right now
• Quote Hebrews 4:12 in full, stressing piercing, dividing and discerning.
• Original words: living is zōn (alive); active is energēs (giving off energy right now).
• The issue isn’t that the word lacks power, but whether it has entered into me.
• Application: when reading, ask that God’s word pierce the thoughts and intentions of my heart.

brief21.title: Three Marks of Understanding
notes: The same passage suddenly makes sense
The same sentence suddenly pierces the heart
The same truth becomes the power of life
“He opened their minds” (Luke 24:45)
• Bring out the lesson’s three marks one by one: it makes sense, it pierces, it becomes power.
• Luke 24:32 — weren’t our hearts burning within us while he opened the Scriptures to us?
• Luke 24:45 — Jesus opened their minds; the original dianoigō means to open up what was tightly shut.
• Acts 8:30–31 — the eunuch said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?”
• Reading is the letter; understanding is revelation.

brief21.title: The Letter Is Raw Rice; Revelation Is Cooked
notes: Raw rice starch is hard for us to digest
Add water and heat, and it can be absorbed
Without understanding, hard to digest; with it, growth
Mindset, life and daily living change
• The lesson’s picture: the letter is like raw rice; revelation is like cooked rice.
• Scientific support: raw rice starch is tightly crystalline and must be heated with water to about 60–80°C to gelatinise before it digests easily.
• Helander and Fändriks (2014): the absorptive surface of the small intestine is about 30 square metres.
• 321 insight: without understanding, hard to digest; with understanding, able to grow.
• The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; Romans 12:2 — transformed by the renewing of your mind.

brief21.title: 3. Understanding Is Not by Cleverness
notes: Understanding comes not by cleverness but by humility
“You hid these things from the wise
and understanding, and revealed them to infants”
(Matthew 11:25) “Revealed”: revelation
• Lesson point: understanding comes not by cleverness but by humility.
• Matthew 11:25 — “revealed” is apokalyptō, revelation; “infants” is nēpios.
• God gives revelation not to those who think they understand, but to those who admit they don’t.
• 321 core: pride is leaving our originally intended position to replace God; humility is returning to it and letting God be God.

brief21.title: Why the Pharisees Didn’t Understand
notes: “Seeing they may see, and not perceive;
hearing they may hear, and not understand” (Mark 4:12)
Because of pride, because they thought they knew
The humble get revelation; the proud, knowledge
• Mark 4:12 — eyes fine, ears fine, minds fine; what was broken was the heart.
• Dunning and Kruger’s 1999 study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
• Leary and colleagues (2017): the intellectually humble weigh evidence better and are willing to revise.
• 1 Corinthians 2:14 — the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit.
• Psalm 119:18 — Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.

brief21.title: Meditate Repeatedly, Chew It Day and Night
notes: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth,
but you shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8)
“Meditate”: to recite over and over in a low voice
Like a tree sending roots into streams (Psalm 1:2–3)
• The setting of Joshua 1:8: Joshua taking up the baton, about to cross the Jordan.
• “Meditate” is the Hebrew hagah, basically meaning to recite in a low voice, to murmur to oneself.
• Isaiah 31:4 uses the same word for the low growl of a lion over its prey.
• Psalm 1:2–3 — like a tree planted by streams of water; a tree doesn’t go looking for water, it sends its roots into it.
• Ebbinghaus (1885): without review, only about a third remains after a day.

brief21.title: Five Steps to Understanding
notes: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do
Revelation deepens, faith grows
and life changes
Not people pushing you, but God’s word driving you
• Explain the five steps: See (Acts 17:11, examining daily), Listen (Nehemiah 8:8, giving the sense).
• Think: Cepeda and colleagues’ 2006 meta-analysis showed spaced repetition beats one-off study.
• Speak: Fiorella and Mayer (2013) — those who teach others understand more deeply.
• Do: James 1:22, be doers of the word, not only hearers; Matthew 13:23, hears the word, understands it, bears fruit.
• Jeremiah 20:9 and Colossians 1:29 — it isn’t you holding on; it is God’s word and power at work within you.

brief21.title: Practices for Daily Living (1)
notes: Don’t just read; seek revelation every day
Write down one sentence God speaks to you today
Meditate repeatedly; carry it all day
Share what you received with one person
• Practice 1 matches “from Information to Revelation”: change the goal from finishing to hearing.
• Stress writing it down — an admission that this sentence is what God has said to me today.
• Practice 2 matches “Conviction” and “Repetition”: think it over on the commute, at the red light, before sleep.
• Practice 3 matches “Multiplication”: when spoken, the word moves from brain to mouth, then back down into the heart.

brief21.title: Practices for Daily Living (2)
notes: Deliberately live out one truth
Before reading, ask the Spirit to open you
Eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction,
Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
• Practice 4 matches “Implementation, Evaluation, Correction”: evaluate after doing; correct where you got stuck.
• 1 Timothy 4:15 — be diligent in these things, give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all.
• Practice 5 is the foundation of the other four: before reading, bow for thirty seconds and ask the Spirit to open you.
• Recite all eight stages, reminding them the last stage is Multiplication.

brief21.title: Summing Up the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard
Humility overcomes pride; selflessness, Satan
Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry
920: live selflessly; 235: share and multiply
• The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; this lesson is the second.
• Humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan; Galatians 2:20 — no longer I, but Christ lives in me.
• The fivefold change begins with the mindset; perspective shifts from man’s, earthly, temporary to God’s, heavenly, eternal.
• 920: live selflessly before every “2”, bearing the ninefold fruit.
• 235: 2 spiritual companions, 3 spiritual parents and children, 5 fivefold ministry team — establishing God’s system.

brief21.title: Closing and Call
notes: Spirit alone drifts; add Understanding, and it is steady
God’s word is no longer a book,
but the power of your life
Not you holding up service, but the word holding you
• Return to the sailing boat: however strong the wind, without a rudder it only spins in circles.
• Jeremiah 15:16 — your words were found, and I ate them.
• 1 Thessalonians 2:13 — it is in truth the word of God, which also works in you who believe.
• Three calls: from finishing to hearing; kneel before God’s word; live it out and pass it on.
• The destination: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Lord, open my eyes, open my heart and mind
Bring me from the letter into revelation
From knowledge into life, living out your word
May Jesus be King and receive all the glory
• Lead the brothers and sisters in praying together, slowly, leaving pauses.
• Follow the lesson’s declaration: not only reading your word, but understanding and living it out.
• Intercede for humility: ask the Lord to take away the veil over our hearts.
• Blessing: may God’s word be like fire within you, holding up your service and making it last.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we read Lesson 164 together, titled “From the Letter into Revelation” — the second station on the Path of Serving: Understanding. The second of the Three Foundations is: the Bible is my standard. Our theme verse is 2 Corinthians 3:6: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” I often compare serving to a sailing boat. The Holy Spirit is the wind; the Bible is the rudder. Wind without a rudder, and the boat drifts; wind and a rudder together, and the boat reaches the shore.

Brothers and sisters, I want to ask a question that may sting a little. How many years have you believed in the Lord? How many times have you read the Bible through? How many hundreds of sermons have you heard? We carry more knowledge inside us than any generation before. But has our life really changed? I know a brother who never lost a Bible quiz, yet his wife said with tears, “He understands everything — except how to say one gentle word to me.” Where does the problem lie? The lesson says: one key thing is missing — understanding. Information cannot change a life; only revelation can change a life.

Paul wrote this verse around AD 56, to the church in Corinth. At the time, some people were carrying letters of commendation and questioning Paul’s credentials. How did Paul answer? He said: you are our letter, written not on tablets of stone, but on tablets that are hearts of flesh. Brothers and sisters, in the original, “letter” means a written code, and “Spirit” is simply the Spirit. A code carved on stone can only condemn; only when the Holy Spirit writes on the tablet of the heart can a person live.

The first teaching: Spirit and Understanding must be in balance. The lesson says that Spirit without Understanding loses its foundation, and Understanding without Spirit turns into mere knowledge. Stress only experience, and you drift from the true way; stress only doctrine, and you end up correct but cold. What is the right pattern? John 3:34 says, “For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure.” Speaking the words of God is truth; giving the Spirit is power. In Jesus, truth and power are perfectly one.

So Matthew 9:35 says that Jesus went about “preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.” Truth in one hand, power in the other. The apostles were the same. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down, Peter stood up and preached, and nearly his whole sermon was quotation from the Old Testament. And the result? “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” Brothers and sisters, not power alone, and not preaching alone, but the Holy Spirit and the word of God at work together. The Spirit lets people experience God; Understanding lets people know God.

The second teaching: from the letter to revelation. What does it mean to stop at the letter? It means we recognise every word and have ticked off the reading plan, yet not one sentence has stayed in our hearts. The Lord Jesus said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.” What proceeds out of God’s mouth is a living word. Hebrews 4:12 says, “For the word of God is living and active.” In the original, that means: alive, and at work right now. The question has never been whether the word has power, but whether it has entered into us.

The lesson uses a very good picture: the letter is like raw rice, uncooked; revelation is like cooked rice that can be eaten. Scientifically, this is very accurate. The starch in raw rice is tightly packed, and we can barely digest it; only when water is added and it is heated does the starch loosen so the body can absorb it. The same verse, without prayer and without the Holy Spirit, is just hard information. The 321 insight says: without understanding, hard to digest; with understanding, able to grow. And when truth becomes revelation, the mindset changes, the life changes, and daily living changes.

The third teaching: how do we gain understanding? The lesson says: not by cleverness, but by humility. The Lord Jesus said, “You hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.” In the original, “revealed” is the very word for “revelation”. Why did the Pharisees, who had read so much Scripture, fail to understand? Because of pride, because they assumed they already understood. In 1999 Dunning and Kruger’s research also found that the least competent people are the most likely to overestimate themselves. Brothers and sisters, the proud receive knowledge; the humble receive revelation.

The second key is repeated meditation. Joshua 1:8 says, “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night.” The Hebrew word for “meditate” basically means to recite over and over in a low voice, like a lion standing over its food and refusing to let go. The process of understanding has five steps: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. When you meditate repeatedly, open your mouth and share, and actually put it into practice, revelation will deepen, faith will grow, and life will change. And then you will discover: it is not people pushing you to serve; it is God’s word within you that drives you.

Let’s look at today’s practices — five in all. First, each day when you read the Bible, ask: Lord, what do you want to say to me today? Write down one sentence. Second, meditate on that sentence again and again all day. Third, open your mouth and share what you have received with one person. Fourth, deliberately live out one truth. Fifth, pray before you read, asking the Holy Spirit to open you up. These five correspond exactly to the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Brothers and sisters, the one most easily skipped is Repetition.

The lesson’s closing words say: if the Path of Serving has only “Spirit”, it drifts; add “Understanding”, and it becomes steady. However strong the wind, without a rudder the boat only spins in circles. When you enter into Understanding, God’s word is no longer just a book; it is the power of your life. You are no longer just doing service; you are living out the truth. And in the end you will discover a truth that brings rest: it is not you holding up your service; it is God’s word within you holding you up. As Paul says, it is in truth the word of God, which also works in you who believe.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I declare: I will not only read your word; I will understand your word and live out your word. May your Holy Spirit open me up, so that I move from the letter into revelation, from knowledge into life. Give me a humble heart, so that I meditate on your word day and night and live it out. Take away the veil over my heart, and give my service a foundation and power. May Jesus reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we read Lesson 164 together, titled “From the Letter into Revelation”. 321 often says the Path of Serving has five stations: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. In the last lesson we talked about “Spirit”; today we take a step forward into the second station, Understanding — which is the second of the Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard. Our theme verse is 2 Corinthians 3:6: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” And “the Spirit” here may also be read as “the Holy Spirit”.

Brothers and sisters, let me begin with a few questions that may sting a little. How many years have you believed in the Lord? How many times have you read the Bible through? How many hundreds of sermons have you heard? Getting hold of Bible information has never been so easy. But I have to ask, honestly, one more question: after all these years, has our life really changed? I know a brother who had been in the church for over twenty years and almost never lost a Bible quiz. Yet his wife said privately, with tears in her eyes, “He understands everything — except how to say one gentle word to me.” Brothers and sisters, where does the problem really lie?

The lesson puts its finger right on it: one key thing is missing — there is no “understanding”. If truth stays only in the head, it is information; when truth enters the heart, it becomes revelation. Information is what someone else tells you; revelation is what God himself says to you. Information means you know one more thing; revelation makes you a new creation. That’s why 321 says: information cannot change a life; only revelation can change a life. Brothers and sisters, please hold this sentence in your heart; this morning we are going to walk into it together.

Let’s look at the background first. The author is the apostle Paul, generally thought to have written around AD 56, on his way to Macedonia, to the church in Corinth that he himself had planted. At the time a group of self-styled apostles had come into the church carrying letters of recommendation and questioning Paul, saying he had no letters of commendation and was unimpressive in person. How did Paul answer? He said: you are our letter, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh. Brothers and sisters, remember this contrast: tablets of stone and tablets of the heart. A code carved on stone can only condemn; only when the Holy Spirit writes on the tablet of the heart can a person live.

Now to the first teaching: the balance of Spirit and Understanding. The lesson says that Spirit without Understanding loses its foundation, and Understanding without Spirit turns into mere knowledge. In church history we have seen far too many distortions. Some stress only experience, promptings and gifts but make light of the Bible; they burn hot for a season and a few years later have drifted from the true way. Others stress only doctrine, system and rigour but refuse the work of the Holy Spirit; they end up correct but cold, like a very neatly built tomb. What is truly healthy service? It is the power of the Holy Spirit together with the word of God.

What, then, is the right pattern? The answer is Jesus. John 3:34 says, “For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God; for God gives the Spirit without measure.” See how perfect the structure is: speaking the words of God is truth; giving the Spirit without measure is power. So Matthew 9:35 records that he went about “preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.” In one hand he held the truth, in the other he carried power, and both hands worked together.

The apostles did the same. On the day of Pentecost the Holy Spirit came down and the disciples spoke in other languages — that was a display of power. But what happened next? Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice and preached, and nearly his whole sermon was quotation from the Old Testament: Joel, Psalm 16, Psalm 110. And the result? “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.” Please notice especially: the three thousand were not baptised because they saw tongues of fire; it was those who received his word who were baptised.

I often use a picture: the Holy Spirit is like electricity, and the Bible is like the wiring. Electricity without wiring is a lightning strike — a flash and it’s gone; wiring without electricity is just a heap of useless copper. But when the current runs through the wires, the lights come on. John Calvin said in his Institutes of the Christian Religion that our eyes are dim, and Scripture is like a pair of spectacles: put them on, and the works of God come clearly into view. To see anything, we need two things: light, and focus. The Holy Spirit is the light; the Bible is the focus. The 321 insight says: the Spirit lets people experience God, Understanding lets people know God, and neither can do without the other.

The second teaching: from the letter to revelation. The lesson says that many people read the Bible and stop at the letter. What does it mean to stop at the letter? It means the eyes have run over the page, we recognise every word, we have finished the passage, we have ticked off the reading plan — yet not one sentence has stayed in our hearts. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.” Notice the words “that proceeds out of God’s mouth”. God’s word is not a fossil lying on paper; it is a word spoken from God’s mouth right now, carrying breath and carrying life.

The writer of Hebrews says: “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” “Living” in the original simply means “alive”; “active” means at work, giving off energy right now — the English word “energy” comes from it. Brothers and sisters, the question has never been whether God’s word has power, but whether it has entered into us.

When the Holy Spirit opens you up, the lesson says you will experience three things: the same passage of Scripture suddenly makes sense; the same sentence suddenly pierces the heart; the same truth becomes the power of life. That is Understanding. The two disciples on the road to Emmaus said to each other afterwards, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” Why were their hearts burning that day? Because “he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.” Then there was the Ethiopian eunuch, reading Isaiah. Philip asked him, “Do you understand what you are reading?” He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” Brothers and sisters, reading is the letter; understanding is revelation.

The lesson uses a very down-to-earth picture: the letter is like raw rice, uncooked; revelation is like cooked rice that can be eaten. Scientifically, this is remarkably accurate. The starch in raw rice is packed in a tight crystalline structure that the body’s amylase can barely touch; only when water is added and it is heated to around 60 to 80 degrees Celsius does the starch gelatinise, so that digestive enzymes can get in. The same grain of rice means something utterly different cooked or uncooked. Brothers and sisters, when we read the Bible, do we give God’s word that kind of cooking? The 321 insight says: without understanding, hard to digest; with understanding, able to grow. When truth becomes revelation, the mindset changes, the life changes, and daily living changes.

The third teaching: how do we gain understanding? The lesson says understanding comes not by cleverness but by humility. Our easiest mistake is to think that understanding is the preserve of clever people. But what did the Lord Jesus say? “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants.” In the original, “revealed” is the very word for “revelation”, and “infants” means little children not yet able to speak. The ones to whom God gives revelation are not those who think they understand, but those who admit they don’t.

So why did the Pharisees, who had read so much Scripture, fail to understand? The Lord Jesus quoted Isaiah: “seeing they may see, and not perceive; and hearing they may hear, and not understand.” Their eyes were fine, their ears were fine, their minds were fine; what was broken was the heart — because of pride, because they assumed they already understood. In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University found that the least competent people tend to overestimate themselves the most; and in 2017 research by Mark Leary and colleagues showed that people with intellectual humility are better at weighing evidence and more willing to revise their views. So before every time we read the Bible, let us first pray: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law.”

The second key is repeated meditation. Before Joshua took up the baton and crossed the Jordan, God said to him: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it.” God didn’t say, “Win more battles”; God said: meditate on my word day and night. The Hebrew word for “meditate” basically means to recite in a low voice, to murmur to oneself; it is even used of the low growl of a lion standing over its prey. So meditating day and night is not sitting and staring into space; it is keeping God’s word in our mouths and chewing it over and over. Psalm 1 uses the same word: such a person is like a tree planted by streams of water. A tree doesn’t run off to look for water; a tree sends its roots down into the water.

The lesson gives us a very clear process: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. See is examining the Scriptures daily, like the Bereans. Listen is growing still and asking: Lord, what do you want to say to me today? Think is repetition — in 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus’s memory experiments found that without review, only about a third is remembered after one day. Speak is opening your mouth to share — in 2013 Logan Fiorella and Richard Mayer’s research showed that people preparing to teach others understood and retained the material markedly better. Do is living it out — James says: be doers of the word, and not only hearers. When you meditate repeatedly, share and put it into practice, revelation will deepen, faith will grow and life will change. And in the end you will discover: it is not people pushing you to serve; it is God’s word within you that drives you.

Brothers and sisters, let’s now look at the lesson’s five practices. First, don’t just read the Bible; seek revelation every day. Don’t rush to finish; ask, Lord, what do you want to say to me today? Then write down one sentence. Please change the goal of your Bible reading from “finishing” to “hearing”. Second, meditate repeatedly. Today, choose one verse and carry it with you all day: think it over on your commute, again at the red light, and meditate on it once more before you sleep. Third, open your mouth and share. Today, share what you have received with one person. When you say it, it moves from your brain to your mouth, and then from your mouth back down into your heart.

Fourth, take real action and let the truth become life. Today, deliberately live out one truth, then evaluate: did I live it out today? Where did I get stuck? Then correct it, and go again tomorrow. Fifth, stay humble. Before you open the Bible, bow your head for thirty seconds and say, “Lord, please open my eyes; I need you to teach me.” Brothers and sisters, these five practices correspond exactly to the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. The stage most often skipped is Repetition.

Let’s draw the main threads of 321 together. The second of the Three Foundations is: the Bible is my standard. A standard is not a reference book; it is a measuring rule — when my feelings conflict with the Bible, I adjust my feelings. That is letting God be God. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan: pride is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place; humility is returning to our originally intended position, letting man be man and letting God be God. The fivefold change begins with the mindset: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Our perspective has to move house too: from man’s to God’s, from the temporary to the eternal. 920 is living selflessly before every “2”, bearing the ninefold fruit of the Spirit; 235 is sharing with spiritual companions, building spiritual parents and children, and becoming a fivefold-ministry team. If the revelation you have received is not passed on to the next person, the cycle is not yet complete.

The lesson’s closing words are beautiful: if the Path of Serving has only “Spirit”, it drifts; add “Understanding”, and it becomes steady. Come back to that sailing boat: however fierce the wind, without a rudder the boat only spins in circles; but when the helmsman grips the tiller, that same wind becomes the force that drives you forward. When you truly enter into Understanding, two things will happen. First, God’s word is no longer a book; it is the power of your life. Jeremiah says, “Your words were found, and I ate them.” He didn’t just read these words; he ate them. Second, you are no longer just doing service; you are living out the truth. And in the end you will discover: it is not you holding up your service; it is God’s word within you holding you up.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I declare: I will not only read your word; I will understand your word and live out your word. May your Holy Spirit open me up, so that I move from the letter into revelation, from knowledge into life. Forgive me for so often reading your word with my head while refusing to listen with my heart to what you say; forgive me for assuming I already understood. Today I bring my pride before you; please take away the veil over my heart. Give me a humble heart, so that I meditate on your word day and night and live it out. May your word be like a burning fire within me, holding me up and driving me on. May Jesus reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

sections.heading: Introduction: Without Life, Service Has No Influence
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to picture two scenes in your heart.

The first: the night sky on Lunar New Year’s Eve. A firework shoots upward — bang! — and the whole sky bursts into golden flowers, while tens of thousands of people below look up at once and gasp, “Wow!” But three seconds later? The light has scattered, the smoke has thinned, and the sky is pitch black again, as though nothing had ever happened.

The second: the mouth of the stove in an old family home out in the countryside. A lump of charcoal, glowing quietly red. It doesn’t dazzle anyone, it draws no gasps, and it will never make it into a single photograph. Yet slowly the pot of water comes to the boil, slowly the whole room full of people grows warm, a whole night passes, the dawn comes — and when you brush aside the ash, it is still glowing red.

Brothers and sisters, I want to ask you a question, and I ask it of myself too: is our service a firework, or a charcoal fire?

I have seen far too much firework service in the church. A special conference: tears flow, decision cards are filled in, the prayer is so fervent it seems about to lift the roof off, and everyone says, “This time it’s different!” Yet three months later the people have disappeared; six months later, no one can even remember what moved them in the first place.

I have also seen charcoal-fire service. There was a sister who, for twenty years without a break, came to church an hour early every Lord’s Day. She boiled the water, straightened the chairs and wiped the floor of the children’s Sunday school room. She couldn’t preach; her testimony was over in three minutes. Yet half the people in that church, in the very hardest stretch of their lives, were held up by a bowl of noodles she had cooked, a pair of hands she had held, an afternoon she had sat with them in silence.

Why is some service like fireworks, and some like a charcoal fire?

This lesson puts its finger on the key right at the start: many people have been moved, have received revelation, and love the Lord dearly — so why doesn’t the influence of their service last? Because one word is missing: “Life.”

In the 321 vision, the Path of Serving has five stations: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”; Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”; Life is “Jesus is my role model”; Service is “let Jesus be King”; God is “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

In the last two lessons we walked together through “Spirit” and “Understanding”. We saw that if service does not begin with the Holy Spirit, it is all just human zeal, human talent and human effort; and we saw that if truth stops at the letter, stops in the head, it can never change a person’s life.

This morning we come to the third station: “Life”.

Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest station on the whole road. Why? Because the journey from “Spirit” to “Understanding” runs from the outside in; but the journey from “Understanding” to “Life” runs from the inside back out. Receiving costs nothing; living it out always costs something. To hear a sermon takes you an hour; to live out a single sentence of it may take you a lifetime.

James puts it very bluntly: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” (James 2:17)

Notice the word James uses: “dead”. The Greek is nekros (νεκρός) — the “dead” of a corpse. Brothers and sisters, a corpse is not without form. A corpse has hands and feet and a face, every feature in place, everything there — except one thing: there is no breath. At the end of the same chapter James says it even more plainly: “For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.” (James 2:26)

A faith that has the stirring of the Spirit and the knowledge of Understanding, yet never comes to be lived out, looks just like that in God’s eyes: everything complete, except that it doesn’t move.

Spirit and Understanding, but no action; being moved and receiving revelation, but never living it out — a faith like that is still stuck in the head and the feelings. It has not yet entered life.

True service must walk all three steps: from Spirit, to Understanding, and on to Life. Only when truth becomes life does real influence follow.

This morning, let’s reflect together on three things: first, from revelation to life — living the truth out; second, the change of life — renewal from the inside out; third, the witness of life — passing on life by life.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Books, Two Settings, One Question
sections.html:
This lesson has two theme passages, one from the letter of James and one from the Gospel of John. They were written nearly half a century apart and addressed different people, yet both point to the same thing: a faith that has not entered life does not count.

Let’s look at James first.

The author of this letter, James, is generally held to be the Lord Jesus’ own younger brother in the flesh. Matthew 13:55 records the people of Nazareth talking about Jesus and saying, aren’t his brothers James, Joses, Simon and Judas? John 7:5 tells us with great honesty: “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” In other words, James did not believe at first. It was only after the risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7) that this younger brother became a disciple. Later he became a leader of the church in Jerusalem; in Galatians 2:9 Paul names him, together with Cephas and John, as a pillar of the church; and at the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15, it was he who gave the closing word.

James is generally dated to around AD 45–50, which may well make it one of the earliest books of the New Testament to be written. Its recipients, according to James 1:1, were “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” — Jewish believers scattered abroad by persecution. They lived as guests under other people’s roofs, suffered endless discrimination, and spent their days in the tension of a yawning gap between rich and poor, under the hand of oppressors. In a setting like that, what does faith most easily turn into? Words. Because words cost nothing.

So the whole of James really says just one thing: true faith is always visible. In 2:15–16 he gives a very pointed example: if a brother or sister has no clothes to wear and nothing to eat, and you say to them, “Go in peace. Be warmed and filled,” yet don’t give them what the body needs — what good is it?

Brothers and sisters, please note: James is not saying that works save us. Paul puts it as clearly as it can be put in Ephesians 2:8–9: “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.” What James is saying is that saving faith will always bear the fruit of works. An apple cannot turn a tree into an apple tree — but an apple tree will always bear apples. Works are not the ticket that gets you in the door; works are the evidence that someone lives in the house.

Next, let’s look at John 6.

The author of John’s Gospel is the apostle John, and it is generally dated to around AD 85–95, very probably written in Ephesus. The setting of chapter 6 is especially important, because it is practically a living textbook for the third key point of this lesson.

That day Jesus fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish (John 6:1–13). The crowd took one look and thought: isn’t this the one we’ve waited a thousand years for? They wanted to take him by force and make him king (6:15). The next day the crowd crossed the lake by boat and searched for him high and low. Jesus saw right through them and said, “You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.” (John 6:26)

From there Jesus began to speak more and more deeply. He said, “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.” (John 6:35) He even spoke of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many of his disciples, when they heard this, said, “This is a hard saying! Who can listen to it?” (John 6:60)

It was at that very moment that Jesus spoke our theme verse for today: “It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” (John 6:63)

Brothers and sisters, the verse that follows close on its heels is chilling to read: “At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.” (John 6:66)

The very people who had cheered over the bread yesterday and wanted to crown him king turned their backs and left today, because of one saying that was hard to understand and hard to live. Jesus turned to the Twelve and asked, “You don’t also want to go away, do you?” (John 6:67) Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.” (John 6:68)

The same miracle, the same preaching, the same Jesus. Some left, some stayed. Where was the difference? The difference lay in that one word: Life. Those who left had come to get something; those who stayed were ready to hand over their whole lives.

Brothers and sisters, put these two passages side by side and you have what God wants to say to us this morning: faith that stops at the lips is dead; truth that stops in the head cannot give life. Only when it enters life does service have roots, have strength, and last.

Key Point 1: From Revelation to Life — Living the Truth Out

“It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” (John 6:63)

Brothers and sisters, notice one word in what the Lord Jesus says here: “life”.

New Testament Greek has more than one word for “life”. Bios (βίος) is the biological, visible kind of life that gets used up — our physical strength, our span of years, our family fortune. But the word the Lord Jesus uses here is zōē (ζωή): the life that comes from God, eternal, with the very nature of God in it.

The Lord Jesus’ meaning is clear: the words I speak are not meant to add data to your head; they are meant to put the life of God inside you.

But where do so many people stop? This lesson nails it: they stop at “hear the sermon, be moved, the end.”

The morning message is wonderful. As you listen your heart grows warm, and your eyes may even mist over. But you walk out the door, take a phone call, sit through a whole day of meetings, get home — and that stirring has evaporated without a trace. The next day you hear another sermon, are moved again, and it evaporates again. Fifty-two Lord’s Days a year, moved fifty-two times — and your life hasn’t budged.

But that is not God’s intention. God’s intention is this: hear the word, understand it, do the word, and so it becomes life.

The Lord Jesus’ own conclusion was: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24)

The Greek word for “wise” here is phronimos (φρόνιμος). It doesn’t mean someone with a high IQ or a quick mind; it means someone with foresight, who knows how to plan for the future. And notice: the Lord Jesus didn’t say “everyone who hears these words of mine and understands them”, nor “everyone who hears these words of mine and is moved by them”. He said, “and does them”.

Two verses later the Lord Jesus says, “Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.” (Matthew 7:26)

Brothers and sisters, look carefully: the wise man and the foolish man heard the same sermon. The difference wasn’t in the hearing; the difference was in the doing.

Luke records an even more direct question from the Lord Jesus: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46) And James says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Notice James’s phrase: “deluding your own selves”. The greatest danger for someone who only hears and never does is not that other people are fooled, but that they are fooled by themselves — thinking they already have what they don’t.

Two professors at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business, Jeffrey Pfeffer and Robert Sutton, published a book in 1999 called The Knowing-Doing Gap. They studied a great many companies and reached this conclusion: the problem in the vast majority of organisations is not that they don’t know what to do, but that they know and still don’t do it. They found that the more meetings a company holds, the more polished its presentations and the more persuasive its reasoning, the more easily an illusion sets in — that “we’ve talked about it” is the same as “we’ve done it”.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t this even worse in the church?

Psychology offers a deeper explanation. In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of cognitive dissonance: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t match, an uncomfortable tension arises inside. There are two ways to resolve that tension. The first is to change your behaviour to fit your beliefs; the second is to change your beliefs to accommodate your behaviour. In an experiment with a colleague in 1959, Festinger found that people very often choose the second — quietly lowering the standard and persuading themselves that “it isn’t really that serious”.

What a frightening thing that is. When someone hears the word for years and never does it, the end is not a conscience that hurts more and more, but a conscience that hurts less and less. The truth didn’t lift his life up; instead his life dragged the truth down.

That is why this lesson’s insight is so well put: it isn’t how much you know, but how much you live out.

Let me use a very ordinary picture. You have a cookbook at home, beautifully printed, with mouth-watering photos. You read it cover to cover — three times, even — and you can recite the steps of every dish. Tell me: are you full? No. To be fed, you have to walk into the kitchen, wash the rice, light the stove, heat the oil, put up with the smoke and wash that pile of pots and pans. Reading the cookbook is comfortable; cooking is a bother. But only cooking can feed anyone.

Brothers and sisters, far too many of us spend our whole lives reading the cookbook.

Let me change the picture. You sit your driving test and score a hundred per cent on the written exam. Traffic rules, road signs and markings, who’s liable in an accident — you know them backwards. But that sheet of paper won’t drive the car for you. The real test is the moment you’re in the driver’s seat, the traffic is jammed at the crossroads and the car behind you keeps blasting its horn. Faith is like that too. Being able to recite “love is patient” is the written exam; still holding your patience the third time a family member talks back to you — that’s the road test.

In 321 language, this is the first checkpoint of the five-fold change. The five-fold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. But brothers and sisters, for a mindset to become life, there is a door to pass through, and that door is “Implementation”.

Among the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — “Information” comes before “Understanding”, “Revelation” is the stage of “Understanding”, and “Implementation” is exactly where “Life” begins. Many people spend their whole lives going round and round the first three stages — gathering information, waiting for revelation, being convinced in their hearts — and simply refuse to take the fourth step.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to say this with all sincerity: God doesn’t owe us a new revelation; God is waiting for us to give him an old obedience.

When you begin to live it out, the truth moves from “outside” to “inside”, from “mindset” to “life”.

Key Point 2: The Change of Life — Renewal from the Inside Out

Brothers and sisters, we might say: but I’ve tried. I really did try to live it out, and I failed.

Yes — and that is exactly the second thing we need to talk about. Because living it out has never depended on us gritting our teeth. The word of God itself has power to change a person’s life.

“Yahweh’s law is perfect, restoring the soul. Yahweh’s covenant is sure, making wise the simple.” (Psalm 19:7)

David’s words here are beautiful in Hebrew. “Restoring the soul” is literally “bringing back the soul” (meshivat nephesh), and the root of “restoring” is shuv, meaning to turn back, to return. Brothers and sisters, here is a picture: a person’s soul has wandered far off, has scattered, has got lost — and when the word of God comes, it leads that soul back to its originally intended position.

This is exactly what 321 means by humility — returning to our originally intended position. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The word of God is not a burden pressed down on us; the word of God is the road that leads the runaway heart back to the Father’s house.

Paul describes this process even more clearly: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

There are two key Greek words in this verse, and the contrast between them is striking.

“Conformed” is syschēmatizō (συσχηματίζω), from the root schēma, which refers to an outward pattern, an external shape — like the cut of a garment, changing with every passing fashion.

“Transformed” is metamorphoō (μεταμορφόω), from the root morphē, which refers to the inner essence, the true form. It is the very word Matthew 17:2 uses to describe the Lord Jesus being “changed” — transfigured — on the mountain.

Paul’s meaning is this: don’t let the world, like a mould, press you from the outside into its shape; let God change your very essence from the inside.

And notice that in the original, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is a present passive imperative. Passive — it isn’t you transforming yourself; it is letting God transform you. Present — it isn’t done once and for all; it is happening continually, on and on.

Paul uses the same idea in Colossians: “and have put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator” (Colossians 3:10).

“Being renewed” is anakainoumenon in the original, a present passive participle meaning “continually being renewed” — the Chinese Union Version renders it “gradually renewed”. Brothers and sisters, keep that word “gradually” in your heart. A change of life doesn’t happen in an instant; it is a process of gradual renewal.

One of the greatest temptations of our age is to demand everything “right now”. Web pages must load in a second, parcels must arrive the next day, diets must show results within a week. And so we make the same demand of our lives: one special conference and we should be completely made over; one prayer and we should overcome for ever. When it doesn’t happen, we lose heart, we give up, and we say, “I suppose I’m just not cut out for this.”

That isn’t how God works.

Let me use an old picture. In the old days, when a bolt of white cloth was to be dyed blue, you didn’t just toss it in the dye vat for a soak. It went into the vat, up onto the rack, out to dry and oxidise — then back into the vat, up onto the rack, out to dry again. Dipped again and again, exposed to the light again and again. Each time it looked only a shade darker, but after thirty times that cloth was blue through and through, and no washing could get it out.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what the word of God does in us.

Science also offers us a remarkable piece of supporting evidence. People used to think that the adult brain was fixed and could no longer change. But research by Professor Eleanor Maguire of University College London and her colleagues, published in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), found that London taxi drivers, because they have to memorise the city’s whole tangled web of streets, have noticeably more grey matter in the posterior hippocampus than most people — and the longer they had been driving, the more marked the difference.

In other words, when someone walks the same road over and over for years, that road really does get engraved into his brain.

Another study is worth remembering too. Research by Phillippa Lally of University College London and her colleagues, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that it takes on average sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit — ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days depending on the person and the behaviour.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: sixty-six days. Not six days, and not six hours.

These two studies can’t prove the Bible, and the Bible doesn’t need science to prove it. But they let us see that this is simply how God made human beings — we can be changed, and change takes repetition. That is precisely the meaning of the “Repetition” stage among the eight.

So this lesson reminds us of two things: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; from relying on ourselves, we turn to relying on Christ.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very core of 321. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. The essence of the old self is “self” — my opinions, my rights, my face, my credit. The essence of the new self is selflessness — “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Please note: selflessness doesn’t mean turning yourself into zero, into nothing. Selflessness is entering into the fullness without limit and living it out. Because when that limited “I” steps aside, the limitless Christ lives himself out within me.

We often say it too: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Everything we do flows from the heart. Many people can’t change, not because they don’t try hard enough, but precisely because they try too hard — relying on the brain, relying on themselves, gritting their teeth and forcing it until, in the end, they are the first to collapse.

Real change happens like this: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18)

Brothers and sisters, notice the three movements in this verse. First, “with unveiled face” — the veil taken away, no more covering up, no more pretending. Second, “seeing the glory of the Lord” — fixing our focus on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. Third, “are transformed into the same image” — and that “transformed” is, in the original, once again that word metamorphoō.

So here is the order: not first striving to change and only then daring to look at the Lord, but first looking at the Lord with unveiled face — and then being changed.

This is the insight of this lesson: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Brothers and sisters, when your life changes, your service will naturally have power. Not power you squeeze out of yourself, but power that flows out from within you.

Key Point 3: The Witness of Life — Passing On Life by Life

Jesus’ service was not just preaching; it was something he lived out with his life.

He lived it before our eyes. He died it before our eyes.

Of a life of thirty-three and a half years, only three and a half were spent in public ministry. And during those three and a half years he didn’t stand on a platform directing his disciples by remote control. He ate with them, lived with them, walked the roads with them, slept in the boat with them, and got caught in the same rain. The disciples saw how he prayed, and they saw how he grew weary; they saw how he worked miracles, and they saw how he wept.

On the last night he took off his outer garment, tied a towel round his waist, and stooped down to wash the disciples’ feet — including the feet of the man who would betray him. Then he said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15)

Brothers and sisters, the Greek word for “example” here is hypodeigma (ὑπόδειγμα), meaning “a sample set down below for people to see”. The Lord Jesus didn’t hang the standard up high for us to gaze up at; he got down on the floor and did it once in front of us.

Peter later wrote: “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21). The word for “example” here is hypogrammos — the copybook children used in ancient times to learn to write. The teacher would write out a line first, and the child would trace over it, stroke by stroke.

But this lesson reminds us of something unusual and sobering: many people followed him because of the miracles, and then left him when hard times came.

We’ve already read it. In John 6, the crowds who wanted to crown him king yesterday scattered today over one saying that was hard to live: “At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.” (John 6:66)

What does this tell us? It tells us that with only Spirit and Understanding, the influence is short-lived; add Life, and there is a foundation.

The Lord Jesus’ own conclusion comes at the very end of the Sermon on the Mount: “The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” (Matthew 7:25)

Notice: the wise man’s house wasn’t spared the storm. The rain still fell, the floods still came, the winds still blew. The difference wasn’t the weather; the difference was the foundation.

Speaking of foundations, there is a real-life observation well worth pondering. In Arizona there is a famous enclosed ecological research facility called Biosphere 2. The researchers found that the trees inside grew fast and tall, yet toppled over one after another before they reached maturity. Scientists later pointed to one important reason: inside that glasshouse there was no wind. Trees in the natural world stand firm because they are buffeted by wind year after year, and so grow a strengthened tissue commonly called “stress wood”, which makes the trunk tougher and drives the roots deeper.

Brothers and sisters, a tree that has never faced the wind grows fast but cannot stand.

It isn’t that God doesn’t love us when he lets the wind blow. The wind is God’s tool for driving our roots downward. Spirit and Understanding are growing upward; Life is putting down roots. The part that grows upward everyone can see; the part that goes down only God can see — yet what decides whether a tree will stand is the part no one sees.

So what truly influences people’s lives is not doctrine but life. This is what 321 means by passing on life by life — life influencing life.

Psychology gives us a very clear confirmation of this. The American psychologist Albert Bandura, in a series of studies at Stanford University — including the famous “Bobo doll experiment” of 1961, and the “social learning theory” he set out systematically in 1977 — pointed to one and the same conclusion: people, and children above all, mainly do not do what adults “say”; they do what adults “do”. The power of watching and imitating is far greater than that of spoken instruction.

Brothers and sisters, in the family and in the church alike, this is brutally accurate. Our children won’t grow up into what we say; they will grow up into how we live.

Albert Schweitzer is generally believed to have said something like this: example is not the main thing in influencing others — it is the only thing.

So why were the apostles able to change the world?

Not because they were eloquent. Paul himself tells us that some criticised him, saying, “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10). They changed the world because they didn’t merely preach; they lived out Jesus, even to the point of being willing to lay down their lives.

Paul’s words to the church in Thessalonica are the finest commentary on passing on life by life: “Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” (1 Thessalonians 2:8)

Brothers and sisters, listen to that: not the Good News only, but our own souls as well — our very lives. The Good News is a message; our souls are our life. To give only the message is to pass on the word; to give your life along with it — that is to pass on life.

Church history bears witness to this again and again. Around AD 155, Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was brought to the stake. The proconsul urged him to deny Christ and save his life. The old man replied: eighty-six years I have served him, and he has never done me wrong — how can I blaspheme my King who saved me? That day Polycarp left behind no sermon; what he left behind was a life lived out. And a life like that multiplies into more lives. That is why Tertullian, in his Apology, could write the line usually rendered “the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church”.

Closer to us is the Canadian missionary George Leslie Mackay. He arrived in Tamsui in March 1872, and in Taiwan he practised medicine, pulled teeth, preached and founded schools; in 1901 he died of illness in Taiwan and was buried there. He is generally believed to have left us this saying: “Rather burn out than rust out.” Brothers and sisters, to burn out is to give your life away; to rust out is to keep your life for yourself.

The Lord Jesus said it long ago: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

So this lesson’s insight says: what has the most influence is not eloquence but life.

In the 321 vision, this is the 920 practice and the 235 relationships.

What is 920? Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2” — your spouse, your children, your colleagues, your neighbours, the elderly person you pass at the end of the lane in the early morning. Before every “2”, we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life, letting the self-centred “self” step aside so that Christ may live himself out in me; and so we bear the “9” — the fruit the Holy Spirit produces, in all nine of its expressions: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

What is 235? When you pass on life by life, God places people around you: first a “2”, one or two selfless spiritual companions who hold each other up; then a “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children, one generation passing it on to the next; and at last a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together to establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, notice the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Not first finding people to get things done, but first living out life. When the life is right, the relationships will be right; when the relationships are right, the ministry will follow naturally. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Life Means Letting Jesus Live Himself Out in Me
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set what we have seen today back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal is: establish God’s system.

The five stages of the Path of Serving — Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — correspond exactly to these Three Foundations and Two Core Values. Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”; Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”; Life is “Jesus is my role model”; Service is “let Jesus be King”; God is “let Jesus receive all the glory”.

Today we stand at the third station. “Life” is the place where the words “Jesus is my role model” actually come true.

A role model isn’t a portrait hanging on the wall; a role model is the line in the copybook that I trace over, day after day. God’s intention has never been for us to admire Jesus, but for us to become like Jesus: “For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” (Romans 8:29)

So what stops us from becoming like Jesus?

The self-centred life.

The mark of the old self is being self-centred; the mark of the new self is selflessness. When we are self-centred, we keep score — who spoke better, who got noticed, who got the applause, who got the short end of the stick. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Brothers and sisters, the biggest breach in our service has never been a lack of ability; it is an “I” that is too big.

So to enter “Life”, we must first pass through the cross. Paul says: “always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body” (2 Corinthians 4:10). First death, then life; first selflessness, then Christ. And that is precisely the lesson we will go deeper into next time — the denying of self that holds nothing back.

To enter “Life” also takes a great reversal of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective, from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective, from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

Brothers and sisters, why do so many people refuse to live the truth out? Because from a human, earthly, temporary point of view, living it out is a very bad deal. If I forgive him, don’t I lose out? If I tell the truth, won’t it cost me? If I spend my time keeping that person company, won’t I fall behind schedule?

But from God’s, heaven’s, eternity’s point of view, everything is turned the other way round. Loss on earth is a deposit in heaven; losing out today is gain for eternity. That is why Paul could say, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21)

Finally, don’t forget that the direction of “Life” is multiplication. God gives us life not so that we can store it away for ourselves, but so that we will pass it on. This is the last of the eight stages — Multiplication — and it is what 920 and 235 look like in practice: living out selflessness before every “2” and bearing the fruit of the Spirit; letting spiritual parents bring forth spiritual children, letting one overcomer walk alongside others until there are many more overcomers — until God’s system is established, the Lord’s Prayer is fulfilled, and we press on into the end time revival.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Eight Stages into Daily Living
sections.html: This lesson gives us five practices. We’ll take them one by one in their original order, and deepen each using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

sections.heading: 1. Choose to Act: Live Out One Truth
sections.html:
Each day, don’t just receive; choose one truth and put it into practice. Practice: today, deliberately live out one word of God — for example, loving others, forgiving, being patient.

This practice corresponds to the fourth of the eight stages — Implementation. Brothers and sisters, notice that the practice says “choose one”, not “all of them”. Biting off more than we can chew is an old habit of ours: today we resolve to love others, to forgive, to be patient, to be humble, to get up early — and in the end we manage none of them.

This morning, just choose one sentence. Write it on a piece of paper and stick it somewhere you’ll see it. Then, before today is over, find one concrete thing to do that puts it into action. Not being moved by it, not agreeing with it — doing it.

sections.heading: 2. Examine Your Life: See Whether Inside and Outside Match
sections.html:
Reflect on whether what you believe is already alive in your daily living. Practice: ask yourself, “Did I live out what I believe today?”

This practice corresponds to the fifth stage — Evaluation.

Evaluation isn’t self-accusation. Satan’s accusation drives people to despair; the Holy Spirit’s rebuke turns people back. Evaluation means placing yourself in the light and looking honestly: is the person who speaks the same person who lives?

Brothers and sisters, I suggest you set aside three minutes before bed at night and ask just three questions: In what did I live out Christ today? In what did I slip back into the old self today? If I could do it over again, what would I do?

sections.heading: 3. Keep Being Renewed: Let Your Life Change Day by Day
sections.html:
Let the word of God adjust your thinking and your behaviour. Practice: each day, write down one mindset that needs to change.

This practice corresponds to the sixth and seventh stages — Correction and Repetition.

We said earlier that it takes on average sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become a habit. Brothers and sisters, don’t give up because you fall on the third day. Falling isn’t the end; giving up is.

“The new man, who is being renewed in knowledge” (Colossians 3:10) — that “gradually”, as the Chinese Union Version renders it, is God’s grace to us, and God’s patience with us too. Get yourself a little notebook and each day write down one mindset that needs to change. Look back a year from now, and you’ll see what a work God has done in you.

sections.heading: 4. Live Out an Example: Influence Others with Your Life
sections.html:
Don’t just preach; let people see Jesus in you. Practice: today, live out the likeness of Christ in one matter.

This practice corresponds to the eighth stage — Multiplication — and it is the 920 practice itself.

The Lord Jesus said, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) Notice the last phrase: the glory doesn’t go to us; it goes to the Father. This is the second of 321’s Two Core Values — let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, start today with the “2” closest to you. Family is often the hardest, yet also the most honest exam room there is.

sections.heading: 5. Be Willing to Pay the Price: Let Your Life Be Shaped by the Lord
sections.html:
Following Jesus always has a cost, but it also brings real life. Practice: today, in one thing that isn’t easy, choose to obey God.

This practice corresponds to the third stage — Conviction.

Conviction is saying “yes” before you have seen the outcome. In the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus said, “Not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) That night his sweat was like drops of blood. That wasn’t an easy obedience; it was an obedience that bled.

Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to look for some earth-shaking deed today. Just choose to obey in one small thing that isn’t easy — the phone call you’ve never wanted to make, the apology you’ve never been able to get out, the right you’ve never been willing to lay down.

A Gentle Reminder

Service without life has three marks: quick, hot, but it doesn’t last.

Service with life also has three marks: steady, rooted, and influential.

Brothers and sisters, the key isn’t how much you do, but how much you live out.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Living Out Jesus with Our Lives
sections.html:
If the Path of Serving stops at “Spirit” and “Understanding”, it is still incomplete. It must enter “Life”.

When you enter life, truth is no longer just something you hear but something you live out; faith is no longer just a mindset but a life.

And in the end you’ll discover something wonderful: it isn’t you who influences people; it is the life of Christ influencing people through you.

The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

The branch doesn’t have to strain to manufacture fruit; the branch only has to stay joined to the vine. Fruit is the natural overflow of life, not the product of a forced will.

So this morning, the call isn’t for you to push harder, but to draw closer. It isn’t for you to do a little more, but to let Jesus live a little more.

Brothers and sisters, let Jesus be King — and a king is not a consultant; a king is the one whose word is final. Let Jesus receive all the glory — all of it, keeping none back for ourselves.

This is the deepest power of service: living out Jesus with our lives.

keyVerses: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” (James 2:17)
“It is the spirit who gives life. The flesh profits nothing. The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life.” (John 6:63)
practices: Choose to act: today, deliberately live out one word of God — for example, loving others, forgiving, being patient.
Examine your life: before bed, ask yourself, “Did I live out what I believe today?”
Keep being renewed: each day, write down one mindset that needs to change.
prayer: Lord Jesus, I declare: I don’t only want to understand your word; I want to live out your word.

Lord, forgive me. So often I have stopped at being moved, stopped at knowing, and never stepped into doing. I have heard so much and lived out so little. This morning I no longer ask for a new revelation; I want to offer you an old obedience.
Let your life grow within me, carrying me from knowledge into life, from receiving into living it out.
I am willing to be changed by you — to put off the old self and put on the new self, day by day, being gradually renewed, living out the likeness of Christ.
Lord, I place my “self” in your hands. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Make my life a witness, so that life influences life; may everyone around me be able to see you in me.
Reign as King in my home, reign as King in my service, reign as King over my whole life.
All glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.

What is holding you back — is it inconvenient, is it a bad deal, or are you simply unwilling?

“Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.” (1 Thessalonians 2:8) Share: in your own life, is there someone who has “influenced you with their life”? What did they do? This week, whose “someone” is God calling you to be?
