script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we reflect together on “The Path of Serving · Life (Part 2): Denying of Self Without Holding Back — Living Out the Life of Jesus”. Listen to today’s theme verse, Romans 8:32: “He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?” God’s love towards us holds nothing back; Jesus’ giving of himself for us holds nothing back. What we are to learn today is not how to do more, but how to live out a life like this, a life that holds nothing back.

Brothers and sisters, first, a true story. In 1949 a twenty-two-year-old young man wrote in his journal: he is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose. His name was Jim Elliot. Seven years later, on 8 January 1956, he and four companions were speared to death while trying to bring the gospel to the Waodani people of Ecuador. It looked like a total waste. But later their wives went back to the same tribe, and years afterwards, the hands that had killed were baptising others in that same river. What matters most in service? Not ability, but life.

Brothers and sisters, notice the words “didn’t spare”. In the original of Romans 8:32 they mean to begrudge, to be unable to let go. And in the Greek translation of the Old Testament, Genesis 22:12 uses the very same word: you have not withheld your only son. On Mount Moriah, Abraham raised the knife and the angel stopped him; on the hill of Golgotha, God the Father raised the knife, and no one stopped him. So please remember: the first one in the whole Bible to hold nothing back was not us; it was God. Our giving is only ever a response to him.

The first teaching: denying of self is the only road into selflessness. Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not a slogan; it is built up from one choice to deny ourselves after another. What is denying of self? Just three phrases: for Jesus, for others, not for myself. The Lord said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” (Matthew 16:24) “Deny himself” in the original means to disown utterly. When Peter said of the Lord, “I don’t know the man,” that was failure; when the Lord calls us to say of the old self, “I don’t know him,” that is victory.

There are two groups of people in the Bible. The first is on the shore of Galilee: Peter and Andrew immediately left their nets; James and John immediately left the boat and their father. The nets were their skill, the boat their livelihood, their father their fallback. The key for them was not being more spiritual but holding nothing back. The second group is just one man, the rich young ruler. He had good conduct, moral standing and a hunger, yet he went away sad, for he had great possessions. Brothers and sisters, it isn’t how much you do that decides your life; it is how much you hold back that decides whether you can follow the Lord.

The second teaching: holding nothing back is a resolve that does not fear death. The Lord said, “He who loses his life for my sake will find it.” (Matthew 10:39) This is the law of the kingdom of heaven: what you clutch, you will lose; what you let go of, you will gain. It’s like grabbing sand — the tighter you grip, the faster it runs out; open your palm, and it stays. What does holding nothing back look like? Four “no fears”: no fear of loss, no fear of being hurt, no fear of paying the price, no fear of death. Brothers and sisters, most of what we hold back isn’t because we’re greedy; it’s because we’re afraid.

Daniel is the finest example. He was only a youth when he was carried off, and by the time he walked into the lions’ den he was in his eighties. The decree only lasted thirty days; he only had to close his window, and nobody would have known. But the Bible says he knelt before God three times a day and prayed, “as he did before”. Brothers and sisters, remember those words. Someone who holds nothing back doesn’t need to change for a crisis. In the end God shut the lions’ mouths, and a pagan king decreed: “His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed.” Daniel didn’t influence the world by ability, but by a life that did not fear death.

The third teaching: living out the selfless life through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Brothers and sisters, denying of self isn’t far away at all; it is hidden in five choices every day: what to look at, what to listen to, what to think, what to say and what to do. These five are the steering wheel of your life. When you see through your own eyes, listen by your own standards and think by your own ideas, you are living in the self-centred life; when you see through God’s eyes, listen to God’s voice and think with God’s truth, you enter into selflessness. And the starting point is not outside but in the Spirit: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. It doesn’t depend on effort; it depends on connection.

The Lord said, “I am the vine. You are the branches… apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) Have you ever seen a branch dripping with sweat, trying to bear fruit? Never. It simply stays connected. So joy is a fruit, not a fruit juice; juice is squeezed out, fruit grows. Brothers and sisters, if the more you serve the more tired you get, the more you do the more bitter it feels, and your joy is draining away, usually it isn’t because there’s too much to do, but because there’s been no denying of self. True joy isn’t things going smoothly; it is a life brought into alignment.

This week, please practise three things. First, make one choice to deny yourself each day: where you wanted to react from your emotions, choose gentleness; where you wanted to fight for yourself, choose to let go; where you wanted to run away, choose to obey. Second, check your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing each evening: was what I looked at today of God or of the world? Did what I said build people up or hurt them? Third, use joy to test your direction: when you have no joy, don’t blame yourself; just ask one question — have I chosen myself again? Then choose afresh: for Jesus, for others, not for myself.

Brothers and sisters, the key to service isn’t how much you have done, but whom you have lived out. As you choose to deny yourself again and again, step by step you enter into selflessness; as you live out selflessness, people will see Jesus in you. The focus is not on ourselves, not on ministry, not on people, but on Jesus alone. Today I’m not calling you to go and do more; I’m calling you to hand over the throne of your heart. Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. Don’t go away sad. Put down the nets today.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I am willing to lay myself down and choose to follow you. I will no longer live for myself; I will live for you, and live for others. I declare: as I choose to deny myself, I live out the selfless life; as I choose humility, I let Jesus reign as King within me. Holy Spirit, guide my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing today. Let my life be a life that draws people, so that they see the glory of Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless every brother and sister to live out the life of Christ today.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we reflect together on “The Path of Serving · Life (Part 2): Denying of Self Without Holding Back — Living Out the Life of Jesus”. This series follows a road: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Today we come to the third station, Life. Listen to the theme verse, Romans 8:32: “He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?” And listen to John 3:16: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” God’s love towards us holds nothing back; Jesus’ giving of himself for us holds nothing back.

Let’s begin with a diary. On 28 October 1949, a twenty-two-year-old American wrote one sentence: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” His name was Jim Elliot. Seven years later, on 8 January 1956, he and four companions were speared to death on a river beach while trying to bring the gospel to the Waodani people in the jungles of Ecuador. In the eyes of the world, it was a total waste. But their wives went back to the same tribe and settled there. Years later, the very men who had speared their husbands were baptising others, with their own hands, in that same river.

Brothers and sisters, this is today’s lesson. On the road of service, what matters most is not ability but life. Many people think service means doing lots of things, giving lots of time and completing lots of tasks. But what the Lord Jesus values has never been the outward ministry; it is the life within us. “Life” is the life of Jesus, and at its heart is not the self-centred life but selflessness; not living for ourselves, but living for Jesus and living for others. Let me ask you a question right at the start, and please don’t answer it too quickly: is there anything that, to this very day, you have still not truly handed over?

Let’s first go back to the scene of the text. Paul wrote Romans around AD 56–57, in Corinth, to a church he had never visited. Chapter 8 is the summit of the letter. He says: he who didn’t spare his own Son. Brothers and sisters, “didn’t spare” in the original means to begrudge, to be unable to let go. And the Greek translation of the Old Testament uses this very word in Genesis 22:12: “you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.” On Mount Moriah, Abraham raised the knife and the angel stopped him; on the hill of Golgotha, God the Father raised the knife, and no one stopped him. The first one in the whole Bible to hold nothing back was not us; it was God.

The first teaching: denying of self is the only road into the selfless life. Brothers and sisters, nobody wakes up one morning and finds they’ve become selfless. Selflessness isn’t a fruit that drops from the sky; selflessness is a road, and every step on that road is called denying of self. What is denying of self? Just three phrases: for Jesus, for others, not for myself. This is the way of the cross. The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, and whoever will lose his life for my sake will find it.”

“Deny himself” in the original means to disown utterly, to declare, “I do not know this man.” Brothers and sisters, this word is used in another place too. The Lord said to Peter: tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times. And later Peter really did say: I don’t know the man. The same root. When Peter said of Jesus, “I don’t know the man,” that was failure; yet the Lord calls us to say of ourselves, “I don’t know the man” — and that is victory. Denying of self isn’t turning your temper down a notch; it is pointing at the old self that wants to be king and saying: he is not my master.

There are two groups of people in the Bible. The first is on the shore of Galilee. When Peter and Andrew heard the Lord say “Come after me”, they immediately left their nets; James and John immediately left the boat and their father. The nets were their skill, the boat their livelihood, their father their family ties and their fallback. And twice the Bible uses the word “immediately”. The second group is just one man, the rich young ruler. He had good conduct, moral standing and a hunger, but when the Lord told him to sell what he had, he went away sad, for he had great possessions. Brothers and sisters, his biggest problem wasn’t that he was rich; it was that he held something back.

The Lord Jesus gave us the most beautiful picture: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” Botany gives us a vivid footnote: for a seed to germinate, it must take in water and swell, its seed coat must split, and the nutrients in its endosperm must be completely used up before the new shoot can grow. The seed coat is the seed’s sense of security, but as long as it doesn’t split, the root can never come out. Brothers and sisters, the condition of many of us is that of a well-preserved seed. We protect our time, our face, our rights, our wounds — and in the end we have preserved ourselves but borne no fruit. Viktor Frankl, a survivor of the concentration camps, wrote in Man’s Search for Meaning that the more a person forgets himself and gives himself to a mission or to someone he loves, the more he fulfils himself.

The second teaching: holding nothing back is a resolve that does not fear death. In Luke 14 the Lord says three times over, “can’t be my disciple”: if you don’t love me above your own life, you can’t; if you don’t bear your own cross and follow me, you can’t; if you don’t renounce all that you have, you can’t. Here we need to clear up a misunderstanding. Where some translations read “love me more than”, the original actually reads “hate”. Does the Lord really want us to hate our parents? Of course not. When Hebrew wants to say “love A more than B”, it says “love A, hate B”. The Lord’s meaning is clear: only one can sit on the throne of your heart.

Then the Lord states the law of the spiritual world: “He who seeks his life will lose it; and he who loses his life for my sake will find it.” Brothers and sisters, keep this in your heart: what you clutch, you will lose; what you let go of, you will gain. It’s like grabbing sand — the tighter you grip, the faster it runs out; open your palm, and the sand stays. What does holding nothing back look like? It looks like four “no fears”: no fear of loss, no fear of being hurt, no fear of paying the price, no fear of death. Let’s be honest: much of what we hold back isn’t because we’re greedy; it’s because we’re afraid. But the Bible says perfect love casts out fear.

Daniel is the finest example. He was carried off to Babylon around 605 BC, when he was only a youth; the lions’ den took place in the reign of Darius, after 539 BC. The Daniel who walked into the lions’ den was an old man in his eighties. The decree only lasted thirty days; he only had to close his window, and nobody would have known. But the Bible says he knelt on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, “as he did before”. Please remember those words. In the end God shut the lions’ mouths, and a pagan king decreed: “His kingdom is that which will not be destroyed!” Daniel didn’t influence the world by ability, but by a life that did not fear death.

It is the same today. People aren’t drawn by your eloquence; they’re drawn by your life. The Lord said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” The very next verse explains: he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die. Brothers and sisters, Jesus’ most compelling moment was not when he worked miracles, but when he hung on the cross, looking utterly powerless. Revelation describes the overcomers of the last days: they didn’t love their life, even to death. As the Father gave holding nothing back, so the overcomers give back holding nothing back. The last card in Satan’s hand is death; against someone who doesn’t fear death, he has no card left to play.

The third teaching: living out the selfless life through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Many people imagine that denying ourselves is very far away, as if it had to mean martyrdom. In fact, denying of self is hidden in the choices of everyday life. Every day we make five choices: what to look at, what to listen to, what to think, what to say and what to do. These five are the steering wheel of your life. When you see through your own eyes, listen by your own standards and think by your own ideas, you are living in the self-centred life; when you see through God’s eyes, listen to God’s voice and think with God’s truth, you begin to enter into selflessness.

How important are these five choices? Look at how the Lord Jesus himself lived. About seeing, the Lord said: the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. About listening and doing, the Lord said: as I hear, I judge, because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me. About speaking, the Lord said: as my Father taught me, I say these things. Brothers and sisters, the Lord who became flesh — not one bit of his seeing, listening, thinking, speaking or doing started from himself. The selfless life isn’t a slogan we invented; it is the pattern Jesus lived out in person.

And the starting point of all this is not outside, but in the Spirit. The 321 Path of Serving is: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. As the Holy Spirit guides me, I can see and listen rightly, and this brings me into Understanding; when I see rightly, listen rightly and think rightly, my life is shaped, and this is Life; once there is life, there can be Service, and in the end everything returns to God. Brothers and sisters, this doesn’t depend on effort; it depends on connection. The Lord says: apart from me you can do nothing. Have you ever seen a branch dripping with sweat, trying to bear fruit? Never; it simply stays connected. The psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in 1949 that neurons that fire together wire together. Walk it once and you’ve crossed a lawn; walk it ten thousand times and it becomes a highway.

As you keep choosing to deny yourself in your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, you will experience one sign: joy. The Lord said: that my joy may remain in you. Paul lists joy second among the fruit of the Spirit. Notice: joy is a fruit, not a fruit juice; juice is squeezed out, fruit grows. So joy is the dashboard of the spiritual life. If the more you serve the more tired you get and the more you do the more bitter it feels, please don’t immediately blame yourself; first look at what the dashboard is telling you. Usually it isn’t because there’s too much to do, but because there’s been no denying of self. The psychologist Martin Seligman also found that sensory pleasure is the most fleeting, while using your strengths in the service of something bigger than yourself brings the deepest and most lasting satisfaction. Brothers and sisters, true joy isn’t things going smoothly; it is a life brought into alignment.

Brothers and sisters, hearing the word isn’t hard; doing it is. This week, please practise three things. First, one choice to deny yourself each day: where you wanted to react from your emotions, choose gentleness; where you wanted to fight for yourself, choose to let go; where you wanted to run away, choose to obey. Start with small things, and your life begins to change. Second, practise bringing your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing into line with God. Each evening, take five minutes to ask: was what I looked at today of God or of the world? Was what I listened to the Holy Spirit or my emotions? Was what I thought faith or fear? Did what I said build people up or hurt them? Was what I did for the Lord or for myself?

Third, use joy to test the direction of your life. When you have no joy, don’t blame yourself; just ask one question: have I chosen myself again? Then choose afresh: for Jesus, for others, not for myself. 321 teaches us to go deeper using the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. You have already received the information today, but information doesn’t change people; revelation does. So ask the Holy Spirit to point out “that one thing” you have never been willing to let go of. And finally, find someone to practise with you; that is Multiplication.

Let’s place today’s message into the map of 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself and became obedient to the point of death; the Bible is my standard — what to give up and what to keep must follow the Bible; the Holy Spirit is my guide — denying of self without the Holy Spirit is nothing but gritted teeth. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. At its heart, denying of self is a change of king, because there is only one throne in the heart. The Goal: establish God’s system. Then there is the 920 practice: everyone you have a relationship with is your “2”; before them you live out the selfless “0”, and the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows. And there is the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things.

Brothers and sisters, let’s come back to the question we started with. The key to service isn’t how much you have done, but whom you have lived out. As you choose to deny yourself again and again, step by step you enter into selflessness; as you live out selflessness, people will see Jesus in you. The focus is not on ourselves, not on ministry, not on people, but on Jesus alone. So this early morning, I’m not calling you to go and do more; I’m calling you to hand over the throne. Please ask yourself quietly: in my heart, who is sitting on that chair? Brothers and sisters, don’t go away sad. Today, put down the nets, and follow him.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, I am willing to lay myself down and choose to follow you. I will no longer live for myself; I will live for you, and live for others. Lord, I confess that there are still things I am holding back; today I place them in your hands. I declare: as I choose to deny myself, I live out the selfless life; as I choose humility, I let Jesus reign as King within me. Holy Spirit, guide my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing today. Let my life be a life that draws people, so that they see the glory of Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord bless every brother and sister: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Problem Is Not Serving, but “Who Is Doing It”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. In this morning’s devotion I want to begin with a very practical question: have you ever had this experience — you are clearly serving God, and yet your heart grows heavier and heavier?

I know a sister who served in her church for twelve years. Sunday school, the choir, welcoming, visitation, the kitchen — wherever there was a need, she was there. One day she sat in my office and said to me, “Pastor, I don’t want to do it any more.” I asked her why. She was silent for a long time, and then she said something I have never forgotten: “It’s not that I don’t love the Lord. I’m just so tired. I feel like I’m holding it all up on my own.”

She said, “I’m holding it all up on my own.” Those few words are the truest confession in the hearts of many who serve — and the one they least dare to say out loud.

Brothers and sisters, if you have ever felt this way, please hear one thing clearly: the problem usually is not serving itself. Serving is one of the greatest graces God gives us. The problem lies somewhere deeper — in “who is doing it”.

If I am the one doing it, what is the result? Pressure, burden, comparison, frustration. Because my strength is limited, my wisdom is limited, my patience is limited. When I do well, I become proud; when I do badly, I blame myself; when someone else does better than me, I become jealous; when others don’t appreciate me, I get hurt. Everything revolves around that “I” — and that “I” cannot hold it all up.

If Jesus is the one doing it, what is the result then? Lightness, joy, power, fruitfulness. Because his strength is limitless, his wisdom is limitless, his love is limitless. He works, I cooperate; he reigns, I obey; he receives the glory, I receive rest.

So the heart of “Service” has never been a question of ability. It is a question of sovereignty.

This is the one sentence to grasp in this lesson: the key to serving is not how much ability I have, but how much sovereignty Jesus has in my service.

When Jesus truly reigns as King, serving changes from “people doing things” to “God doing his work”. The difference between the two is not a difference of degree; it is a difference of nature. When people do things, they do them until their strength runs out; when God works, he works until glory comes. When people do things, what they see is results; when God works, what we see is life. When people do things, people get the applause; when God works, God gets the glory.

Peter puts it very clearly: “If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11). Notice the two keys in this verse. First, the source of the strength is “which God supplies”. Second, the aim of serving is “that God may be glorified”. The source is not me, and the aim is not me. If neither the beginning nor the end is me, then surely the part in the middle shouldn’t be me either.

Today we are going to take up two key questions: first, what is true service? Second, how do we let Jesus reign as King in our service?

On the 321 Path of Serving we have been climbing five steps: “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God”. Spirit is the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding is the Bible is my standard; Life is Jesus is my role model; Service is let Jesus be King; God is let Jesus receive all the glory. The first three steps are the “inflow” — receiving. The fourth step, “Service”, is the “outflow” — pouring out. Today we stand on the fourth step.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A Letter Written to Those Who Suffer
sections.html:
To truly understand 1 Peter 4:11, we first need to get to know this letter.

The Author and the Date

The author of this letter calls himself “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:1). He is Simon, the fisherman from Galilee; the disciple who denied the Lord three times in the high priest’s courtyard; the man whom the Lord asked three times by the Sea of Tiberias, “Do you love me?” and who was given his commission afresh. The Lord said to him, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

By the time he wrote this letter, Peter was no longer young. He calls himself “a fellow elder” (1 Peter 5:1). Most evangelical scholars hold that the letter was written between AD 62 and 64, from “Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13), generally taken to be a code name for Rome. In other words, not long after this letter was written, Nero’s persecution fell, and Peter himself was martyred in Rome.

This matters a great deal: the man who wrote this letter was not a scholar sitting in his study discussing theory, but an old servant about to lay down his life for the Lord. Every word he wrote was made ready with his blood.

The Readers and Their Situation

Peter writes “to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1). All five regions were in Asia Minor — the north-central part of what is Turkey today.

The word for “living as foreigners” is the Greek παρεπίδημος (parepidēmos), meaning “a temporary resident from elsewhere” — people with no citizenship, no property and no social standing. In Roman society they were already on the margins; after they believed, they were slandered by their neighbours, shut out by their relatives and watched by the authorities. They were a company of “suffering believers”.

In this letter Peter mentions “suffering” sixteen times and “glory” ten times. He binds suffering and glory together, because that is exactly the road Jesus walked.

Brothers and sisters, keep this background in mind: when Peter speaks about serving, he is not speaking to people with plenty of resources and strength to spare; he is speaking to people who can barely keep themselves going, people who have been crushed. That means the serving Peter describes can never be something piled up by human strength. How can people with no resources serve? There is only one answer — “as of the strength which God supplies”.

The Context

1 Peter 4:7–11 is one complete unit.

Verse 7: “But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.” This is the overarching principle: an end-times awareness.

Verse 8: “And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.” This is the motive: love.

Verse 9: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.” This is the attitude: willingness.

Verse 10: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” This is the identity: stewards.

Verse 11: “If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.” This is the standard and the purpose.

Do you see the order? First an end-times perspective, then the motive of love, then a willing attitude, then the identity of a steward — and only last of all the method and the purpose. This is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Peter doesn’t open his mouth by talking about ministry. He starts from life, goes through relationships, and only at the end comes down to serving.

Two Key Words in the Original

The word for “managers” in verse 10 is the Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonomos), a servant who manages a household’s estate — a steward. The most important quality in a steward is not capability but faithfulness, because nothing a steward manages belongs to him. The gifts are the master’s, the time is the master’s, the fruit is the master’s too. A steward who treats his master’s estate as his own is an unfaithful steward.

The word “supplies” in verse 11 is the Greek χορηγέω (chorēgeō). In the ancient Greek city-states this word had a special use. When a city held a drama festival, it needed a large chorus, and the chorus’s training, costumes, instruments and meals were all paid for by one wealthy citizen. What this sponsor did was called chorēgeō. In other words, Peter is saying: God is the great sponsor who covers every expense — all you have to do is go on stage and sing.

Brothers and sisters, what a beautiful picture this is. Many who serve run dry because they are trying to be both the one who sings and the one who pays. God says: I am the one who pays. You just sing.

sections.heading: 3. The First Teaching: A Life without “Service” Is a Stagnant, Even a Dying, Life
sections.html:
1. All “inflow” and no “outflow” — life is bound to stagnate

The purpose of “Spirit, Understanding, Life” is not to stop at the growth of our own life; it is to move on into “Service”.

Brothers and sisters, picture this scene. Israel has two famous bodies of water, and they drink from the same river — the Jordan.

The one in the north is the Sea of Galilee. The Jordan flows in from the north and flows out again at the southern end. Its water is alive: there are fish in the lake and grass along the shore. Two thousand years ago Peter fished there, and today it is still a fishing ground.

The one in the south is the Dead Sea. The Jordan flows in and never flows out again. It is the lowest point on the earth’s land surface, its surface about 430 metres below sea level. Water can only evaporate, so salt keeps building up, until the salt content reaches around thirty per cent — nearly ten times that of ordinary sea water. And the result? No fish, no water plants; even bacteria struggle to survive. That is why people call it the “Dead Sea”.

The same source of water, the same sky, the same sunshine. There is only one difference: one has an outlet, and the other has none.

That is a picture of spiritual life. A pond that only takes water in and never moves will go foul; a life that only absorbs and never gives will dry up.

Some brothers and sisters have believed for many years. They keep listening to sermons, keep receiving, keep learning. They have filled several notebooks and sat through dozens of talks — and yet they notice something very strange: they are moved less and less, their passion is lower and lower, their life is more and more stagnant.

Why? Not because the word is poor, but because there is no outlet.

Because life was designed from the start to be this: receive, pour out, receive again, pour out again. That is the cycle of “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service”.

2. Letting Scripture interpret Scripture: the Lord himself says so

The Lord Jesus said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38).

Notice the word the Lord uses: not “pools” but “rivers”. A pool stores; a river flows. The Lord never promised to turn us into reservoirs. He promised to turn us into rivers.

The vision the prophet Ezekiel saw is even clearer. The water flowing out from under the threshold of the temple grew deeper and deeper: “It will happen, that every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, will live. Then there will be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea will be healed, and everything will live wherever the river comes” (Ezekiel 47:9).

Brothers and sisters, notice the phrase “wherever the river comes”. Where the water doesn’t reach, nothing lives. The fruit of life always appears where the water flows to — never where the water sits still.

When the Lord Jesus sent out his disciples, he said, “Freely you received, so freely give” (Matthew 10:8). “Receiving” and “giving” belong together. If you only receive and never give, what you have received will spoil — like the manna in the wilderness, which bred worms and stank when it was kept until morning.

The Lord also said, “Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you. For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38). We pour out so that we can receive more.

3. Evidence from science and psychology

This spiritual principle can be seen in our own bodies too.

An adult heart, at an average of seventy beats a minute, beats roughly a hundred thousand times a day. Why must the heart keep beating without a break? Because once the blood stops flowing, we die. And the heart has one striking feature: it never keeps blood for itself. Blood comes in and is immediately pumped out; it comes in again and is pumped out again. The heart is not an organ for storing blood; it is an organ for sending it. God has written the principle “only what flows has life” into every beat in our chests.

Psychology bears this out as well. In 2005 Professor Stephen Post of Case Western Reserve University in the United States published a review in the International Journal of Behavioral Medicine showing that altruistic, helping behaviour is significantly associated with better physical and mental health and greater life satisfaction. Put simply: people who give live better.

But an important caution needs adding here. Professor Adam Grant of the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, in his book Give and Take (2013), points to a paradoxical finding: in the workplace, the worst performers are “givers” — and so are the best performers. The same giving, so why such opposite outcomes? The key is that the givers who burn out are giving from their own reserves, while the givers who are blessed over the long haul know how to attend to their own replenishment and boundaries at the same time.

Brothers and sisters, this confirms Peter’s words from the other side. If you serve with “your strength”, sooner or later you will become that burnt-out giver; if you serve “as of the strength which God supplies”, you will always have something to give. Because the one paying is the great sponsor, not you.

4. A 321 Insight

Life is not meant to be hoarded; life is meant to flow.

It is not how much you know, but how much flows out of you.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the fivefold change 321 speaks of: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Many people get stuck at the second step and go no further — they want their life to grow, but they won’t move on into relationships and ministry. Yet the order God designed is this: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you move into ministry. Ministry is not an extra burden. Ministry is the natural outlet of a maturing life.

When you begin to serve, you will discover three things: you need God more, you rely on God more, you experience God more.

Why? Because “Service” will draw you into a deeper life. If you don’t serve, you will never know how limited you are; the moment you serve, you immediately hit the end of yourself. And the end of man is exactly where God begins.

This is also the true meaning of “the 920 practice”. Every person you are in relationship with is your “2”; before each “2”, you practise living a life of selflessness (0), and you bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions (9). Serving doesn’t wait until you have become perfect before it begins; serving is itself the training ground for selflessness. Your co-workers, the members of your group, that family member who is hardest to get along with — they are all the “2” God has measured out to you.

5. An illustration from daily life

I once urged a brother who had been spiritually low for years to go and visit an elderly man in hospital. He said, “Pastor, I can’t even look after myself — how am I supposed to look after someone else?” I said, “You’re not going because you have something. You’re going because he does.”

He went. He sat by the hospital bed, didn’t know what to say, so he read a psalm aloud — and when he finished, he wept. Three months later he told me, “Pastor, that day I thought I was going to give. It turned out I was going to receive. In that hospital room I met God again.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the river of living water. You think you are giving, but in fact God is pouring more water into you so that you have something to let flow. If you don’t let it flow, he has no need to keep pouring.

sections.heading: 4. The Second Teaching: Service without “Spirit, Understanding, Life” Is Incomplete Service
sections.html:
1. True service contains three elements

If the first teaching was about “whether anything flows out”, the second is about “what it is that flows out”.

Because not all busyness is service, and not all service is complete service. True service always contains three elements together: Spirit — the guidance of the Holy Spirit; Understanding — the truth of God’s word; Life — the life of Jesus.

None of the three can be missing. Lose any one of them and service is bent out of shape. Let’s look at them one at a time.

2. Understanding without Spirit

This kind of service looks like this: a gifted preacher, someone who knows the Bible well, someone with a great deal of knowledge. They can get a Bible study group going, they can speak the theological terms, they know the references by heart.

But there is no presence of the Holy Spirit.

And the result? It cannot touch hearts, it cannot bring life. There is only doctrine, without power.

The listeners nod and say, “That was a great talk,” and then go home exactly as before. The message got into their heads but couldn’t get into their hearts.

Brothers and sisters, Scripture itself warns of this danger. Paul says, “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). The Lord Jesus said to those who were best at searching the Scriptures, “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life” (John 5:39–40).

So it turns out that Bible knowledge can exist apart from the Holy Spirit — but life cannot.

Paul himself was one of the most learned men of his day, an outstanding student under Gamaliel. Yet what did he say when he came to Corinth? “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).

Notice Paul’s reason: not that eloquence is unimportant, but “that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men”. If people are persuaded by your eloquence, their faith rests on you; and one day when you can no longer preach, their faith collapses too. The work of the Holy Spirit is to rest people’s faith on God.

An illustration from daily life: there is such a thing as wax fruit. Set on the dining table, its colours are bright and its shape is perfect — it looks better than the real thing. But bite into it and you know the difference at once: no juice, no flavour, no nourishment. Service that has Understanding without Spirit is spiritual wax fruit. Lovely to look at, impossible to eat.

A saying worth remembering: the nineteenth-century evangelist D. L. Moody is generally credited with saying something like this — don’t speak God’s word with your mouth; let God’s word speak out of your life. Whatever its true source, the point is right: truth that has not passed through the fire of the Holy Spirit is only cold ash.

3. Spirit without Understanding

The second distortion is exactly the opposite. This kind of service looks like this: deeply moved, full of passion, rich in experiences.

Tears in the meetings, fire in prayer, always ready to tell you a string of signs and wonders.

But there is no foundation of truth.

And the result? Instability, a tendency to drift off course, easily swayed by circumstances.

If they feel moved today, they do it; if they don’t feel moved tomorrow, they don’t. If one meeting has a strong feeling, they keep going; if another church has no feeling, they never come back. More dangerous still, they take their own emotions for the leading of the Holy Spirit and their own desires for the will of God.

Scripture is not vague about this at all. John says, “Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1).

And what do we test them with? With God’s word. The Bereans are our example: “Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so” (Acts 17:11).

Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit and the Bible never fight each other, because the Bible is inspired by the Holy Spirit. “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). If your “prompting” clashes with the clear teaching of Scripture, that is not the Holy Spirit — it is something else.

An illustration from daily life: a ship has a sail, and it also has a rudder. The sail receives the push of the wind; the rudder sets the direction. A ship with a sail but no rudder is in more danger the stronger the wind blows, because it will only be blown where it should never go. “Spirit” is the sail; “Understanding” is the rudder. God never wants us hoisting the sail on a ship with no rudder.

Evidence from psychology: since the 1970s psychologists have done a great deal of research on “emotion regulation”. The process model of emotion regulation put forward by Professor James Gross of Stanford University shows that our emotional responses are deeply shaped by “cognitive appraisal” — how you interpret something determines how you feel about it. In other words, feelings don’t come from nowhere; they follow the mindset you hold. This corresponds exactly to the first of the changes 321 speaks of: change the mindset and you change the life. If the mindset (Understanding) is not right, the feelings (whether or not you sense the Spirit moving) will be misled.

4. Spirit and Understanding, but no Life

The third distortion is the most hidden and the most regrettable. These people have gifts, knowledge and experiences — they lack nothing.

But their life has not been dealt with.

And the result? They easily become proud, they offer no example to follow, and they cannot pass on life.

Brothers and sisters, this is the most dangerous kind of all. Because others can spot the first two distortions, but nobody can spot this one — only God can see it.

Gifts are a present God gives; life is a project God builds. A present can be handed to you in a day; a project takes a lifetime to build. And Scripture says plainly that the gifts are not taken back: “For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). So a person can go on having gifts while their life has already gone wrong.

The Lord Jesus spoke some of his most solemn words about this: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven; but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity’” (Matthew 7:21–23).

Notice that these people were not lying — they really did preach, cast out demons and do mighty works. The problem was not in the ministry but in the relationship: “I never knew you.”

Paul also says, “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal” (1 Corinthians 13:1). What is special about brass and cymbals? They are very loud, and empty inside.

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. For someone who serves with gifts but whose life has not been dealt with, the greatest temptation is to grab God’s rights into their own hands: the pulpit is mine, the ministry is mine, the people are mine. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

An illustration from daily life: a fine instrument can play moving music; but if its strings are out of tune, the louder it plays, the more obvious the wrong notes. The gift is the instrument; life is the tuning. God will allow circumstances to tune us. The process is often uncomfortable, but it is so that we play true.

An analogy from science: a redwood can grow to nearly a hundred metres tall, yet its roots are not deep. What keeps it standing in the wind is that its roots intertwine with one another as the trees grow together in groves. Without those connected roots, height becomes a danger. If the depth of a life cannot keep pace with the height of its gifts, the higher it grows, the more dangerous it becomes.

5. True service: life touching life

So true service is three in one: the guidance of the Holy Spirit (Spirit), a foundation of truth (Understanding), and the witness of a life (Life).

Service like this is not merely teaching; it is “life touching life”.

What does Paul say? “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). And again: “Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:8).

Brothers and sisters, notice that Paul gave two things: the gospel, and his own life. Giving the gospel without giving your life is a lecture; giving the gospel together with your life — that is service.

As Scripture says, “But we have Christ’s mind” (1 Corinthians 2:16).

The first half of that verse is: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he should instruct him?” Paul is quoting Isaiah 40:13, whose original meaning is that no one can instruct God. But Paul immediately follows it with an astonishing declaration — “But we have Christ’s mind.” The word “mind” here is the Greek νοῦς (nous), meaning one’s thinking, way of thinking, the angle from which one sees things.

Brothers and sisters, this is the very heart of 321: turning from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. To have the mind of Christ is to see people, things and ourselves through Christ’s eyes.

6. A 321 Insight

It is not I who serve; it is Christ who serves in me.

It is not passing on knowledge; it is passing on life.

This is the reality of Galatians 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness. Only when I am no longer “I” do I begin to become the person God wants me to be. A single drop of water on its own will evaporate; but once a drop enters the ocean, it will never dry up again. Selfless service is placing this drop that is me into God’s ocean.

This is also the foundation of “the 235 relationships”: becoming a “2” with a selfless person, as spiritual companions to each other; establishing the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and finally becoming the “5”, a team of spiritual comrades — a fivefold-ministry team working together. Life touching life is not a slogan; it is a road you can actually walk.

sections.heading: 5. The Third Teaching: Service That Begins with the “Spirit” Brings Authority and Power
sections.html:
1. Ask the Holy Spirit first; don’t start with methods

True service always begins with the “Spirit”.

Don’t start by thinking about how to do it; start by asking: what does the Holy Spirit want me to do?

Brothers and sisters, this order matters enormously. Our natural reaction is this: first we see a need, then we think up a plan, then we find the people, then we fix the schedule, and only at the very end do we pray and ask God to bless the plan we have already decided on. That is not seeking guidance — that is asking God to sign off on it.

How did the Lord Jesus himself serve? “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise” (John 5:19).

Notice: Jesus is the Son of God and has all power, yet he chose not to act on his own. He first “sees” what the Father is doing, and only then does it. The order is: first see, then act.

Moses understood this too. When God said he could send an angel to lead the Israelites up into Canaan, Moses answered, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). Moses would rather not move at all than have success without God going with him.

2. Four things “right” when the Holy Spirit is in charge

Scripture says, “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Mark 13:11).

The full context of this verse is: “When they lead you away and deliver you up, don’t be anxious beforehand, or premeditate what you will say, but say whatever will be given you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (Mark 13:11).

The setting in which the Lord said this was the time when the disciples would face trial and persecution. At the moment when people are least sure of themselves, the Lord’s assurance is not “make sure you are well prepared” but “it is not you who speak”.

When the Holy Spirit is in charge, you will experience four things being “right”: at the right time, to the right person, you say the right words and do the right thing.

Philip is the best example. The Holy Spirit said to him, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot” (Acts 8:29). And he obeyed. The result? On a road in the wilderness he met the Ethiopian eunuch, who was reading Isaiah 53 without understanding it. The right time, the right person, the right passage, the right words. Philip did only one thing: he listened, and then he went.

Brothers and sisters, this is not technique; this is guidance. Technique can be learned; guidance can only be asked for. Technique helps you get things done; guidance lets you accomplish the things of God.

3. Service like this carries power

“For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

The word “strongholds” is the Greek ὀχύρωμα (ochyrōma), meaning a fortress or citadel. Behind the city of Corinth towered a great citadel rock about 575 metres high — a natural stronghold almost impossible to take in the ancient world. When Paul used the word “strongholds” in writing to the Corinthians, all they had to do was look up and they could see that mountain.

So what are today’s strongholds? Paul explains it himself: “imaginations”, “every high thing”, “every thought”. It turns out that the real fortresses are not outside; they are in people’s thinking.

So true service is not surface change; it is throwing down patterns of thought, renewing mindsets and setting lives free. This is spiritual warfare.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly why 321 stresses “changing the mindset” from the very start. Behind a person’s behaviour are their habits; behind their habits are their values; behind their values is their mindset. If you only change the behaviour, in a couple of days it springs back; change the mindset and the life is turned around from the root. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

And what is the key to all this? Praying in the Holy Spirit and using God’s word: “And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; with all prayer and requests, praying at all times in the Spirit, and being watchful to this end in all perseverance and requests for all the saints” (Ephesians 6:17–18).

See how Paul puts two things side by side: the word of God, and prayer in the Spirit. Isn’t that exactly “Understanding” and “Spirit”? However sharp the sword, without a hand to hold it, it cuts nothing; however strong the hand, without a sword it is only swinging empty fists.

4. Three times “not you, but God”

When you let Jesus reign as King, you will discover three things.

It is not you who are striving; it is God who is at work. “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

It is not you who change people; it is God who changes them. “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

It is not you who serve; it is Jesus who serves. “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Brothers and sisters, the story of Gideon shows this most clearly. Thirty-two thousand men were ready to fight the Midianites, and God said there were too many; ten thousand were left, and God still said there were too many. “Yahweh said to Gideon, ‘The people who are with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel brag against me, saying, “My own hand has saved me”’” (Judges 7:2). In the end only three hundred were left, and what they carried were jars, torches and trumpets.

God was not afraid of too few people; he was afraid of too many — so many that they could take the credit for themselves.

When David faced Goliath, he too said, “For the battle is Yahweh’s” (1 Samuel 17:47).

And the prophet Zechariah left us these words that never go out of date: “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6).

5. Evidence from psychology: where burnout comes from

Modern psychology has done quite solid research on the fact that “serving for a long time wears you out”.

From 1981 onward, Professor Christina Maslach of the University of California, Berkeley, developed the well-known Maslach Burnout Inventory, which identifies three core dimensions of burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (treating people as tasks to be processed), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. In 2019 the World Health Organization, in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, formally defined burnout as “a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed”.

Brothers and sisters, notice Maslach’s second dimension — depersonalisation. The most obvious sign of a burnt-out servant is this: they begin to treat people as items on a to-do list. The list has to be got through, the visits have to be got through, the meetings have to be got through. People have become tasks.

And how clearly 321 puts it: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. When someone starts putting “ministry” ahead of “relationships”, burnout has already begun.

In addition, the “self-determination theory” developed by the psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan from the 1980s shows that when people act from intrinsic motivation, and their three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — are met, both their engagement and their persistence rise significantly; whereas if their actions are driven mainly by external pressure, they tire easily. In spiritual terms: what you do out of love you can do for a lifetime; what you do under pressure won’t last long.

6. A 321 Insight

To serve relying on the brain is to rely on yourself, and the result is pressure; to serve relying on the heart is to rely on the Holy Spirit, and the result is power.

Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. Because “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Let Jesus be King, and serving becomes light.

The Lord himself said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

Brothers and sisters, notice that the Lord didn’t say “take the yoke off”; he said “take my yoke upon you”. A yoke is made for two oxen — one lighter, one heavier, one older, one younger. The old ox leads in front; the young ox learns alongside. The Lord’s meaning is not that you don’t have to work, but this: you don’t have to pull alone.

“I’m holding it all up on my own” — those words have never been the Lord’s heart for you.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: 321 on the Path of Serving
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set what we have seen today back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. He said, “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). He took up a basin and a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). Our role model for serving is not a set of methods; it is a person.

The Bible is my standard. If service has no foundation of truth, zeal turns into distortion. Only by examining the Scriptures daily do we know what God wants, and what I merely think God wants.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Don’t start by thinking how to do it; start by asking what the Holy Spirit wants me to do. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6).

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. This is the very theme of this lesson. What does it mean to be King? It means to have the right to decide. In your service, who has the final say? The calendar? Your gifts? People’s expectations? Or Jesus?

Let Jesus receive all the glory. Peter states this with absolute firmness: “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever” (1 Peter 4:11). Glory is something that cannot be divided. Take a share of it, and God has that much less. John the Baptist’s attitude is the healthiest one: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

The Goal

Establish God’s system. Service is not running one event after another; it is establishing on earth a system in which Jesus reigns as King — a family in which people are loved, built up and sent out. The building materials of this system are lives, not programmes; relationships, not organisational charts.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

Brothers and sisters, the most piercing line in this lesson is this one from the text: if serving makes you more and more tired, it is not that you are doing too much — it is that “self” is doing too much.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. In service, pride wears many disguises: I won’t let go, because others won’t do it well; I’m so busy, because I’m the only one who can do it; I’m hurt, because nobody sees what I put in. The subject of every one of those sentences is “I”.

Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Letting God be God means no longer carrying for God what he himself means to carry; letting man be man means accepting our own limits, and accepting the limits of others too.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When a team of co-workers splits apart, it is usually not because they disagree; it is because two “I”s both want to be King at the same time.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When I step back to zero, God’s fullness has a channel to flow out through.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

What mindset is this lesson meant to change? The mindset that “serving is me doing things for God” must change into “serving is God doing things through me”.

Once the mindset changes, the life changes: you no longer need results to prove yourself. Once the life changes, daily living changes: you have rest, you have rhythm. Once daily living changes, relationships change: you begin to see people, not just tasks. Once relationships change, ministry changes: your service begins to give birth to life, not merely to activities.

A Shift in Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s: not asking “Does this work?” but “Does this please God?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: not asking “What do others think of me?” but “How does the Lord see me?”

From the temporary to the eternal: not asking “How much did I get done this year?” but “Will this person still be standing twenty years from now?”

From the worldly to the godly: not relying on methods, connections and resources, but on the Holy Spirit.

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice: every person you are in relationship with is your “2”. Before each “2”, practise selflessness (0), and you will bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). In the end, the fruit of your service is not measured by how many meetings you ran, but by how many of these fruit you lived out before those people.

The 235 relationships: first find a selfless companion, and become a “2”; then have spiritual parents above you and spiritual children below you, and become a “3”; and finally work together within the fivefold ministry, and become a team of “5”. Brothers and sisters, if today you feel “I’m holding it all up on my own”, that is not just a matter of physical strength; it is a matter of relationships. God never designed anyone to serve alone. When the Lord sent out his disciples, he sent them out two by two (Mark 6:7).

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Letting Jesus Truly Reign as King in Our Service
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work each of them out one by one.

Practice 1: Before every time you serve, return first to the “Spirit”

Don’t rush to act; first be still before God.

Pray: Lord, today it’s not about what I want to do — what do you want to do?

Learn to wait first, then act.

Information: first know this truth — Jesus said, “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19). Even the Son of God, when he served, first looked at what the Father was doing.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see how much of your past service has been “decide first, pray afterwards”. That moment of seeing is revelation.

Conviction: say to God in your heart: I agree, this is right, I need to change.

Implementation: starting this week, before every time you serve, give God five minutes. Just be still, and just ask one question: Lord, what do you want to do?

Evaluation: after a week, look back — have those five minutes changed the spirit in which you serve?

Correction: if you can’t manage five minutes, start with two; if you often forget, set a reminder.

Repetition: four weeks in a row, without a break. A new habit needs time; a new mindset needs repetition.

Multiplication: bring a co-worker along. Be still together before you serve, and ask this one question together.

Practice 2: Practise “not I, but Christ”

As you serve, keep reminding yourself: it is not I who speak, it is the Holy Spirit who speaks; it is not I who do it, it is Jesus who does it.

Turn your focus from “me” to “Jesus”.

Information: memorise Galatians 2:20 — “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Revelation: as you serve, when you notice you are tense, or notice you are enjoying the applause, stop and ask God to show you who the subject of the sentence is at that moment.

Conviction: admit that the “I” is really there; don’t pretend you are already selfless.

Implementation: every time before you go on stage, every time before you open your mouth, say silently in your heart: not I, but Christ.

Evaluation: has this sentence changed the way you react to applause and to criticism?

Correction: if you find you still care a great deal about what others think of you, change your prayer to this: Lord, please take away my fear of people.

Repetition: let this sentence become your catchphrase — become your very breathing.

Multiplication: share this practice in your small group, and invite everyone to use this sentence to remind one another.

Practice 3: Use “the fruit” to test whether you are letting the Lord be King

Examine your service: is it pressure or joy? Does it rely on methods or on the Holy Spirit? Is it surface change or change of life?

If serving makes you more and more tired, it is not that you are doing too much — it is that “self” is doing too much. Hand the sovereignty back to Jesus again.

Information: know the Lord’s promise — “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). The Lord never intended to crush you.

Revelation: face your answers to these three questions honestly. Don’t dress them up, don’t spiritualise them.

Conviction: admit that exhaustion is not glory; exhaustion is often a warning sign.

Implementation: take a sheet of paper and list everything you are serving in right now. Next to each item write: did God give me this, or did I take it on myself?

Evaluation: go over this sheet with your pastor or your spiritual companion.

Correction: lay down what should be laid down; hand over what should be handed over. Laying something down is not unfaithfulness; letting go is trusting God.

Repetition: review it again every quarter.

Multiplication: once you have learned a healthy rhythm of serving, go and hold up a co-worker who is about to fall.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please keep these few sentences in your heart.

Serving is not proving yourself; it is displaying Jesus.

Don’t hold up your service with your own ability; let the Holy Spirit lead.

You are not the source; Jesus is.

Hudson Taylor, founder of the China Inland Mission, is generally credited with this saying: God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply. That is exactly Peter’s chorēgeō — the one who pays for everything is God.

The psalmist said it long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain” (Psalm 127:1). In vain — not because people didn’t work hard, but because they worked hard for the wrong object.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we have seen three things together.

First, a life without “Service” is a stagnant, even a dying, life. Life is not meant to be hoarded; life is meant to flow.

Second, service without “Spirit, Understanding, Life” is incomplete service. True service is life touching life.

Third, service that begins with the “Spirit” brings authority and power. It is not you who are striving; it is God who is at work.

So true service is not about how impressive you are, but about how much room you give Jesus.

This is a very simple yet very deep measuring rod. It does not measure how great your gifts are; it measures how much room you have yielded. Yield a little, and he reigns a little; yield everything, and he reigns completely.

When you let Jesus be King, your service has power, your service bears fruit, your service has joy.

The focus is not on yourself, not on methods, not on results. Only on Jesus.

Letting Jesus be King is the most powerful service there is.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to invite you to make a decision.

If you are already exhausted, please stop holding it all up. Put that burden of “I’m holding it all up on my own” into the Lord’s hands. He says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

If you have been receiving all along but have not yet let anything flow out, ask the Lord to give you an outlet. Even if it is just one phone call, one visit, one time of keeping someone company. From today, let the living water flow out.

If you are serving, but have realised that all these years you have been sitting in the Lord’s seat, please give up that seat today. Let Jesus be King: give the pulpit back to him, give the ministry back to him, give the people back to him, give the glory back to him.

Because “to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen” (1 Peter 4:11).

keyVerses: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms. If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.” (1 Peter 4:10–11)
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord Jesus, I am willing to hand the sovereignty of my service over to you.
I will no longer rely on myself; I will rely on the guidance and power of the Holy Spirit.
I declare: it is not I who serve, but Christ who serves in me; it is not I who receive the glory, but Jesus who receives all the glory.
My service will bring power, life and change.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Use “the fruit” to test whether you are letting the Lord be King
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
Thank you — you are the King who serves. Though you were in the form of God, you took up a basin and a towel and washed your disciples’ feet. You are my role model in serving.
Lord, I confess that in my service there has been far too much “me”. I have held it up with my own strength, done it my own way, measured myself by my own results. I am tired, and I have run dry.
Lord, today I hand the sovereignty of my service back to you.
Forgive my pride; forgive me for taking your seat. Put that “I” in me that wants to be King on the cross, and bring me into selflessness, so that your fullness can flow out from within me.

Holy Spirit, please guide me. Teach me not to rush to act, but first to be still and wait; teach me not to start with methods, but first to ask for your will. Plant your word deep within me, to be my standard.

Lord, let my service be not merely the completing of tasks but the passing on of life; not merely surface change, but the throwing down of strongholds, the renewing of people’s mindsets and the setting free of their lives.
Give me, too, people to walk alongside me — a spiritual companion, spiritual parents, spiritual children — so that I am no longer holding it all up on my own.
May my service bring power, life and change. May you, in all things, receive all the glory through Jesus Christ.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: “Every living creature which swarms, in every place where the rivers come, will live. Then there will be a very great multitude of fish; for these waters have come there, and the waters of the sea will be healed, and everything will live wherever the river comes.” (Ezekiel 47:9) Please share: is your spiritual life right now more like the Sea of Galilee or more like the Dead Sea?
