Key points:
• The heart of “lead” is being together (Mark 3:14) — let them see the real you.
• “Accompany” is the hardest, because you must put up with them doing it worse than you; every time you take over, they take one step back.
• Education: scaffolding theory (Wood, Bruner, Ross, 1976) — the value of scaffolding is that it finally comes down.
• Medical training motto: see one, do one, teach one (generally traced to Halsted’s residency system).

brief21.title: An Example of Letting Go
notes: Slide text:
Barnabas brought Saul to the apostles
Later it became “Paul and his company”
“He must increase, but I must decrease”
(John 3:30)
Key points:
• Acts 9:27, 11:25–26: Barnabas took Saul in and served alongside him in Antioch for a whole year.
• From “Barnabas and Saul” in Acts 13:2 to “Paul and his company” in 13:13 — his name stepped back behind.
• Barnabas went on to lead Mark; 2 Timothy 4:11: “he is useful to me for service”.
• Light from 321: not holding on to people but building them up; not controlling people but setting them free.

brief21.title: Three Practices
notes: Slide text:
Ask daily: whom did I influence?
Care, accompany, draw people to God
Find one person: lead, accompany, release
Don’t be afraid they won’t do it well
Key points:
• Practice 1: replace “How much did I get done today?” with “Whose life did I influence today?” and write down one name each night.
• Practice 2: stay ten minutes after the meeting, ask “How have you been lately?”, and end by praying together.
• Practice 3: the Lord Jesus too led only twelve, and among them three in a special way.
• Draw up a timetable; there must be a date for “release”, or accompanying becomes dependence without end.

brief21.title: The Eight Stages, All the Way
notes: Slide text:
Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation
Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication
The last stage is Multiplication
Only multiplication completes the course
Key points:
• Information: write the three key points as three sentences; Revelation: ask the Lord to show what I am clinging to.
• Conviction: admit that I have been doing tasks, not raising up people; Implementation: write down the first name tonight.
• Evaluation and Correction: look back after a week — have I taken the task back into my own hands again?
• Repetition: Hebrews 5:14, senses exercised by use; Multiplication: they begin to lead someone else.

brief21.title: Summing Up with the 3-2-1 Vision
notes: Slide text:
Three Foundations, Two Core Values, the Goal
The old self is self-centred; the new self selfless
Life first, then relationships, then ministry
From the temporary to the eternal
Key points:
• The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.
• The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory; the Goal: establish God’s system.
• Being self-centred makes the ministry an extension of me; selflessness lets me fall into the earth like a grain of wheat (Galatians 2:20).
• The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry; the 235 relationships, from 2 to 3 to 5.
• The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

brief21.title: Leave Life, Not Just Work
notes: Slide text:
Not how much you did
But how much life you leave behind
Not on tasks, people or results
Only on Jesus
Key points:
• A gentle reminder: don’t just be a good co-worker — become a spiritual parent; don’t just complete tasks — build up lives.
• On that day the Lord will ask: those people I put into your hands — where are they today?
• The three-step call: open your hand, write the name down, turn your focus back to Jesus.
• Point to the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

brief21.title: Prayer of Response and Blessing
notes: Slide text:
Lord, give me a parent’s heart
Willing to build people up and set them free
Reign as King in my service
May all the glory be yours
Key points:
• Lead the congregation in prayer together, asking the Lord to forgive our clinging and our fear.
• Ask the Holy Spirit to place one name on our hearts today.
• Declaration: I am not someone who only does tasks; I am someone who passes on life; I am not building a ministry; I am building disciples.
• Blessing: may the Lord’s life flow out from you and be passed on from generation to generation. Amen.

script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we are reflecting together on the second talk on the Path of Serving: passing on life and multiplying disciples. Before he ascended, the Lord Jesus said: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Brothers and sisters, the ultimate goal of serving is not to get things done well, but to pass on life.

Please be still for three seconds and answer one question in your heart: if the Lord took you home tomorrow morning, what would the service in your hands leave behind? A to-do list — or someone who can already stand on their own? We often measure service by three indicators: growing numbers, expanding ministry and power on display. None of these is bad, but none of them is the goal the Lord spoke of. What the Lord said was — make disciples of all nations. Not bigger meetings, but disciples made. There was a sister who led the children’s Sunday school for twenty years. For family reasons she had to step away for three months, and the Sunday school came to a standstill. With tears she said: “So for these twenty years I’ve been doing the work, not raising up people.” Brothers and sisters, the greatest danger in serving is not doing it badly, but doing it too well — so well that nobody else can get a hand in.

Let’s look at the background. The scene is a mountain in Galilee. Scripture records honestly that the disciples worshipped him, but some doubted; those the Lord sends have never been perfect people. In the original language this passage has only one main verb in the imperative: “make disciples”. “Go”, “baptizing” and “teaching” are all participles. Making disciples is the goal. A “disciple” means “a learner”; in the Jewish world, being a disciple didn’t mean attending classes — it meant living with your teacher. Brothers and sisters, discipleship is not a course; it is a road walked together.

Our first key point: the purpose of serving is not a display of power. In serving we often see miracles, being deeply moved, power. These are all real, but none of them is the final goal. If someone experiences many miracles and is often deeply moved, yet their life hasn’t changed and they can’t go and influence others, then that kind of service is still stuck at the level of “Spirit”. In Matthew 7:22–23, people say to the Lord: didn’t we prophesy, cast out demons and do mighty works in your name? The Lord doesn’t deny their power. What the Lord says is: “I never knew you.”

So what is true service? Three things: helping people’s lives to change, helping people to follow Jesus, helping people to go and influence others. Paul says: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). This is a chain: I imitate Christ, you imitate me, and you in turn lead others to imitate Christ. Paul also says to commit these things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2) — there are four generations there, and four generations is multiplication. The psychologist Bandura’s social learning theory tells us that people are changed mainly not by lecturing, but by example. Brothers and sisters, receiving life is not the finish line; passing life on is the goal.

Our second key point: the heart of serving is not doing tasks. On his last night on earth, the Lord Jesus did something that has shaken every generation since — he washed his disciples’ feet. He said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). In that era, washing feet was the work of Gentile slaves. The first thing the Lord did was kneel down. Scripture says he knew that the Father had given all things into his hands — and so he was able to bend low. Brothers and sisters, humility is not low self-esteem; humility is something only a person secure in their identity can do.

Behind this “task” of washing feet lay two purposes. First, to restore our relationship with God. The Lord said: “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean” (John 13:10). The original uses two different words: bathing is the whole body; washing the feet is only part. The bath is the salvation the Lord accomplished once for all on the cross; foot-washing is the cleansing we need every day. Second, to build our relationships with one another. The Lord said: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). So tasks are the tool; relationships are the goal. Many problems in serving are not that the task wasn’t done well, but that a relationship has broken. Harvard University’s study of adult development, running since 1938, found that what best predicts a person’s health and happiness is good relationships. Brothers and sisters, people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than results.

Our third key point: with a parent’s heart. Paul says: “Though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers” (see 1 Corinthians 4:15). A co-worker watches progress; a parent watches maturity. A parent’s heart has one mark: a willingness to build others up, even to let them surpass you. A heart like this always involves denying of self. The Lord Jesus said: “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). This is the highest level of service: I die, so that you may live.

The Lord drove it home with a picture: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). When a grain of wheat is buried in the soil, its seed coat swells and splits, all the nourishment stored inside is used up, and only then can the new shoot grow. Without dying, there is no multiplying; without denying of self, there is no legacy. Passing on life has three stages: lead — do it while they watch; accompany — let them do it, while you stand alongside to support and correct; release — let go, and let them go and lead others. Educational psychology tells us that the value of scaffolding is that in the end it must come down. Barnabas once brought Saul to the apostles, and later Scripture’s record changed from “Barnabas and Saul” to “Paul and his company”. Brothers and sisters, not holding on to people, but building them up; not controlling people, but setting them free.

Today there are three practices. First, ask yourself one question every day: not how much did I get done today, but whose life did I influence today? Write down one name each night. Second, practise building life relationships: care about the other person’s life, walk alongside their growth, and help them draw closer to God. Stay ten minutes longer after the meeting; don’t just ask, “Can you come next week?” — ask, “How have you been lately?” Third, begin to practise lead, accompany, release. Find one person: lead them, accompany them, release them. Don’t be afraid that they won’t do it well, because growth always goes through a process. The very last of the eight stages of changing our mindset is Multiplication. Only with multiplication is the course complete.

Brothers and sisters, truly successful service is not how much you did, but how much life you leave behind. One day, standing before the Lord, he will ask: those people I put into your hands — where are they today? So don’t just be a good co-worker; become a spiritual parent. Don’t just complete tasks; build up lives. The focus is not on tasks, not on people, not on results — only on Jesus. Today I invite you to do three things: open your hand, write the name down, and turn your focus back to Jesus. This is letting Jesus be King, and letting Jesus receive all the glory.

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, you are the first grain of wheat that fell into the earth. Forgive our clinging, forgive our fear. Give us a parent’s heart, willing to build people up, willing to set people free. Holy Spirit, please place one name in our hearts today, so that we may lead them, accompany them, and, on the right day, release them. May you reign as King in our service, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord’s life flow out from you, and be passed on from generation to generation.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we are reflecting together on the second talk on the Path of Serving: passing on life and multiplying disciples. Let’s first read our theme passage. Before he ascended, on a mountain in Galilee, the Lord Jesus said: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:19–20). Please hold today’s first sentence in your heart: the ultimate goal of serving is not to get things done well, but to pass on life.

Let’s begin with a question. Please be still for three seconds and answer honestly: if the Lord took you home tomorrow morning, what would that area of service in your hands leave behind? What comes to most people’s minds is a to-do list. But please think one layer further down: apart from these “tasks”, is there a “person” who, because you have walked alongside them, can now stand up and take the baton from you? There was a sister who led the children’s Sunday school for twenty years. For family reasons she had to step away for three months, and the Sunday school all but collapsed. When she came back she said with tears: “So for these twenty years I’ve been doing the work, not raising up people.”

We often measure service by three indicators: growing numbers, expanding ministry and power on display. None of these is bad in itself. But the Lord’s last command before he ascended was not “make the meetings bigger” but — make disciples of all nations. Not bigger meetings, but disciples made; not getting the job done, but passing on life. Brothers and sisters, the greatest danger in serving is not doing it badly, but doing it too well — so well that nobody else can get a hand in. True service does not make people depend on you; it helps people follow Jesus, just as you do. A lamp is lit so that other lamps can be lit too.

Let’s look at the background. Matthew’s Gospel was written by the apostle Matthew, generally thought to be between AD 50 and 70, mainly for Jewish believers. The scene is a mountain in Galilee — the Lord’s ministry began in Galilee, and after the resurrection he brought the disciples back to the starting point to send them out afresh. Scripture records honestly: some doubted. Those the Lord sends have never been perfect people. First the Lord says: all authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. The Great Commission is built on the Lord’s authority, not on our ability. In the original language this passage has only one main verb in the imperative: “make disciples”; “go”, “baptizing” and “teaching” are all participles. A disciple means “a learner”; being a rabbi’s disciple didn’t mean attending his classes — it meant living with him.

Our first key point: the purpose of serving is not a display of power. In serving we often see miracles, being deeply moved, power — these are all grace, but they are not the final goal. Imagine someone who has experienced many miracles, and when he shares his testimony the whole room is shaken; yet five years go by, his temper hasn’t changed, his family hasn’t been influenced, and there isn’t one person around him who loves Jesus more because of him. Service like that is still stuck at the level of “Spirit” — feelings without life. The Lord himself said: in that day many will say, didn’t we prophesy, cast out demons and do mighty works in your name? But the Lord will say: I never knew you (see Matthew 7:22–23).

So what is true service? Three levels: helping people’s lives to change, helping people to follow Jesus, helping people to go and influence others. This is a conveyor belt of life: people are changed, people are placed in the Lord’s hands, people are sent out to change others. Brothers and sisters, leave out the third, and life stops at my station. When God called Abraham he said: “I will bless you and make your name great. You will be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2). The blessing God gives is not a terminus; it is a relay station.

Paul said something extraordinarily bold: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). In the original, “imitate” doesn’t mean “agree with my ideas”, but “live the way I live”. Paul dared to say this not because he thought himself perfect, but because he knew that making disciples doesn’t depend on passing on ideas, but on passing on life. Here is a chain: I imitate Christ, you imitate me, and you in turn lead others to imitate Christ. 2 Timothy 2:2 puts it more fully: commit these things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also. Count them — there are four generations in that verse. Four generations — that is multiplication.

How is life passed on? Scripture says that the first purpose for which the Lord chose the twelve was “that they might be with him” (Mark 3:14). First with him, then sent out. The psychologist Bandura’s social learning theory and his Bobo doll experiment confirmed that people are changed mainly not by lecturing, but by models. Children don’t do what adults say; they do what adults do. Church history bears witness too: Irenaeus said that as a young man he heard Polycarp preach, and Polycarp had walked with the apostle John. The gospel did not reach the second century through one huge evangelistic rally, but through one old man leading one young man. The first light is this: receiving life is not the finish line; passing life on is the goal.

Our second key point: the heart of serving is not doing tasks. On his last night on earth the Lord did something that has shaken every generation since — he washed his disciples’ feet. John 13:1 says that, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. He did not settle his property or arrange an organisation; the first thing he did was kneel down. He said: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). In that era, washing feet was the work of Gentile slaves, the lowest task in society.

There is an important detail here. Scripture says that Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God — and then he rose from supper, wrapped a towel around his waist and washed their feet (see John 13:3–4). Notice where the word “knowing” appears. Precisely because he knew his identity completely, he was able to kneel down. Brothers and sisters, humility is not low self-esteem; humility is something only a person secure in their identity can do. Someone who is still trying to prove themselves cannot kneel down. 321 puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position.

Behind this act of washing feet lay two purposes. First, to restore our relationship with God. The Lord said: “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean” (John 13:10). The original uses two different verbs: bathing is washing the whole body; foot-washing is washing part of it. The whole-body bath is accomplished once and valid for ever — that is the salvation of the cross; but foot-washing is a daily matter, because our feet pick up dust and we need to come before the Lord every day. Second, to build our relationships with one another. The Lord said: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15).

So we must distinguish clearly: tasks are the tool; relationships are the goal. Many problems in serving are not that the task wasn’t done well, but that a relationship has broken. The choir’s problem is seldom singing out of tune; mostly it is that someone feels overlooked. The leaders’ meeting’s problem is seldom a poor proposal; mostly it is that after the meeting, two people stopped speaking to each other. Harvard University’s study of adult development, begun in 1938 and running for more than eighty years, points out that what best predicts whether a person will be healthy and happy in later life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships. The second light is this: people matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than results. Don’t hurt people to get things done; build people through getting things done.

Our third key point: with a parent’s heart. A co-worker looks at who is going to do this job; a parent looks at how this person is going to grow up. A co-worker cares about progress; a parent cares about maturity. A co-worker wants the task finished; a parent wants the other person one day to no longer need them. Paul says: “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News” (1 Corinthians 4:15). The “tutor” was, in Roman times, a household servant who took children to and from school — he had duties but no bond of flesh and blood. To the Thessalonian church Paul was like a nursing mother cherishing her children, and like a father exhorting his own; he even said, I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you (Galatians 4:19).

A heart like this always involves denying of self. The Lord Jesus said: “Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). Remember the setting of those words — the disciples were arguing over the seats on his right and left. This is the highest level of service: I die, so that you may live. The Lord also said: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). When a grain of wheat is buried in the soil, its seed coat swells and splits, and all the nourishment stored inside is broken down and used up, just to supply the tiny shoot that has only just appeared. By the time the new seedling breaks through the soil, the grain of wheat can no longer be found. Without dying, there is no multiplying; without denying of self, there is no legacy.

How do we walk the road of passing on life? Three stages: lead, accompany, release. First, “lead” — do it while they watch. The key is being together. Don’t start by tossing them an instruction manual; let them stand beside you and watch how you pray, how you care for people, how you keep your mouth shut when you are misunderstood. Second, “accompany” — let them start doing it, while you stand alongside to support, encourage and correct. This step is the hardest, because you have to put up with them doing it worse than you. At this point a voice will rise up in your heart: I’d better just do it myself. Brothers and sisters, please hold that hand back, because every time you take over, they take one step back. Educational psychology’s idea of “scaffolding” reminds us: the value of scaffolding lies not in how firmly it is put up, but in this — in the end it must come down.

Third, “release” — let go, and let them go and lead others. “Release” takes the most faith, because releasing means I am no longer needed. The most beautiful example in Scripture is Barnabas. When Saul had just come to faith, the disciples were all afraid of him; it was Barnabas who took him in and brought him to the apostles. Later Barnabas went all the way to Tarsus to look for him and brought him to Antioch, where they served together for a whole year. On the first mission Scripture writes “Barnabas and Saul”; before long it has become “Paul and his company”. Barnabas then took on Mark, who had given up halfway; many years later Paul wrote from prison: take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service. And Mark went on to write the Gospel of Mark. John the Baptist said: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). The third light: not holding on to people, but building them up; not controlling people, but setting them free.

If we understand the teaching but it never lands in our daily living, tomorrow everything will carry on as before. So there are three practices. First, ask yourself one question every day: not “How much did I get done today?” but “Whose life did I influence today?” Write down one name each night. Second, practise building life relationships: care about the other person’s life, walk alongside their growth, and help them draw closer to God. Stay ten minutes longer after the meeting; don’t just ask, “Can you come next week?” — ask, “How have you been lately?” Third, begin to practise lead, accompany, release. This very week, find one specific person — not a group of people, one person. Give yourself a timetable, and there must be a date for “release”. Don’t be afraid that they won’t do it well, because growth always goes through a process.

For a mindset to become life, it has to go through all eight stages. Information: write the three key points as three sentences. Revelation: ask the Lord to shine his light — in my service, what have I been holding on to and won’t let go? Conviction: say “yes” to the Lord in your heart. Implementation: write down the first name tonight. Evaluation: after a week, look back honestly — have I taken the task back into my own hands again? Correction: if you’re too hurried, slow down; if you have no time, hand over one area of ministry. Repetition: life lessons are learned through repeated practice. Multiplication: when the person you are leading begins to lead someone else, only then has your mindset truly run its full course. Brothers and sisters, multiplication is the destination of changing our mindset, and the destination of serving too.

Let’s sum up with 321. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — the Lord said, “I have given you an example”; the Bible is my standard — the ruler for measuring service is “make disciples of all nations”; the Holy Spirit is my guide — so we dare to let go, because the one who keeps the disciples is the Holy Spirit, not us. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The greatest temptation in serving is to make ourselves king; the deepest obstacle to passing on life is the fear of others surpassing me. The Goal: establish God’s system. The watershed of this lesson is self-centredness versus selflessness: when the old self is self-centred, the ministry becomes an extension of me; only when the new self is selfless can I fall into the earth like a grain of wheat. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. And the order must never be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Brothers and sisters, truly successful service is not how much you did, but how much life you leave behind. One day, standing before the Lord, he will not ask how many special conferences you ran, nor on how many posters your name was printed. What the Lord will ask is: those people I put into your hands — where are they today? Are they more like me? So don’t just be a good co-worker; become a spiritual parent. Don’t just complete tasks; build up lives. The focus is not on tasks, because tasks pass away; not on people, because people change; not on results, because results are in God’s hands. The focus is only on Jesus. Today I invite you to make three decisions: open your hand, write the name down, and turn your focus back to Jesus.

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You are the first grain of wheat that fell into the earth; you gave up your own life so that we might receive eternal life. Lord, forgive our clinging, forgive our fear, forgive that bit of pride in our hearts that doesn’t want to be surpassed. Give us a parent’s heart: willing to build people up, willing to set people free, willing to let people go further than we have. Holy Spirit, please place one name in our hearts today, so that from this week we may lead them, accompany them, and, on the right day, release them. May you reign as King in our service, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen. May the Lord’s life flow out from you, and be passed on from generation to generation.

sections.heading: Introduction: At the End of the Road of Service, There Is Only One Question
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to be still for half a minute and call one picture to mind.

Think of a time of service you took part in that went extremely well. Perhaps it was a meeting packed to the doors, perhaps a time of worship in song that moved the whole room, perhaps a sharing that many people praised. Hold that picture in your heart, and then honestly ask yourself one question —

After the meeting ended that day, what was the very first thought that rose up in your heart?

Was it, “Thank you, Lord, you did all of this,” or was it, “Good thing I prepared,” or “Lucky I was here today”?

Brothers and sisters, that thought looks small — so small that no one else will ever know about it. Yet in God’s eyes, that one small thought is the last and most decisive checkpoint on the whole road of service.

The Path of Serving in Kingdom 321 has five stations.

The first station is “Spirit” — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit’s guidance, everything we do is merely religious activity.

The second station is “Understanding” — the Bible is my standard. Without the foundation of truth, zeal will carry us off in the wrong direction.

The third station is “Life” — Jesus is my role model. Without a changed life, service is just a performance.

The fourth station is “Service” — let Jesus be King. When a life has been changed, practical giving and service will inevitably flow out of it.

The fifth station is “God” — let Jesus receive all the glory. This is the destination, and the purpose of the whole road.

Right at its opening the lesson sums up the entire road: the starting point of service is Jesus; the process of service is Jesus; the end point of service is still Jesus.

But brothers and sisters, we cannot avoid facing a heartbreaking reality.

In church history, far too many people have walked the first four stations beautifully. They had the Holy Spirit’s leading, the foundation of truth, a changed life and practical service; their preaching had power, their prayers were answered, and revival broke out wherever they went. And yet at the very end, they fell. They did not fall for lack of gifts, nor for lack of fruit. They fell because — the glory went to themselves.

Why? Because the last and most decisive station was missing: “God” — giving all the glory to God.

If, at the end of the road of service, the focus has turned to ourselves, then even the greatest ministry becomes the beginning of ruin.

So this morning, let us go together into the deepest core of all.

The end point of service is not success; the end point of service is glorifying God.

The final question on this road is just one question, and it has only one right answer: to whom does the glory go?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Men, Two Endings
sections.html:
Today’s theme passages set two men before our eyes: Herod, seated on a throne, and John the Baptist, standing in the wilderness. One wanted glory and lost his life; the other laid glory down and was called by the Lord the greatest of all born of women. And between them stands Paul, whose whole life of toil gives us the best commentary on both.

The first passage is John 3:30.

The Gospel of John was written by the disciple whom the Lord loved, the apostle John; it is generally thought to have been completed between AD 80 and 90, and its place of writing is most often held to be Ephesus in Asia Minor. John himself states his purpose for writing: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

“He must increase, but I must decrease” — these words were not spoken in quiet meditation. They were spoken in a deeply awkward situation. John 3:23 records: “John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came, and were baptized.” At that point John’s ministry was at its height. But his disciples came running to him with news they could not accept: “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptizes, and everyone is coming to him.” (John 3:26)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the point of what the disciples said — “everyone is coming to him.” Put into today’s words, it means: Teacher, we’re losing our people, and the meeting across the way keeps getting bigger.

This is a temptation every servant of God will face sooner or later: when someone else flourishes, what do I do?

John’s answer comes in three layers. The first concerns the source of everything: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27) The second concerns his own position: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29) The third is the declaration that has shaken the ages: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The second passage is Acts 12:23.

The Acts of the Apostles was written by Luke, Paul’s co-worker and the beloved physician, and the book is addressed to Theophilus (Acts 1:1). The Herod of chapter 12 is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled over all Judea from about AD 41 to 44. To please the Jews, he killed James, John’s brother, with the sword (Acts 12:2), and then moved to arrest Peter.

The event took place in Caesarea. Scripture records: “On an appointed day, Herod dressed himself in royal clothing, sat on the throne, and gave a speech to them. The people shouted, ‘The voice of a god, and not of a man!’” (Acts 12:21–22) Then come these fearful words: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)

The Jewish historian Josephus records the same event in Book 19 of his Antiquities of the Jews: Herod wore a garment woven of silver that glittered in the early-morning sun; the crowd flattered him as a god; he was at once seized by violent pain in his belly and died a few days later. The year was AD 44. Scripture and the historical record confirm one another.

The third passage is 1 Corinthians 15:10.

1 Corinthians is the letter Paul wrote from Ephesus to the church in Corinth around AD 55. Corinth was a prosperous and chaotic port city, and the church there had factions and quarrels — some exalted Paul, others exalted Apollos. Chapter 15 is the greatest chapter on the resurrection in the whole Bible. Paul first lists the witnesses of the resurrection, and then speaks of himself: “and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.” (1 Corinthians 15:8) Immediately after comes his moving account of himself.

Two men, two endings. One kept the glory for himself and died on the spot; the other yielded the glory to Christ and was exalted in the Kingdom of Heaven. Brothers and sisters, today’s message begins right here.

sections.heading: 1. Not Giving the Glory to God Is the Beginning of Spiritual Ruin
sections.html:
1. One Verse, One Solemn Law

Scripture gives us a very solemn warning:

“Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)

Notice that Scripture does not say Herod spoke badly. It does not say he governed incompetently, or that he did anything wrong that day. That day he wore his royal robes, sat on his throne, and the people cheered — from a human point of view it was the most glorious day of his life.

What he did wrong was not a lack of ability; it was keeping the glory for himself.

Here is a spiritual law: the greater our ability and the wider our influence, the easier it is to give the glory to ourselves.

Someone nobody knows finds it hard to take the glory for himself, because no one is giving him any. But when the applause comes, when the fruit appears, when people start saying, “This is the voice of a god” — that is the moment of the real exam.

2. The Original Meaning of Glory Is “Weight”

The word “glory” is well worth pausing over. In Greek it is doxa, which corresponds to the Old Testament Hebrew kabod, and the root meaning of kabod is “heavy,” “weighty.”

So the glory of God originally means God’s weight, God’s substance, God’s true being made visible.

Brothers and sisters, this explains something: why is it that as soon as a person gives the glory to himself, things go wrong?

Because glory has weight. When someone hoists onto his shoulders a weight that doesn’t belong to him, there is only one outcome — he is crushed.

What Herod took on that day was not a weight he was meant to bear. His shoulders could not carry the title “god,” and so he fell.

God said long ago: “I am Yahweh. That is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to engraved images.” (Isaiah 42:8)

God does not withhold his glory from false gods because he is stingy; he does it out of mercy. He knows that what has been created cannot bear the weight of the Creator.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: From Nebuchadnezzar to the King of Tyre

This law appears again and again in the Bible.

Nebuchadnezzar was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon when he said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30) Scripture goes on: “While the word was in the king’s mouth, a voice came from the sky, saying, ‘O king Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: “The kingdom has departed from you.”’” (Daniel 4:31) Before he had even finished speaking, his kingdom was gone. Thank the Lord, Nebuchadnezzar later repented, and he said: “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” (Daniel 4:37)

And the king of Tyre? God said through Ezekiel: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” (Ezekiel 28:17a) Notice “corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor.” Splendour itself was not the fault; the fault was that his eyes were dazzled by his own splendour.

Isaiah 14 records the five “I will”s in the heart of the shining morning star: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14) Those five “I will”s are the whole story of every fall in miniature.

So Scripture’s conclusion is perfectly clear:

“Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5b)

4. An Illustration from Life: The Moon Never Shines

Let me take an illustration from the sky.

The moon is the brightest body in the night sky, yet the moon itself gives off no light at all. Its albedo is only about 12 per cent: of the sunlight that falls on the lunar surface, only about one-eighth is reflected back. Of all the clear moonlight we admire, not one particle belongs to the moon.

The moon is at its loveliest when it keeps to its place and faithfully reflects the light of the sun.

And when is the moon at its worst? When it moves between the sun and the earth and blocks the sun — that is called an eclipse. At that moment the moon stands in the most “central” position, and plunges the whole earth into darkness.

Brothers and sisters, it is the same for those who serve. If we keep to our place as reflectors, people see the beauty of God; if we step in between God and people and block his light, that isn’t called shining — it’s called eclipsing.

5. Confirmation from Psychology: Taking the Credit Is Instinct

Psychology has a classic finding called the “self-serving attribution bias.” In 1975 two scholars, Miller and Ross, published a widely cited review article in the Psychological Bulletin, bringing together a large body of research and showing that people generally tend to attribute their successes to their own ability and effort, and their failures to outside circumstances and bad luck.

Another related finding is the study Kruger and Dunning published in 1999 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology: those with weaker abilities are often the most likely to overestimate themselves, because they lack the very ability needed to recognise their own shortcomings.

Brothers and sisters, together these two studies point to one thing: taking the credit for ourselves doesn’t need to be learned. It’s instinct.

In other words, “giving the glory to ourselves” is not an occasional slip; it is the old self’s automatic reflex. We don’t have to work at being proud. If we simply do nothing, pride will grow all by itself.

The British writer C. S. Lewis, in the chapter on “The Great Sin” in Book Three of Mere Christianity, calls pride the most fundamental evil, the state of mind that is completely opposed to God. He is right. Pride is not one sin among many; pride is the root of every sin.

6. Applying 321: Pride Is Leaving Our Originally Intended Position

This is exactly the core truth that 321 teaches.

The mark of the old self is the self-centred life; the mark of the new self is selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem.

What is pride? 321 gives a very precise definition: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take the place of God.

That is exactly what Herod did that day. The people said, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” He did not deny it. He left his originally intended position as a man and sat down in the seat of God.

What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In a serving team, as soon as one person starts grabbing glory, others start defending themselves, comparing, competing, until everyone is worn down. On the other hand, as soon as one person sincerely gives the glory to God and yields the credit to a brother, the whole atmosphere of the team relaxes.

So the 321 insight the lesson gives us is this —

It isn’t failure that destroys people; it is pride in the midst of success.

It isn’t a question of ability; it’s a question of where the glory goes.

When we begin to feel “I did it,” “it was my effort,” “I’m brilliant,” we have already drifted off course.

The real danger has never been outside us; it lies in “the focus of the heart.”

sections.heading: 2. Only When Everything Is Grace Can We Live in True Humility
sections.html:
1. How Paul Saw Himself

Paul was a man God used mightily in the New Testament. Thirteen letters, three missionary journeys, countless churches — all came through his hands. But how did he see himself?

“For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10)

Brothers and sisters, listen closely to the structure of what Paul says here. It is the most beautiful specimen of spiritual maturity.

First, he acknowledges the facts: “I worked more than all of them.” Paul isn’t being falsely modest. He really did labour harder than anyone. The Greek for “worked” is kopiaō, the kind of toil that leaves you utterly exhausted. He doesn’t deny what he gave.

Second, he immediately disowns the credit: “yet not I.”

Third, he returns everything to its source: “but the grace of God which was with me.”

Do you see it? True humility doesn’t say, “I did nothing” — that would be a lie. True humility says, “I did it, but it wasn’t I who did it.”

The Greek for “grace” is charis, meaning a free gift that is utterly undeserved. Paul’s whole life of theology could be condensed into that one word.

2. Humility Is Not Belittling Ourselves; It Is Seeing the Truth

Many people misunderstand humility. They think humility means talking yourself down, hiding your gifts, and hurrying to deny it whenever someone praises you. That isn’t humility; sometimes it’s just another form of self-preoccupation — still thinking about ourselves.

The lesson puts it very precisely: humility isn’t belittling ourselves; it is seeing the truth clearly.

What truth?

All my abilities were given by God.

All my opportunities were given by God.

All my fruit was produced by God.

What does Scripture say? “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)

Three questions, each one cutting deeper than the last. First: who makes you different? Second: what do you have that you didn’t receive? Third: since you received it, what right do you have to boast?

James says too: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow.” (James 1:17)

And John the Baptist puts it all in a single sentence: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” (John 3:27)

Brothers and sisters, even the very fact that we are able to serve is grace. If God had not chosen you, you wouldn’t even have the opportunity to stand here and serve.

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Clay Jars, Unworthy Servants, the God Who Works in Me

Scripture says the same thing from every angle.

From the angle of the vessel: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) Clay jars were the cheapest, plainest containers of the day. God deliberately put the treasure in clay jars so that people would see the treasure, not the vessel.

From the angle of the servant: “Even so you also, when you have done all the things that are commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy servants. We have done our duty.’” (Luke 17:10) Only doing everything commanded counts as doing our duty. So there is never any room for us to claim credit.

From the angle of motivation: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13) Even the very desire to serve was put there by God first.

From the angle of weakness: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9a)

From the angle of conclusion: “that, as it is written, ‘He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.’” (1 Corinthians 1:31)

4. Illustrations from Life: The Postman and the Light Bulb

Let me use two very everyday illustrations.

The first: the postman.

Suppose a postman delivers a registered letter, and inside the envelope is a cheque for ten million. The recipient is so delighted that he throws his arms round the postman and won’t let go, thanking him again and again. Now, would that postman say, “You’re welcome — that ten million is my gift to you”?

Of course not. He knows perfectly well: I’m the one delivering it, not the one paying it.

Brothers and sisters, every bit of grace, every word of comfort, every passage of truth we hand out in our service — not one of them is our own. We are the postman, not the benefactor.

The second: the light bulb.

A light bulb gives light, but a light bulb doesn’t generate electricity. Pull the plug, and the most expensive bulb in the world is just a piece of glass.

Jesus said it even more thoroughly: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “Apart from me you will do a little less,” but “you can do nothing.” Zero.

5. Confirmation from Psychology: Gratitude Is the Ability to See the Truth

Since everything is grace, the most natural response of a life lived in grace is gratitude.

In 2003 the psychologists Emmons and McCullough published a well-known study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, “Counting Blessings Versus Burdens.” They divided participants into groups: one group wrote down each week things they were grateful for, another wrote down hassles, and another neutral events. The group that kept recording gratitude scored markedly higher in overall well-being and optimism about the future, and also reported fewer physical complaints.

Brothers and sisters, this study tells us something: gratitude isn’t just good manners. Gratitude is an ability — the ability to see the truth.

Ungrateful people aren’t worse; they’re blinder. They can’t see the grace that holds them up every day, so they assume they earned everything themselves.

6. Applying 321: Change the Mindset and the Life Changes

321 says the fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

“Everything is grace” is a mindset. But once that mindset truly enters the heart, the whole life turns over.

The mindset changes: everything I have, I have received.

The life changes: I no longer need to prove myself by performance.

Daily living changes: I no longer compare myself with others, or fear that someone is better than me.

Relationships change: when others flourish, I can sincerely rejoice.

Ministry changes: I serve not to be seen but so that God will be seen.

This is precisely the shift of perspective that 321 speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one; from a temporary perspective to an eternal one; from the Worldly perspective to God’s perspective.

The lesson’s 321 insight says it so well —

It’s not that I deserve it; it’s that I’ve received mercy.

It’s not that I can; it’s that God can.

It’s not what I have done; it’s what God has done in me.

When you truly see “grace,” you won’t be proud; instead you’ll become more grateful and more humble.

sections.heading: 3. Letting Jesus Increase Is the Highest Expression of a Selfless Life
sections.html:
1. The Most Stunning Words

John the Baptist spoke one of the most stunning sentences ever spoken:

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

The Greek of this sentence is worth a close look. “Increase” is auxanō, which basically means to grow, to multiply — the word used for a plant growing or a child growing up. “Decrease” is elattoō, which means to lessen, to become smaller.

And the word “must” in the sentence is the Greek dei, meaning “it is necessary, it ought to be, this is how it should be.”

Notice that John is not sighing, “Oh dear, what a pity I have to get smaller.” He is declaring: “This is right, this is fitting, this is how things were always meant to be.”

Brothers and sisters, this sentence is selflessness at its very height.

It isn’t that I am seen; it is that Jesus is seen.

It isn’t that I am exalted; it is that Jesus is exalted.

It isn’t that people remember me; it is that people come to know Jesus.

2. The Friend of the Bridegroom: Knowing Who We Are

How could John say such a thing? Because he knew who he was.

“He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. This, my joy, therefore is made full.” (John 3:29)

In Jewish wedding custom, “the friend of the bridegroom” was a role with real duties, much like today’s best man. He ran errands for the bridegroom, prepared the wedding feast, escorted the bride, and was busy right up to the last moment. But when the bridegroom’s voice rang out and the feast began, the best man had only one thing left to do: step aside and stand there rejoicing.

The best man’s greatest joy is hearing the bridegroom’s voice.

Brothers and sisters, there’s an extremely serious warning hidden here: if the best man falls in love with the bride, the whole wedding is ruined.

The church is the bride of Christ, not ours. We are the best man, not the bridegroom. We may give everything for this wedding feast, but we must never take possession of the bride’s heart.

Scripture says: “He is the head of the body, the assembly, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might have the preeminence.” (Colossians 1:18) Preeminence in all things — that is Jesus’ right, not ours.

The Lord himself also said: “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.” (John 7:18)

3. A Thorough Check of Our Motives for Serving

The lesson honestly points out that many people serve in order to be affirmed, to be needed and to be seen.

Brothers and sisters, we have to admit that these three things have an enormous pull. Being affirmed makes us feel valuable; being needed makes us feel irreplaceable; being seen makes us feel we exist.

But the Lord Jesus spoke very sternly about that kind of service:

“Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1)

“Therefore when you do merciful deeds, don’t sound a trumpet before yourself, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may get glory from men. Most certainly I tell you, they have received their reward.” (Matthew 6:2)

“They have received their reward” — this is the most chilling final reckoning in the whole Bible. The moment the applause rings out, the account is settled, and there is nothing left on deposit in heaven.

So what is true service? The lesson puts it beautifully: true service is helping people forget you and remember only Jesus.

The Lord Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16)

The Lord didn’t tell us to hide our light. He wants us to shine — but the purpose of shining is that people give glory to the Father, not to us.

4. Illustrations from Life: The Lighting Technician and the Windowpane

I want to use two illustrations to say the same thing.

First, the stage lighting technician. When a performance ends, all the applause goes to the people on stage. The best lighting technician is the one nobody in the whole audience noticed. If the audience keeps looking at the lighting, it means the lights were done badly.

Second, the windowpane. The value of a window lies in its transparency. The cleaner the window, the less you see the window and the more you see the sunlight outside. A window that keeps drawing your attention to itself is usually dirty.

Brothers and sisters, you and I are people who pass on the fire, not people who light it.

5. The Arithmetic of the Kingdom: The Smaller, the Greater

There is something wonderful here.

John said, “I must decrease.” Did he really decrease? From an earthly point of view, yes. He was thrown into prison and finally beheaded. His disciples scattered, and his name left behind no school, no building.

But what did the Lord Jesus say of him?

“Most certainly I tell you, among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer; yet he who is least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater than he.” (Matthew 11:11)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? The man who willingly decreased was called by the Lord the greatest of all born of women.

This is the arithmetic of the Kingdom: the more you decrease, the greater you become. The further you step back, the higher you are lifted.

“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” (1 Peter 5:6)

Notice the words “in due time.” Lifting up is not our work but God’s; it runs not on our timetable but on God’s. We have only one responsibility: to humble ourselves.

6. Applying 321: Selflessness Is Not Having Nothing — It Is Entering into the Infinite

321 has a saying that gets right to the heart of this: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

Many people are frightened as soon as they hear the word “selflessness.” They think it means erasing themselves and becoming someone with no value, no personality, no presence. Not at all.

Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“It is no longer I who live” moves the limited “I” out of the way; “but Christ lives in me” lets the infinite Lord come in.

If a cup is full of its own water, it can’t hold anything else; only when it is emptied of its own water can it hold rivers of living water.

So the lesson’s 321 insight says —

The focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is being filled with Jesus.

True success is letting Jesus be glorified.

Brothers and sisters, the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances. This must become the habit of a lifetime.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: The Last Station on the Path of Serving
sections.html:
Today’s lesson is precisely the fifth station on 321’s Path of Serving — the last one.

Let’s walk the whole road once more.

Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Service begins with the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

Understanding — the Bible is my standard. Service is corrected by the truth.

Life — Jesus is my role model. Service flows from a changed life.

Service — let Jesus be King. Service means letting the King reign, not letting me be master.

God — let Jesus receive all the glory. The end point of service is that God is glorified.

Brothers and sisters, notice that 321’s Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. These two core values are two sides of one coin. If Jesus truly reigns as King, the glory will naturally go to him; if the glory goes to me, that proves it is still I who sit on the throne.

And the Goal is: establish God’s system. The biggest difference between God’s system and the Worldly system lies right here — the Worldly system runs on glorifying self; God’s system runs on glorifying God.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Once the glory goes to ourselves, this order is turned completely upside down — ministry comes first, people become tools, and God becomes a resource. That isn’t God’s system; that is the Babylonian system.

For our practice, 321 gives us two keys.

The first is the 920 practice. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” In every “2” relationship, we practise living out selflessness — the life of “0” — and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (see Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice that fruit is grown, not manufactured; it is the fruit of the Spirit, not my achievement. So not even the fruit can be used for boasting.

The second is the 235 relationships. Becoming a “2” with a selfless person means having a spiritual companion; establishing the “3” means spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming the “5” means a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Only when I no longer need to be exalted can I sincerely lift others up.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad at heart, rely on the brain and you’ll be weighed down. Where the glory goes is precisely a matter of the “heart.” The brain calculates how much I’ve given and how much I’m owed; the heart only says, Lord, you did all of this.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Living a Life That Gives All the Glory to God
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s look at them one by one, and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: After Every Time of Service, Deliberately Give the Glory to God

Whether the outcome is good or bad, after you serve, pray to God: “Lord, you did all of this; the glory is yours.”

Notice the words “whether the outcome is good or bad.” When things go well, give him the glory; when they don’t, give him the glory all the more. Because if we only think of God when we succeed, it shows that the real leading character in our hearts is still results.

Don’t let your heart linger on “how well did I do?”; turn it to “has God received the glory?”

That one turn is the turn from being centred on self to being centred on God, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one.

Practice 2: Practise Tearing Down Self-Centredness in Your Heart

When thoughts like these come up in your heart —

“I did really well.”

“They can’t manage without me.”

“I’m the one who brought the change.”

Don’t argue with yourself, and don’t try to suppress them by willpower. Replace them with the truth at once. The Lord himself said: “apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) So we declare, in line with the Lord’s word: without the Lord, I can do nothing.

Brothers and sisters, you can’t stop thoughts from coming, but you can replace them. An empty heart can’t stay empty; if you don’t fill it with truth, lies will take it over.

Returning the glory to God is a movement we must practise all our lives.

Practice 3: Deliberately Exalt Jesus, Not Yourself

When you share, testify or serve, consciously adjust the proportions: speak more about what God has done and less about what you have done.

A testimony isn’t an autobiography. After a good testimony, people say, “God is so good,” not “You’re amazing.”

What people should see is God’s works, God’s grace, God’s glory.

The Eight Stages: Driving the Truth Deep into Life

Stage one, Information: today you have heard the truth — the glory belongs to God alone. First write it down: copy today’s three passages into your notebook.

Stage two, Revelation: information isn’t yet revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on you and show you one specific scene in your life where you are clinging to glory. Ask the Lord to let you “see” within that scene.

Stage three, Conviction: not just agreeing in your head, but surrendering in your heart. Tell the Lord: Lord, I admit there really is a longing in me to be seen; I need you.

Stage four, Implementation: starting today, do the three things the lesson describes. Especially the first — however your service went today, before you sleep be sure to tell the Lord: you did all of this.

Stage five, Evaluation: each night spend three minutes asking yourself: did I grab any glory in my heart today? Over what?

Stage six, Correction: the moment you notice it, give it back. There’s no need for long self-reproach — dwelling on self-reproach is another form of self-centredness. Simply say: Lord, I’m sorry; this is yours, and I give it back to you.

Stage seven, Repetition: once isn’t enough. Our instinct is self-serving attribution, so this practice must be repeated, every single day. As 321 so rightly says, only repetition turns it into a habit of life.

Stage eight, Multiplication: find a brother or sister, share this lesson with them, remind each other, and ask each other, “Where did the glory go today?” That is the “2” relationship; that is the 920 practice. When the truth bears fruit in you, it should bear fruit in others too.

A Gentle Reminder

Glory isn’t something you can take; glory belongs to God alone.

You can take part, but you cannot take possession.

You are the vessel, not the source.

Brothers and sisters, please keep these three sentences in your heart. The value of a vessel doesn’t lie in how precious it is in itself, but in whom it holds.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Receive All the Glory
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, at the end of the road of service, what counts is not how much you did, nor how successful you were, but one thing only:

To whom does the glory go?

When all the glory goes to God, three things happen.

First, you can go on being used by the Lord. Because God “will not give my glory to another” (Isaiah 42:8), with a vessel that grabs glory, God — precisely to protect that person — dares not use them greatly.

Second, you can go the distance. Those who grab glory run fast but not far, because they keep needing applause to refuel; those who give the glory away may be a little slower, but they can keep going for a lifetime, because their strength comes from grace, and grace never runs dry.

Third, you can live in true victory. 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan fell long ago through pride, and pride is the only weapon he can use against us. A truly selfless person gives the enemy nothing to work with, because there is no handle for him to grab.

So the focus is not on ourselves, not on people, not on tasks — only on Jesus.

Let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory — this is the most glorious ending service can have.

The worship of heaven has long been singing this ending: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honor, and the power, for you created all things, and because of your desire they existed, and were created!” (Revelation 4:11)

“Worthy is the Lamb who has been killed to receive the power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing!” (Revelation 5:12b)

Brothers and sisters, what we do on earth today is simply rehearsing ahead of time what we will do on that day.

Paul says it best: “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)

Of him — he is the beginning. Through him — he is the way. To him — he is the end.

So: “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Today, let us settle this: I will be someone who gives the glory back.

keyVerses: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
“Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)
“But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I am willing to give all the glory to you.
I acknowledge that everything I have is your grace.
I declare: not I, but Christ; not my glory, but Jesus’ glory; he must increase, but I must decrease!
May my life exalt you alone!
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
practices: After every time of service, deliberately give the glory to God
Practise tearing down self-centredness in your heart
Deliberately exalt Jesus, not yourself
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
This morning you have shone on us through your word. We have seen Herod’s end and John’s beauty; we have seen how terrible pride is and how vast grace is.

Lord, please forgive us. Forgive us that in our service we so often, without even noticing, keep the glory for ourselves; forgive us for loving to be affirmed, needed and seen more than we love to see you exalted.

Holy Spirit, shine on our hearts every day, so that the moment we find we have grabbed the glory, we give it straight back. Help us, after every time of service, to make our first words: Lord, you did all of this.
Make us clean, transparent vessels, so that people see you through us, forget us, and remember only you.
Lord, you must increase, and I must decrease. May our families, our fellowship and our church see you increase because we decrease.
Be King, and receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!
discussion: Acts 12:23 says: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” Share a time when, after your service or work went well, the thought “I did it” rose up in your heart. How did you handle it then? What does today’s passage remind you of?

John 3:30 says: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” In your current relationships or service, what is the hardest area in which to let “him increase and me decrease”? Name one specific action you’re willing to practise this week, and ask the group to pray for you.

blog.title: The Last Checkpoint of Service

blocks.x: After the Meeting, What Is Your First Thought?
The last time your service went extremely well, what was the very first thought that rose up in your heart after the meeting ended?
Was it, “Thank you, Lord, you did all of this,” or was it, “Lucky I was here today”?
That thought is small — so small that no one else will ever know about it. Yet in God’s eyes, it is the last and most decisive checkpoint on the whole road of service.
1. He Fell Not in Weakness, but in His Finest Hour

The Acts of the Apostles records a chilling scene. Herod Agrippa I put on his royal clothing, sat on the throne and gave a speech, and the people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” Then Scripture writes these fearful words:
“Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died.” (Acts 12:23)

Scripture does not say Herod spoke badly, or that he governed incompetently. That day was the most glorious day of his life. What he did wrong was not a lack of ability; it was keeping the glory for himself.

The word “glory” — in Hebrew kabod — has the root meaning “heavy”, “weighty”. Glory has weight. When someone hoists onto his shoulders a weight that doesn’t belong to him, there is only one outcome: he is crushed.
Scripture said it long ago: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18)

Psychology calls this tendency the “self-serving attribution bias”. As far back as 1975, Miller and Ross showed in a review in the Psychological Bulletin that people generally attribute success to themselves and failure to circumstances. Taking the credit doesn’t need to be learned. It’s instinct.
2. The Moon Never Shines
The moon is the brightest body in the night sky, yet it gives off no light at all; its albedo is only about 12 per cent. Of all the moonlight we admire, not one particle belongs to the moon.

So when is the moon at its worst? When it blocks the sun — that is called an eclipse. It is the same for those who serve: if we keep to our place as reflectors, people see the beauty of God; if we block his light, that isn’t called shining — it’s called eclipsing.
Paul was used mightily by God, yet this is how he saw himself: “But by the grace of God I am what I am … yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)

Paul acknowledges the facts, yet disowns the credit, and finally returns everything to its source. True humility doesn’t say, “I did nothing” — that would be a lie. True humility says, “I did it, but it wasn’t I who did it.”
3. He Must Increase, but I Must Decrease

When John the Baptist’s ministry was at its height, his disciples came running with the news: “Everyone is coming to him.” John’s reply has echoed through the ages: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)
In the Greek of this sentence, “must” means “it ought to be, this is how it should be”. John is not lamenting; he is declaring: this is right, this is how things were always meant to be.

Because he knew who he was — the friend of the bridegroom, the best man. The best man runs every errand for the wedding, but the moment the bridegroom’s voice rings out, he steps aside and stands there rejoicing. The church is the bride of Christ, not ours.
And what did the Lord say of John, the man who willingly decreased? “Among those who are born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptizer.” (Matthew 11:11a)
This is the arithmetic of the Kingdom: the more you decrease, the greater you become.
Three Things You Can Practise Today
1. After every time of service, whether the outcome is good or bad, deliberately pray: “Lord, you did all of this; the glory is yours.”
2. The moment “they can’t manage without me” comes up in your heart, replace it at once with the truth: without the Lord, I can do nothing.
3. When you share and testify, speak more about what God has done and less about what you have done. After a good testimony, people say, “God is so good,” not “You’re amazing.”
Glory isn’t something you can take. You can take part, but you cannot take possession.
You are the vessel, not the source.
At the end of the road of service, what counts is not how much you did, nor how successful you were, but one thing only: to whom does the glory go?
Question for Reflection
This week, in your family, workplace or service, where is it hardest for you to say, “He must increase, but I must decrease”? Write down one concrete action that gives that glory back to God.

Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God

2. Explain the five stations one by one: Spirit (the Holy Spirit’s guidance), Understanding (the Bible as standard), Life (Jesus as role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (all the glory to him).

brief12.title: Theme Passages and Background

Herod sits on the throne in Caesarea
The people shout: the voice of a god

Key points:
1. Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, ruled over all Judea from AD 41 to 44.
2. Josephus records the same event in Book 19 of Antiquities of the Jews; the year was AD 44.

brief12.title: 1. To Whom Does the Glory Go?
notes: Slide text:
“An angel of the Lord struck him,
because he didn’t give God the glory.”
Glory originally means “weight”
Key points:
1. Read the full verse, Acts 12:23; point out that Herod’s problem was not incompetence but keeping the glory.
2. Original language: Greek doxa corresponds to Hebrew kabod, whose root meaning is “heavy”, “weighty”.
3. Key line: when someone shoulders a weight that isn’t theirs, there is only one outcome — they are crushed.
4. Isaiah 42:8: God withholds his glory from false gods not out of stinginess, but out of mercy.

brief12.title: Pride Goes Before Destruction
notes: Slide text:
Proverbs 16:18
“Pride goes before destruction,
and an arrogant spirit before a fall.”
Not failure, but pride, destroys people.
Key points:
1. Scripture interpreting Scripture: Daniel 4:30–31 — Nebuchadnezzar lost his kingdom before he had finished speaking.
2. Illustration: the moon’s albedo is about 12 per cent; it gives no light of its own; when it blocks the sun, that is an eclipse.
3. Psychology: Miller and Ross (1975, Psychological Bulletin) — the self-serving attribution bias: success to ourselves, failure to circumstances.
4. 321: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to replace God; humility is returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

brief12.title: 2. Not I, but the Grace of God
notes: Slide text:
“By the grace of God
I am what I am.”
(1 Corinthians 15:10)
I did it, but it wasn’t I who did it.
Key points:
1. Read the full passage, 1 Corinthians 15:9–10.
2. Unpack Paul’s three layers: acknowledging the facts, disowning the credit, returning everything to its source.
3. Original language: “grace” is Greek charis, a free, undeserved gift; “worked” means toil to the point of exhaustion.
4. Key line: true humility doesn’t say “I did nothing”, but “I did it, but it wasn’t I who did it”.

brief12.title: Humility Is Seeing the Truth
notes: Slide text:
My abilities were given by God

My fruit was produced by God
“What do you have that you didn’t receive?”
Key points:

2. Illustrations: a postman delivering a ten-million cheque won’t say the money is his gift; a light bulb gives light but makes no electricity.
3. John 15:5: “apart from me you can do nothing.” Not a little less — zero.
4. Psychology: Emmons and McCullough (2003, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) — those who record gratitude show higher well-being and optimism.

Key points:
1. Original language: increase auxanō (grow), decrease elattoō (become smaller), must dei (it ought to be, so it should be).
