script: Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today is the final lesson of the To Serve unit of Morning Devotion 321, and its title is “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — Walking the Victorious Path of Serving”. Our theme verse is Romans 8:6: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” Notice: not “will lead to death”, but “is death”; and not “peace one day in the future”, but “is life and peace”. Today — right here, today.

Brothers and sisters, let me first ask a question: how can a person walk in God’s way for a whole lifetime — without drifting, without drying up, without falling? We have seen people who were on fire for three years and then were gone; people who know the Bible well yet whose lives are parched; and people who served until they collapsed. If an aircraft’s heading is off by one degree, after a hundred kilometres it is about 1.7 kilometres off course. We rarely leave God overnight; we all drift away one degree at a time. The answer is five words: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. These aren’t five stages; this is a road to walk every day. And at its core is one sentence: live the self-centred life, and there is no road; live selflessly, and there is a road. Because the Lord said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

This verse comes from Romans. Around AD 56–57, Paul wrote from Corinth to the Roman church, which he had not yet met. Chapter 7 ends with a cry: “What a wretched man I am!” — the failure of our own effort. As chapter 8 opens, the day breaks: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” — the victory of life by the Holy Spirit. Brothers and sisters, that is exactly where “Spirit” stands — the starting point of the whole road. Then in chapter 12 Paul goes on: “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” — that is “Understanding”; next he speaks of presenting our bodies and serving one another — that is “Life” and “Service”; and at the very end of the book he lifts his voice: to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, be the glory — that is “God”. You see, Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God is not a slogan; it is the direction Romans itself travels.

The first station, Spirit: the Holy Spirit is my guide. In the original, the word “mind” means the habitual direction of our thoughts, like the needle of a compass. So the verse is asking: which way does your heart habitually face? The Holy Spirit’s guidance isn’t only needed for big things. Drivers all use satnav, and the value of satnav isn’t that it knows the destination, but that it recalculates your position every second and, the moment you go off course, says: “Please make a U-turn ahead.” Sadly, we often put it on mute, because we think we know the way. Brothers and sisters, take the first question with you today: at this very moment, what does the Holy Spirit want me to do?

The second station, Understanding: the Bible is my standard. “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” Being conformed is being pressed into a mould from outside; being transformed is changing form from within. And Paul speaks of the renewing of the “mind” — the renewing of our mindset. Change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes. Brothers and sisters, change doesn’t begin with gritting your teeth; it begins with a new way of thinking. But remember this: the Bible is to be our standard, not our decoration. When my thinking differs from the Bible, I am the one who is wrong. Take the second question with you today: what does the Bible say about this thought of mine?

The third station, Life: Jesus is my role model. The Lord said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” Denying of self is not self-torment; it is saying to the old self that wants to be king: you are not my master. And where does denying of self happen? In our everyday seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Hundreds of times a day, and every time a choice: for myself, or for Jesus? But please hear this clearly: Life is not imitation; it is letting Jesus live himself out. A branch doesn’t need to imitate a grape; a branch only needs to stay joined to the vine.

The fourth station, Service: let Jesus be King. Serving is not me doing the work; it is Jesus doing the work in me. I step back, and Jesus steps up. John the Baptist said it best: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Brothers and sisters, the hardest lesson in serving is often not whether we can do it, but whether we are willing to go down. When Jesus is King, serving has power, fruit and life. When I am king, serving is reduced to exhaustion, resentment and collapse. The Lord said: “Take my yoke upon you.” A yoke is carried by two oxen together. He never asked you to pull the cart on your own.

The fifth station, God: let Jesus receive all the glory. Many people reach “Service” and stop there, overlooking the most important step. Without it, we will grow proud, we will snatch the glory, and we will fall. Scripture records that Herod did not give God the glory and was struck down at once. But when a person truly sees that everything is grace and everything is God’s doing, he will naturally live in humility. The Lord Jesus humbled himself utterly and in the end received all the glory; this is our road too: humility, and then being lifted up by God.

Brothers and sisters, remember the lesson’s reminder: only Spirit, and you will drift; only Understanding, and you will dry up; only Life, and you will stall; only Service, and you will burn out; without God, you will certainly fall. So don’t stop at any station. These five stations are not five legs of a journey; they are one circle to be completed every day. Walk it today, and walk it again tomorrow; walk it tomorrow, and walk it again the day after — until the day we see the Lord face to face. Brothers and sisters, ask yourself honestly: of these five stations, which one do I most easily miss?

How do we practise it? Five “every days”. Begin every day with “Spirit”: when you open your eyes, let your first words not be “What am I going to do today?” but “Lord, what do you want me to do today?” Renew your mindset every day with “Understanding”: when you read the Bible, ask one more question — which of my thoughts does this passage want to change? Deny yourself every day in your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing: pick the area where you most easily give way, and ask the Lord for victory there. Let the Lord be King every day: be still for thirty seconds before every meeting. Give the glory to God every day: count three graces before you sleep.

Brothers and sisters, this road is not a sprint; it is a marathon. The full distance is over forty-two kilometres, and the hardest part is hitting the wall at around thirty kilometres; what keeps a runner going then is not stamina, but the goal. Scripture says: lay aside every weight, and look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith. Laying aside every weight is selflessness; looking to Jesus is keeping the focus on him. May each of us one day be able to say: “I have finished the course.”

Let’s pray together. Lord Jesus, you said that you are the way, so we no longer have to find the way ourselves. Please take away the self within us; let the Holy Spirit guide us, let your word be our standard, reign as King in our serving, and let all the glory be yours. Walk with us until the day we see your face. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.

Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today is the final lesson of the To Serve unit of Morning Devotion 321, and its title is “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — Walking the Victorious Path of Serving”. Our theme verse is Romans 8:6: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” Notice Paul’s choice of words. He doesn’t say “will lead to death”; he says “is death”. Nor does he say “peace one day in the future”; he says “is life and peace”. This isn’t about the future; it’s about today. This morning I want to walk this road through together with you, brothers and sisters, and then invite you to walk it every day, starting tomorrow.

Let me first ask a question. How can a person walk in God’s way for a whole lifetime — without drifting, without drying up, without falling? Brothers and sisters, we have all seen these three kinds of people. The first: on fire when they first came to faith, and ten years later, gone. The second: they know the Bible better than anyone, yet their life is parched, and their family can’t stand them. The third: run off their feet in ministry, carrying everything on their own shoulders, until in the end they collapse in the middle of their serving, complaining even as they work. In aviation there is a simple piece of common sense: if the heading is off by one degree, after flying a hundred kilometres you will be about 1.7 kilometres off course. At the moment of take-off, one degree is invisible; but the further you fly, the more deadly that one degree becomes.

Brothers and sisters, we rarely leave God overnight; we all drift away one degree at a time. So is there a road that lets us correct our heading every day? There is. The answer lies in five words: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. Please notice, these are not five stages, as though once you have passed through one you can leave it behind; this is a road of life that goes round and round. And at the heart of this road there is one key, and only one: selflessness. Please remember these two sentences: live the self-centred life, and there is no road; live selflessly, and there is a road. Why? Because the Lord Jesus himself said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” The road isn’t something I carve out; the road is the person of Jesus. When “self” stands in the middle, I have no road; when “self” steps back, the road opens up beneath my feet.

Our theme passage comes from Romans. Paul wrote this letter around AD 56–57 in Corinth, and it was addressed to the church in Rome, a group of believers he had not yet met. Rome was the capital of the world at that time, the centre of power, wealth and idols. Chapter 7 ends with a cry: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” That is the failure of keeping the law by my own effort. As chapter 8 opens, the day breaks: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” For the law of the Spirit of life has set us free. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly where “Spirit” stands — the starting point of the whole road.

The first station: Spirit. “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” The word “mind” here is the Greek phroneō, meaning the orientation of our thoughts, our habitual purpose — like the needle of a compass, always pointing the same way. So what this verse is really asking is: where does your heart habitually face? The starting point of life is not in what we do, but in choosing whom to follow. Brothers and sisters, this isn’t a future verdict; it is a present condition. Someone whose mind habitually faces towards themselves is already living, right now, with the smell of death about them: strained relationships, an unquiet heart, nothing seeming worthwhile.

So “Spirit” means this: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Not relying on our own cleverness, not relying on past experience, but at every moment asking: what does the Holy Spirit want me to do? The Lord Jesus said: “When he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth.” In the original, the word “guide” has the word “road” at its root. The Holy Spirit is not a consultant sitting in the passenger seat offering suggestions; he is the guide who goes ahead and leads the way. But we often make a mistake: we treat the Holy Spirit’s guidance as something needed only for big things. We pray about changing jobs, we pray about getting married; but how to say the first words to our family this morning, how to reply to that infuriating email — those we decide for ourselves. Drivers all use satnav, and the value of satnav isn’t that it knows the destination, but that it recalculates your position every second and, the moment you go off course, says: “Please make a U-turn ahead.” Scripture says: don’t quench the Spirit. Turn the sound off, and the road is still there — but we can no longer hear.

The second station: Understanding. “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” Paul uses two sharply contrasting words. In the original, “conformed” means being pressed into a mould from the outside; “transformed” is metamorphoō, changing form from within — the very word used when the Lord Jesus was transfigured on the mountain. One is pressure from outside; the other is change from within. Brothers and sisters, are you being pressed by the world into its shape, or being changed by the word of God into a new life?

Even more crucial, Paul speaks of the renewing of the “mind”, and the mind is our mindset. He doesn’t say the renewing of your behaviour; he says the renewing of your mind. This is exactly the fivefold change of 321: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Change doesn’t begin with gritting your teeth; it begins with a new way of thinking. Our mindset is the pair of glasses through which we see the world; if the lenses are skewed, everything we see is skewed. Someone convinced that “I only have worth if people notice me” sees someone else being praised and feels a pang of envy; someone convinced that “my worth has already been settled in Christ” is glad. The difference lies not in the event but in the mindset. But remember: the Bible is to be our standard, not our decoration. When my thinking differs from the Bible, I am the one who is wrong.

The third station, Life: Jesus is my role model. Once we have Spirit and Understanding, the next step is not to stop at “knowing”, but to go on into “living it out”. The Lord said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.” Notice the three things the Lord says: deny yourself, daily, take up the cross. The word “deny” is the very word used when Peter three times “denied” the Lord. So denying of self is not self-torment; denying of self is saying to the old self that wants to be king: I don’t know you; you are not my master. And the Lord didn’t say “take it up once”; he said “take it up daily”.

Where does denying of self happen? In five small things every day: seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Wherever the eyes land, the heart follows; whatever the ears feed on, the heart grows into. Scripture says: whatever things are true, honourable, pure and lovely — think about these things; let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up; whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Brothers and sisters, we perform these five actions hundreds of times a day. Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London found in 2010 that the median time for a new habit to become automatic is about sixty-six days. Feeling nothing after a few days of practice doesn’t mean you have failed; what truly changes people is small choices, day after day.

But there is a vitally important distinction here: Life is not imitation; it is letting Jesus live himself out. Imitation is me copying his ways from the outside, and that will wear you out; letting Jesus live himself out is him living out his own life from within. Paul says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” And the Lord says: “Apart from me you can do nothing.” Brothers and sisters, a branch doesn’t need to imitate a grape; a branch only needs to stay joined to the vine. This is what 321 means: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite.

The fourth station, Service: let Jesus be King. Serving is not me doing the work, but Jesus doing the work in me. To put it in one sentence: I step back, and Jesus steps up. John the Baptist is the finest role model. When his disciples came running to say, “Everyone is coming to him,” John was not anxious. He said: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” One is to rise, the other is to go down. Brothers and sisters, the hardest lesson in serving is often not whether we can do it, but whether we are willing to go down. Paul also says: we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord. Who is master and who is servant — once that gets reversed, serving immediately becomes a heavy burden.

When Jesus is King, serving has power, fruit and life, because it is “not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit”. But when I am king, serving is reduced to three things: exhaustion, resentment, collapse. In 2019 the World Health Organization listed “burn-out” as an occupational phenomenon, marked by energy depletion, mental distance from one’s job and reduced professional efficacy. Brothers and sisters, these three are no strangers to us in the serving of the church. Why do we burn out? Often it isn’t because we do too much, but because the sovereignty is in our own hands. If the sovereignty is mine, the burden crushes me. The Lord said: “Take my yoke upon you.” A yoke is carried by two oxen together. He didn’t ask you to pull the cart on your own; he said: come and share one yoke with me — I go in front, and you follow.

The fifth station, God: let Jesus receive all the glory. Many people reach “Service” and stop there, overlooking the last and most important step. Without it, the four stations before it will turn round and harm us: we will grow proud, we will snatch the glory, and we will fall. Scripture records that Herod put on his royal robes and made a speech, and the people shouted, “The voice of a god!” The text says: because he didn’t give God the glory, an angel of the Lord struck him immediately. Notice, it was not because he spoke blasphemy, but because he “didn’t give God the glory”. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, was the same: while the word was still in his mouth, judgement fell. 321 puts it exactly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, grasping power and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down power and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

But when a person truly sees that everything is grace, that everything is God’s doing, he will naturally live in humility. True humility is not forced down; true humility is how we respond once we have seen the truth. Paul asks it well: what do you have that you didn’t receive? Your mind, your health, your family, your gifts — which of these did you not receive? The Lord Jesus’ whole life is our role model: existing in the form of God, he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death; therefore God highly exalted him. He humbled himself utterly, and in the end received all the glory. This is our road too: humility, and then being lifted up by God.

Brothers and sisters, the lesson gives us a very precise reminder. Only Spirit, and you will drift — promptings, but no anchor of truth, like a ship that has never dropped anchor. Only Understanding, and you will dry up — doctrine down to a system, yet hard and cold. Only Life, and you will stall — practising every day, yet unwilling to come out and serve. Only Service, and you will burn out — one task after another, until you have worn yourself dry. Without God, you will certainly fall — the fruit appears, but if you don’t give the glory back, that very fruit becomes the stone you stumble over. So don’t stop at any station. These five stations are not five legs of a journey; they are one circle to be completed every day.

How do we practise it? The lesson gives us five “every days”. First, begin every day with “Spirit”. Ask yourself each day: today, am I following the Holy Spirit, or following myself? When you open your eyes, don’t let your first words be “What am I going to do today?” but “Lord, what do you want me to do today?” Second, use “Understanding” every day to adjust your mindset. Through the word of God, correct your thinking, renew your mindset and align yourself with the truth; don’t let old mindsets run your life. When you read the Bible, ask one more question: which of my thoughts does this passage want to change?

Third, practise denying of self every day in your seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing. Pick the area where you most easily give way — perhaps your tongue, perhaps your eyes — and ask the Lord for victory in that very area. Fourth, let Jesus be King in your serving every day. Don’t ask, “How am I going to do it?” Ask, “Lord, how do you want to do it?” Before every meeting, visit or small group, be still for thirty seconds and lay your crown at the Lord’s feet first. Fifth, give all the glory to God every day. Whether you succeed or fail, declare: it is all grace. Count three graces before you sleep. Then walk it through with the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. The first seven are about us receiving; the eighth is about others receiving.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God is simply 321. Spirit is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”; Understanding is “the Bible is my standard”; Life is “Jesus is my role model” — these are the Three Foundations. Service is “let Jesus be King”; God is “let Jesus receive all the glory” — these are the Two Core Values. And what walking this road accomplishes is the Goal: establish God’s system. The practice of this road is 920: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; as I live out the selfless “0”, the ninefold fruit of the Spirit grows. The companionship of this road is 235: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. This road is long; no one can walk it alone.

Brothers and sisters, this road is not a sprint; it is a marathon. A full marathon is 42.195 kilometres, and the hardest part is not the start but hitting the wall at around thirty kilometres — the glycogen in the body is almost exhausted, and what keeps a runner going at that moment is not stamina, but the goal. Scripture uses exactly the picture of a race for this road: lay aside every weight, run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith. Laying aside every weight is selflessness; looking to Jesus is keeping the focus on him — not on ourselves, not on our circumstances. Keep walking this road, and you will become more and more like Jesus: more and more full of life, of power, of joy and of glory. May each of us one day be able to say: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course.”

Let’s pray together. Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. You said that you are the way, so we no longer have to find the way ourselves. Forgive us for so often walking by our own cleverness. Please take away the self within us, for in the self-centred life there is no road, but in selflessness there is a road. Holy Spirit, be our guide; may your word renew our mindset day by day; help us in our seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing to choose, time after time, to deny ourselves; reign as King in our serving, and guard us so that we give all the glory to you. This road is a marathon; we do not ask to run fast, but to run to the end. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen. Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.

l172.title: Live Out Christ, Become a Victor
l172.subtitle: The Summary of 321
l172.partTitle: Unit 10 · The Necessity for Revival — To Serve
keyVerses: “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).
“He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: A Road Summed Up
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you! Today is Lesson 172 of Morning Devotion 321, the summary of the whole Morning Devotion 321 series. In the last lesson we learned together “Spirit — Understanding — Life — Service — God”: beginning with the guidance of the Holy Spirit, renewing our mindset through the truth of the Bible, following Jesus’ example to live out his life, letting Jesus be King in our serving, and finally giving all the glory to God. Today we want to gather all of the 321 vision we have learned along the way into one clear direction, summed up in a single phrase: live out Christ, become a Victor.

Over these many days we have read a great many lessons, heard a great deal of teaching, and noted down quite a few terms: the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal, the self-centred life and selflessness, 920, 235, the eight stages of changing our mindset, Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God… But brothers and sisters, learning 321 is not just about memorising some concepts, nor just about understanding some teaching. It is about letting the truth enter our lives and letting Jesus be King within us, so that in our everyday lives we become more and more like him.

There was once a medical student who knew human anatomy inside out. He could name every bone and every nerve, and yet he was not yet a doctor. Only when he put on the white coat and cared for patients at the bedside, time after time, did all that knowledge become the power to save lives. Spiritual knowledge is just the same. If 321 stays in our notebooks, it is merely an attractive framework; only when it walks into our homes, our workplaces and our churches does it become life.

So today, let us hold this road of life in our hands with three sentences: the Three Foundations direct us to follow the Lord; the Two Core Values help us honour the Lord as King; the Goal leads us to build together with one heart. And all of this has to be worked out at one key point: turning from the self-centred life to selflessness.

Let us be clear first of all: selflessness does not mean denying our own worth, nor abandoning the responsibilities we ought to fulfil. God created us in his image, and we are precious in his sight; we also have duties to fulfil in our families, our workplaces and our churches. Selflessness means no longer putting ourselves at the centre, no longer insisting on being lord and king ourselves, but willingly letting Jesus rule our lives.

Let us also be clear that being victorious does not mean there will be no more difficulties from now on, or that everything will happen just as we expect. Some people think a victorious Christian is one whose business thrives, whose health is good, whose children do well and whose relationships are harmonious — green lights all the way. No. True victory is to keep trusting the Lord in difficulty, to keep obeying the Lord in temptation, and to keep living out the Lord’s love in our relationships. Our circumstances may not yet have changed, but our lives have already begun to change; the road may still hold challenges, but in our hearts we can stand firm through the Lord.

Why is this possible? Because the foundation of our victory is not in ourselves, but in the Lord Jesus, who loved us, gave himself up for us, and has already risen victorious. This morning, let us come back together into the presence of this Lord.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Romans 8 and the Letter to Laodicea
sections.html:
Today we have two theme verses, one from Romans and one from Revelation. One stands near the beginning of the New Testament letters and the other at the very end, and together they thread the whole victorious life on a single string.

Romans was written by the apostle Paul, generally thought to have been written in Corinth around AD 56–57, to the church in Rome, which he had not yet visited. Chapter 8 is the summit of the whole letter. Chapter 7 ends with a cry: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24). That is the cry of someone who tries to keep the law by their own strength and fails again and again. Then, at the very start of chapter 8, the dawn breaks: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Paul goes on to speak of the guidance of the Holy Spirit, of our becoming children of God, of the groaning of creation and the glory to come; and then, in the second half of chapter 8, like a lawyer making his closing speech in court, he says: “What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

Next, Paul lists a long string of things that might separate us from God: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Romans 8:35). He also quotes Psalm 44: “For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Romans 8:36). Brothers and sisters, this is not empty rhetoric. Less than ten years after the letter was written, in AD 64, came the Great Fire of Rome. The Emperor Nero laid the blame on the Christians, and the believers in Rome really did go through persecution and martyrdom — something even the Roman historian Tacitus recorded in his Annals. When Paul wrote “more than conquerors”, he was not sitting in a comfortable study making fine speeches; the people who received his letter would soon have to prove those words true in the face of the sword.

It is in exactly this situation that Paul says: “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). “More than conquerors” is a single word in the original Greek, hypernikaō, made up of hyper (beyond, above) and nikaō (to conquer, to overcome). It appears only this once in the whole New Testament, and might be called Paul’s own coinage for emphasis: not a narrow win, but a victory that goes far beyond. Then he concludes in the firmest of tones: “For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39).

The second theme verse is Revelation 3:21. Revelation was written by the apostle John while he was exiled on the island of Patmos, traditionally dated around AD 95, during the reign of the Roman Emperor Domitian. Revelation 2 and 3 contain the Lord Jesus’ letters to the seven churches of Asia, and each letter ends with a promise to “him who overcomes”; this word “overcome” is nikaō. Revelation 3:21 is the last of the promises in the seven letters, and also the highest, and it was written to the church in Laodicea.

Laodicea was a very wealthy city. It was a centre of banking and finance, famous for its black wool, and it had a medical school; the surrounding area produced a well-known eye powder. Around AD 60, Laodicea was struck by a great earthquake, and Tacitus records that the city declined Roman aid and rebuilt itself from its own resources. The city had one weakness: it had no good water source of its own, and water had to be brought in by aqueduct from outside. By the time it reached the city it was usually neither cold nor hot, and full of minerals. Nearby Hierapolis had hot springs, and Colossae had cool, fresh water, but Laodicea’s water was lukewarm.

With this background, the Lord’s words to Laodicea become especially clear: “I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were cold or hot. So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3:15–16). “Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing,’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17). A city that had rebuilt itself by its own strength had a church that had also learned to rely on itself. Brothers and sisters, Laodicea’s problem was precisely the self-centred life: I am rich, I need nothing, I can manage by myself.

Yet the Lord did not give up on them. He said: “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten. Be zealous therefore, and repent” (Revelation 3:19). And again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him, and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). The Lord was standing right outside the door of the very church that thought itself rich. And then, right here, comes the highest promise: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21). From knocking outside the door, to dining together, to sitting together on the throne — this is the road of victory walked by those who turn from the self-centred life to selflessness.

sections.heading: 3. Teaching One (Part 1): Victory Begins with the Lord Loving Us First
sections.html:
“No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

Please notice the emphasis of this verse: through him who loved us. Paul does not say “through our willpower”, nor “through our spiritual disciplines”, but “through him who loved us”. The starting point of our victory is that the Lord loved us first.

It is not that we first become perfect and then the Lord accepts us; rather, while we were still weak and still sinful, the Lord laid down his life for us and opened up for us a way to life. In the same letter Paul says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Through the cross Jesus bore our sins, and through the resurrection he gives us new life. When we repent and trust in him, we no longer have to live by the strength of the old self alone; we can rely on the Lord and begin a new life. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus said to his disciples: “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Notice that the Lord says “I have overcome” — the action is already complete. We are not striving for a victory whose outcome is still undecided; we are walking into a victory the Lord has already won. John later wrote as well: “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

So, in learning 321, we must first stand firm on the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model: when something happens, we learn his humility, obedience, holiness and kindness. Paul says: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). When we don’t know how to respond, we ask ourselves one question: if it were Jesus, how would he see this? What would he say? What would he do?

The Bible is my standard: we do not let the trends of the world or our own preferences become the highest standard of right and wrong, but let God’s word correct us. Trends change direction every few years, and our preferences change every day; only God’s word is an unchanging measure. We do not measure the Bible with our own ruler; we let the Bible measure us.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: in prayer we seek the Lord, keep an obedient heart, and follow guidance that is consistent with the truth of the Bible. This point is very important: the guidance of the Holy Spirit will never contradict the Bible. If some “prompting” tells you to do something contrary to the Bible, that is not the Holy Spirit; that is the self.

These Three Foundations help us turn from “what I think” to “what the Lord says”, and from “what I want” to “what pleases the Lord”. At the end of the Sermon on the Mount, the Lord Jesus said that whoever hears his words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock: the rain came down, the floods came, the winds blew, and the house did not fall (Matthew 7:24–25). Brothers and sisters, victory doesn’t suddenly happen on the day the storm arrives; victory is already decided on the ordinary days when we are building the house.

sections.heading: 4. Teaching One (Part 2): The Two Core Values — Returning in Humility to Our Originally Intended Position
sections.html:
Having stood firm on the Three Foundations, we must hold fast to the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Why do we emphasise “let Jesus be King”? Because our problem is often not just that something has been done wrongly, but that the “I” within us wants to be in control. I want others to listen to me, I want things to go my way, I want to prove I am right. And when my own will is blocked, pride, anger and complaining come out all too easily.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that many quarrels are not really about the matter itself, but about “who gets the final say”? A small thing — how the dishes should be washed, how the car should be parked, how a meeting should be run — is no big deal in itself, but as soon as it touches that nerve of “I want to be in charge”, the temper flares. The church in Laodicea said, “I am rich… and have need of nothing”; that is exactly the heart that says, “I can be in charge myself.”

So the practice of victory begins with letting go of self: letting go of our insistence on being in charge, returning to our originally intended position as created beings, and handing over the lordship of our lives to Jesus.

This is what 321 so often calls “returning in humility to our originally intended position”. Humility means letting humans be human and letting God be God. Humanity’s greatest dislocation is wanting to sit in God’s seat; from the Garden of Eden onward, the serpent’s temptation was “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5). Humility is not looking down on ourselves; it is returning to our proper place: I am the creature, he is the Creator; I am the branch, he is the vine.

The Lord Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch bears fruit not because it tries especially hard, but because it is joined to the vine and continually receives the supply of life. Anyone who has grown grapes or walked through an orchard knows that a cut branch, however thick and green it once was, will wither within a few days once it is separated from the trunk. We too must draw near to the Lord and rely on him every day, letting his life work within us.

The second core value is to let Jesus receive all the glory. When the lordship goes to Jesus, the glory must go to Jesus as well. Revelation 4 describes the worship of heaven, where the twenty-four elders “throw their crowns before the throne” (Revelation 4:10), saying, “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, the Holy One, to receive the glory, the honour, and the power” (Revelation 4:11). Even those who have been given crowns lay them down. This gives us a beautiful picture: a Victor is not someone who clutches the crown tightly, but someone who offers the crown to the Lord.

So here is A 321 Insight for this section: victory begins with trusting the Lord; change begins with letting go of self. The Three Foundations give our life roots; the Two Core Values give our life a Lord. The lordship belongs to Jesus, and the glory belongs to Jesus too. Brothers and sisters, with roots we need not fear the wind; with a Lord we will not lose our way.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Two (Part 1): From Knowing the Truth to Living Out Christ
sections.html:
“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Once the foundation is firm, the next step is to live out what we believe. Paul says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Please notice the last phrase of this verse: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” We are able to deny ourselves because he first gave himself up for us. This flows from the same source as “through him who loved us” in Romans 8:37.

Living out Christ is not just about being devout at meetings; it is about letting people see the character of Jesus in our everyday lives. At home, a little more understanding; in conflict, a little more gentleness; when wronged, still holding on to honesty; in serving, a willingness to build one another up. Brothers and sisters, how beautifully a person prays from the platform is not the true measure of their spiritual stature; how they speak to their spouse, their children and their elderly parents when they get home — that is.

A change of life often begins with a renewal of mindset. This is what 321 stresses again and again: change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes. Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). The word “transformed” in the original is metamorphoō, the kind of complete change by which a caterpillar becomes a butterfly; and its starting point is “the renewing of your mind”.

321 teaches us four shifts of mindset: from the human point of view to God’s point of view; from the earthly to the heavenly; from temporary gain and loss to eternal value; from the worldly to the godly. When our mindset turns round, we can respond differently to the very same situation.

Here is an example. In the past we might have thought: “He has upset me, so I’ll show him what I’m made of.” Now we are willing to learn to say: “Lord, please help me live out your life in this situation.” It is the same situation and the same person, but the starting point within us is completely different. This is turning from the self-centred life to selflessness, from the reactions of the old self to the life of the new self.

So how exactly do we practise this? 321 gives us five words: See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do. These are the five channels through which we touch the world every day, and also the five battlefields on which we practise denying self every day.

See: not rushing to find fault, but learning to see people’s needs. Our eyes easily spot other people’s faults, yet fail to see the burdens they carry. Listen: not rushing to contradict, but learning to understand the other person patiently. James says: “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Think: not only calculating for ourselves, but learning to consider the Lord’s heart. Speak: not wounding carelessly, but learning to speak words that build others up. “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). Do: not only seeking our own convenience, but learning to take action in love.

Each of these five words is a small crossroads: is this for myself, or for the Lord and for others? The Lord Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). Notice the word “daily”. Denying self is not one big, once-for-all decision, but small choices made again and again, every day, in our seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing.

sections.heading: 6. Teaching Two (Part 2): The Victory of 920 and Turning Back after Failure
sections.html:
This is also the life practice of 920. The “9” is the ninefold fruit of the Spirit, the “2” is everyone I relate to, and the “0” is the selfless “0”. Before everyone we relate to, we lay down our self-centred insistence and, by the Holy Spirit, bear the fruit of “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Notice that Scripture speaks of “the fruit of the Spirit”: the fruit is not something we squeeze out through gritted teeth, but something the Holy Spirit produces in us when we move the “self” out of the way.

Let me describe a scene that could happen in any family. A family member says something hurtful, and anger instantly rises inside. At that moment we can first stop, and pray in our hearts: “Lord, please rule my heart, and rule my mouth too.” Then we choose to listen well, speak gently and communicate honestly.

The psychologist John Gottman, who has studied marriage for many years and spent a long time observing how couples interact, made a well-known observation: in stable couples, the ratio of positive to negative interactions during conflict is about five to one. Brothers and sisters, this does not mean there can never be a negative word, but that relationships need a great deal of goodwill to carry them. One word of rebuke needs to be balanced by plenty of encouragement, understanding and gentleness. This is consistent with what the Bible teaches.

So overcoming anger is victory; being willing to apologise is victory; letting go of revenge is victory; holding fast to truth while holding fast to love is victory. Paul says: “‘Be angry, and don’t sin.’ Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath” (Ephesians 4:26). So victory does not necessarily happen on a platform or a battlefield; far more often it happens beside the dinner table, in the living room, or in front of the reply box of a messaging app.

Speaking of letting go of revenge, I am reminded of the testimony of Corrie ten Boom. Because her family hid Jews during the Second World War, they were sent to concentration camps, and her sister Betsie died in Ravensbrück. After the war she travelled everywhere preaching forgiveness. Once, at the end of a meeting in Munich, a man who had been a guard at the camp came up to her, held out his hand, told her he had become a believer, and asked for her forgiveness. She later wrote that at that moment she could not raise her hand; all she could do was pray in her heart and ask the Lord to help her. When she obeyed and held out her hand, she experienced a love that came from the Lord. Brothers and sisters, this is the victory “through him who loved us” — not that her love was big enough, but that the Lord’s love flowed through her.

But we must also be clear: denying self is not giving way without limits. Denying self also includes facing problems honestly, setting appropriate boundaries according to the truth, taking responsibility and seeking help. Paul says: “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). We learn Jesus’ gentleness, and we also learn his faithfulness to the truth. Jesus cleansed the temple, and he also prayed on the cross for those who crucified him; in him, gentleness and truth are one. When we face harm or violence, seeking protection and professional help according to the truth is also part of love.

On this road we may still fail. But after failing we can come straight back to the Lord, confess, repent, receive forgiveness and correct our steps. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). Proverbs also says: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). The righteous are not those who never fall, but those who get up again after they fall.

This is exactly the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Hearing the truth is Information; the Holy Spirit driving it home to our hearts is Revelation; being willing to say, “Lord, I yield” is Conviction; doing it in daily life is Implementation; looking back in the evening is Evaluation; adjusting how we do things is Correction; doing it day after day is Repetition; and finally bringing others along with us is Multiplication. Through these eight stages, the truth we have received gradually becomes our way of life, and also a living testimony that can walk alongside others.

A 321 Insight for this section: truth enters our mindset, our mindset shapes our choices, and our choices form our way of life. Denying self is a daily practice; selflessness is letting Christ reign. Victory begins in daily life; change begins with me. Brothers and sisters, not with my spouse, not with my co-workers — with me.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Three: Building Together — From Personal Victory to God’s System
sections.html:
“He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).

This is the Lord Jesus’ promise to the Victors. He calls us to follow him faithfully, and he sets an eternal hope before us: one day to sit with him on his throne and share in the glory of his victory. Notice that this promise was given to Laodicea — the lukewarm church that thought itself rich. The Lord did not save his highest promise for the best church, but gave it to the church that most needed to repent. This tells us that as long as we are willing to open the door and willing to repent, no one is too far from victory.

Notice too that the Lord says “as I also overcame”. How did Jesus overcome? He, “existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7); he humbled himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross. Jesus’ victory was the victory of selflessness. If one day we are to sit with him on his throne, then today we must learn to walk the road he walked.

This promise encourages us to learn today to let him be King: to honour the Lord as great in our choices, to learn to love in our relationships, to be faithful and responsible in our serving, and to keep the faith in difficulty.

And the Goal of 321 is to establish God’s system. God’s system does not begin with organisation charts, buildings or programme schedules, but with a group of people who let Jesus be King. When we are willing to obey the same Lord, to take the Bible as our standard and to work together by the Holy Spirit, we can gradually establish an order of life, relationships and service that accords with God’s heart. This is what the Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

So we must remember: life first, then relationships, then ministry. First cultivate life in the Lord, then build relationships with the love of Christ, and then together shoulder the work the Lord has entrusted to us. Many teams fall apart not because there is too little ministry, but because the order has been turned upside down: first the work, then the relationships, and finally the discovery that life cannot keep up. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. When pushing things forward, cherish people; when dealing with problems, have regard for relationships.

On this foundation we go on to develop the relationships of 235. The “2” is building relationships with spiritual companions who support one another. Ecclesiastes says: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecclesiastes 4:9). The “3” is building relationships of spiritual parents and children, who walk alongside one another in growth. Paul says to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). In a single verse there are four generations. The “5” is building a fivefold ministry team that builds together with one heart: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12).

We also want to keep living out the previous lesson’s “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God” in our serving every day. Spirit: seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Understanding: grasp and obey the truth. Life: cultivate and live out the life of Christ. Service: let Jesus be King, and serve in reliance on him. God: give thanks in everything, and give the glory to God. In this way we not only learn to be victorious ourselves, but can also walk alongside others as they become Victors.

Let us go back to Romans 8. The “all these things” Paul speaks of include oppression, anguish, persecution and peril. Being more than conquerors means that even when we go through these hardships, we can still stand firm through the Lord, and no created thing can separate us from God’s love in Christ. In the second century, Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna, was dragged into the arena in his old age. The proconsul told him that if he would curse Christ he would be set free. According to the Martyrdom of Polycarp, he replied that he had served Christ for eighty-six years and the Lord had never done him any wrong; how could he blaspheme the King who had saved him? This is a Victor who was faithful to the end. The Lord had said to the church in Smyrna: “Be faithful to death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10).

Today we are faithful in love; one day we will meet the Lord with hope. Today we let Jesus be King, today we walk alongside others as they live out Christ, and one day we will sit with the Lord on his throne. A 321 Insight for this section: life brings forth relationships, and relationships carry ministry. Follow the Lord yourself, and walk alongside others as they follow him too. Establish God’s system, so that the Lord’s will is done on earth.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder: Becoming a Victor Is a Lifelong Journey
sections.html:
The lesson gives us a very important reminder: in learning 321, we must let what we have learned keep flowing into our lives. The Three Foundations must become what we follow every day; the Two Core Values must become the choice of our hearts; the Goal must become the direction in which we build together. Every day we practise 920 in our relationships, develop 235 in community, and keep walking the road of “Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God” in our serving.

Brothers and sisters, becoming a Victor is a lifelong journey of relying on the Lord and following the Lord. It is not a graduation ceremony that is over once you have your certificate; it is more like a branch on the vine, which must stay joined to the vine through all four seasons. When we are weak, we can come to the Lord; when we fail, we can repent and stand up again. The Lord’s grace helps us keep going forward.

Please keep these three sentences in your heart: the foundation of victory is in Christ; the strength for victory comes from the Lord; the glory of victory goes to God. The foundation is not in me, so I need be neither proud nor despairing; the strength comes from the Lord, so I need not grit my teeth and struggle on alone; the glory goes to God, so I need not grab the credit. Walked this way, the road of victory is light to travel, and it can be travelled for a lifetime.

sections.heading: 9. Integrating the 321 Vision: From the Three Foundations to Sharing the Throne
sections.html:
Since today is the summary, let us look at the whole picture of 321 once more, from beginning to end.

321 means the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. The Goal: establish God’s system. These are not three sets of slogans to memorise, but a road of following the Lord: with roots, with a Lord, with a direction.

The key to this road is turning from the self-centred life to selflessness. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life puts self at the centre; selflessness lets Jesus return to the centre. And the entrance to selflessness is returning in humility to our originally intended position: letting humans be human and letting God be God.

The focus of this road is Jesus — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:2). When the focus is on ourselves, we easily become proud or feel inferior; when the focus is on others, we easily compare or judge; when the focus is on circumstances, we easily worry or complain; when the focus is Jesus, our hearts find rest.

The method of this road is to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit. Relying on the heart is our part: earnestness and faithfulness. Relying on the Holy Spirit is acknowledging that apart from the Lord we can do nothing. “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

The process of this road is the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Change your mindset and your life changes; change your life and your living changes; and when your living changes, your relationships and ministry change too.

The battlefield of this road is See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do; the practice of this road is 920; the companionship of this road is 235; the order of this road is life first, then relationships, then ministry; the steps of this road are Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God.

And the destination of this road is the hope of sitting with the Lord on his throne. Paul says: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us” (Romans 8:18). Brothers and sisters, from beginning to end, 321 has never been about making us a more impressive version of ourselves, but about making us people who are more like Jesus. For those whom God foreknew, “he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). That is the goal of Romans 8, and it is also the goal of 321.

sections.heading: 10. Putting It into Practice: Living Out Christ and Becoming a Victor Every Day
sections.html:
The lesson gives us five daily practices. Let us place them within the eight stages of changing our mindset, so that the information we hear today can, step by step, become our way of life, and finally become a life that can be passed on.

First, stand firm on the Three Foundations every day. Set aside time every day to draw near to the Lord, read the Bible, pray and reflect on Jesus’ example. When something happens, learn to stop: look at Jesus’ example, judge by the Bible, and seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Let God’s word set the direction for that day’s living. This is “Information” and “Revelation”: letting God’s word come in every day, and asking the Holy Spirit to make it alive in our hearts.

Second, hold fast to the Two Core Values every day. Bring the things you care about most, the things you most want to control, before the Lord. You can pray like this: “Lord Jesus, I hand this matter over to you. I am willing to obey you, and willing to faithfully fulfil my own responsibilities.” When things go well, thank the Lord for his grace; when you meet setbacks, humbly seek him, evaluate and correct. The lordship to Jesus, the glory to Jesus. This is “Conviction”: not just feeling that it makes sense, but actually handing over the lordship.

Third, practise 920 once every day. Choose one person you relate to, and practise denying self in a real interaction: one less word of rebuke, one more word of encouragement; a little less impatience, a little more patience; a little less keeping score, a little more understanding. Let the fruit of the Spirit appear in concrete words and actions. This is “Implementation”: the truth has to land on a specific person and a specific sentence.

Fourth, live every day in the order of life, relationships, ministry. When you are busy, still draw near to the Lord; when you are pushing things forward, still have regard for people. Take the initiative to care for a family member, support a companion, or walk alongside someone in need. Also let yourself be supported by spiritual companions and a team, learning to remind one another, pray for one another and build one another up. Rooted in life, with loving relationships and united service. This is “Repetition” and “Multiplication”: walking together in community, and bringing others onto this road.

Fifth, follow faithfully every day with eternal hope. In the evening, look back over the day and give thanks for the Lord’s grace. Where you have failed, confess it to the Lord; where you have wronged someone, try to make amends; where you have received something, keep putting it into practice. Don’t give up following because of one failure, and don’t stop relying on him because things are going well for a while. This is “Evaluation” and “Correction”. Remember the Lord’s promise and go forward with hope: through him who loved us, we can still stand today; through him who loved us, we will keep following tomorrow.

sections.heading: 11. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, the summary of 321 is this: it brings us back before Jesus, to learn day by day to live out his life. Begin with the Three Foundations, and let your life take root; hold fast to the Two Core Values, and let Jesus be King; head towards the Goal, loving one another and building together with one heart. In everyday life, practise denying self; in every relationship, live out Christ; in every act of service, give the glory to God.

As we keep following the Lord like this, victory will become more and more concrete: those who were quick to anger begin to learn gentleness; those who held on tightly begin to be willing to entrust things to him; those who cared only for themselves begin to reach out to others; those who used to shrink back from difficulty begin to stand firm through the Lord. This is the life of Christ growing within us.

At the end of his life Paul said: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7). He did not say, “I have never fallen”; he said, “I have finished the course.” May each one of us run like this to the very end. “Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

What we have learned in Morning Devotion must keep becoming our daily steps; the truth we have received today must keep becoming tomorrow’s living. Today the Lord is still standing at the door and knocking. Perhaps in this season you have been like Laodicea, lukewarm, holding yourself up by your own strength; perhaps in some relationship you have still not let Jesus be King. Today, open the door to the Lord.

Let us fix our eyes on Jesus all our lives and, through him who loved us, walk the road of victory: live out Christ and become Victors; walk the road of victory together with our families; be faithful to the end, and wait for the day we sit with the Lord on his throne.

May all the glory go to our Lord Jesus Christ, who loves us and saves us!

practices: Stand firm on the Three Foundations every day.
Hold fast to the Two Core Values every day.
Practise 920 once every day.
Live every day in the order of life, relationships, ministry.
Follow faithfully every day with eternal hope.
declarations: Let us declare together:
Lord Jesus, thank you for loving me, for laying down your life for my sins, and for rising from the dead to give me new life.
Today I am willing to hand over the lordship of my life to you.
I declare: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide!
I will let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory, and establish God’s system together with my brothers and sisters!
Renew my mindset and change my life, so that in my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing I learn to deny myself, and your life is lived out through me.
I will practise love in my relationships, learn faithfulness in my serving, and keep the faith in difficulty.
Even when trouble comes, I will still rely on you; even when I am weak for a time, I will still return to you.
For in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us!
Lead me to follow you faithfully all my life, and to walk alongside many more as they live out Christ and become Victors, until the day I see your face.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you. While we were still weak and still sinners, you loved us first, laid down your life for us, and rose again from the dead. The foundation of our victory is not in ourselves, but in you.

Lord, we confess that so often we are like the church in Laodicea, thinking ourselves rich and in need of nothing, holding ourselves up by our own strength, neither cold nor hot. Forgive the “self” within us; forgive the heart that wants to be in charge and wants to grab the glory. Today we are willing to open the door to you; please come in and be King.

Help us stand firm on the Three Foundations: taking Jesus as our role model, the Bible as our standard and the Holy Spirit as our guide; and help us hold fast to the Two Core Values: letting you be King and letting you receive all the glory. In our seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, lead us day by day to deny ourselves, and let the fruit of the Spirit grow in our relationships with our families and companions.

Lord, make us not only follow you ourselves, but also walk alongside others as they follow you; life first, then relationships, then ministry, establishing God’s system together with our brothers and sisters with one heart. When we fall, lift us up; when things go well, keep us still relying on you, until the day we see your face and sit with you on your throne.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen!

May the Lord’s blessing come upon every brother and sister: “Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26).
discussion: Looking back over the whole journey of Morning Devotion 321, which of the Three Foundations (Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide) and the Two Core Values (let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory) has brought the most concrete change to your life? And what is one thing you are still holding on to tightly, which you have not yet truly handed over for the Lord to be King over? Scripture: “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

The Lord said, “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne” — and this promise was given to the lukewarm church in Laodicea. In your family, workplace or service at the moment, in which relationship do you most need to practise 920? Who is your “2”? Over the next month, which brother or sister are you willing to walk alongside on the road of victory? Scripture: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).

blog.title: Victory Is Not Green Lights All the Way

blocks.x: For many people, a “victorious life” means a thriving business, good health, children who do well, harmonious relationships — green lights all the way. If that is true, then Paul was probably a great failure: he was flogged, imprisoned and shipwrecked, and in the end he was martyred in Rome.

And yet it was this very man who wrote the most ringing declaration of victory in the whole New Testament: “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).
“More Than Conquerors”, Written in the Face of the Sword

In the original Greek, “more than conquerors” is just one word: hypernikaō. Nikaō means to conquer or overcome; add hyper in front, and it means “beyond, far above”. This word appears only once in the whole New Testament.

The “all these things” Paul speaks of are the ones he has just listed two verses earlier: oppression, anguish, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril and sword. Less than ten years after the letter was written, Rome burned, Nero blamed the Christians, and the believers in Rome who had received this letter walked straight into those very things.

So being more than conquerors does not mean having no difficulties. It means still trusting the Lord in difficulty, still obeying the Lord in temptation, and still living out the Lord’s love in our relationships. Our circumstances may not yet have changed, but our lives have already begun to change.

And the key lies in the words at the end of the verse: “through him who loved us”. It is not that we first become perfect and then the Lord accepts us; the Lord loved us first, and that is why we have the strength to stand.
Laodicea: A City That Said “I Can Manage by Myself”

In Revelation 3, the Lord Jesus writes to the church in Laodicea. Laodicea was a wealthy city, a financial centre, famous for its black wool, and home to a medical school. The historian Tacitus records that after a great earthquake around AD 60, the city declined Roman aid and rebuilt itself from its own resources.

This “I can manage by myself” spirit quietly crept into the church too. The Lord said: “Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing,’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked.”

Yet the Lord did not give up on this lukewarm church. He stood at the door and knocked, and he gave them the highest promise in all seven letters: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).
How did Jesus overcome? He emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death. So the road of victory turns out to be the road of selflessness.
Victory Often Happens at the Dinner Table

A family member says something hurtful, and anger instantly rises. At that moment, stop for a second and say in your heart: “Lord, please rule my heart, and rule my mouth too.” Then listen well, speak gently and communicate honestly.
Overcoming anger is victory; being willing to apologise is victory; letting go of revenge is victory; holding fast to truth while holding fast to love is victory.

Denying self doesn’t mean giving way without limits, either. It includes facing problems honestly, setting appropriate boundaries, taking responsibility and seeking help. In Jesus, gentleness and truth are one.

What if you fail? Come straight back to the Lord, confess, repent, receive forgiveness and correct your steps. “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.” Victors are not people who never fall, but people who, after falling, are willing to get up again through the Lord.

The foundation of victory is in Christ; the strength for victory comes from the Lord; the glory of victory goes to God. Today let Jesus be King, today walk alongside others as they live out Christ, and one day we will sit with the Lord on his throne.
Question for Reflection
Where in your life are you most like Laodicea — where do you keep saying, “I can manage by myself”? Today, in which relationship are you willing to open the door to the Lord and let him be King?
